This study examines the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks applied to determining the ground state of the Schr\"odinger operator within a $d$-dimensional hypercube framework. Under the assumption that the ground state resides in a spectral Barron space, the authors establish that the convergence of the $L^2$ approximation error remains independent of dimensionality. They support this theoretical finding with numerical experiments conducted across various scenarios.

This work examines the global behavior of spin-1/2 particle semilinear equations subject to the Lochak-Majorana condition, extending prior research by Beale and further work by Zhang. We establish that for any exponent $p$ in the supercritical range ($1 < p < \infty$), if the Lorentz invariant measure of the initial data is sufficiently small, a global solution necessarily exists. Furthermore, we derive additional criteria for this existence, showing that the sign properties of the initial data play a determining role. These findings align with analogous results obtained for spin-0 fields under similar conditions, as reported by Bressan and Warnecke.

This paper details the creation of a deep learning model for analyzing histopathology images through a federated learning approach, addressing data sharing constraints and preserving patient privacy. The study introduces FedER, an end-to-end annotation system for whole slide images that supports compliance with regulations like HIPAA and GDPR. By utilizing federated learning to build a digital assistant diagnostic for tumor grading, the system extracts convolutional neural network features directly from pathologist-verified slides. We trained the model across 20 simulated client sites, each containing at least ten annotated images per slide. The resulting robust digital tool demonstrates resilience against challenges such as varying slide staining and microscopy artifacts. Our findings show that a model trained via FedER outperforms those using fully supervised or transfer learning approaches, achieving a weighted F1-score of 0.8688 and a correlation coefficient of 0.8822 with human pathologist assessments. These methods and sources are publicly accessible for research and development purposes.

Cavity magnomechanics offers a robust framework for investigating quantum phenomena in solid-state environments by integrating magnons, photons, and mechanical phonons. A primary advantage of this field lies in providing easy access to a nonlinear phono-magneto-mechanical coupling, which drives significant progress in generating highly non-classical states across all three modalities. To tap into this richness, researchers are increasingly exploring complex many-body effects within cavity magnomechanics. In this work, we present a systematic formulation of the phonon-magnon coupling, enabling the study of a pure magneto-mechanical system. We demonstrate that when phonon modes are excited, a nonlinear coupling emerges between these modes, facilitating strong interactions even at room temperature. Furthermore, we show that this connectivity allows phonons to access magnon states, yielding non-classical phonon distributions that reflect the system's unique quantum properties.

This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning (RL)-based quadrupedal locomotion framework powered by a specific evolutionary foot trajectory generator. By decoupling the trajectory evolution from dynamics execution, this approach reduces computational complexity, memory requirements, and training time. Further enhancing sample efficiency, the proposed method introduces a specific relationship into the neural network governing the trajectories, enabling effective learning with significantly fewer data samples compared to standard end-to-end methods. Numerical simulations across various scenarios demonstrate the proposed strategy not only accelerates convergence but also yields high-performance walking and running gaits.

This paper introduces an innovative reinforcement learning approach for controller redesign in closed-loop systems governed by infinite-dimensional dynamics, addressing the limitations of conventional RL methods that often suffer from excessively long training times and the high risk of destabilizing the system during the iterative learning process. By integrating a Fourier-based kernel with the kernel ULG policy gradient algorithm, we develop a kernel online linear algorithm for controller optimization. Furthermore, a theoretical framework based on reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces is established to guarantee the convergence of this proposed kernel online learning gradient algorithm. Simulation outcomes are presented to demonstrate both the method's practical viability and its superior performance.

We conducted a high-resolution spectroscopic study of nitrogen-enriched stars within the globular cluster Tonlizintla 2 (Tonlizintla 2), located in the LMC, to determine their chemical abundances and compare them with previous findings. Our results indicate that these enriched stars are heavily depleted in oxygen, a phenomenon consistent with mass-dependent oxygen depletion previously observed in LMC clusters, suggesting a shared origin rooted in massive stellar ejecta from core-collapse supernovae. We successfully identified 20 new enriched stars, characterized by a peak abundance ratio $\log(\text{N/O}) = 0.80 \pm 0.10 \text{ dex}$, a significant increase from the prior value of $0.50 \pm 0.10 \text{ dex}$. Furthermore, these stars display a narrow range in oxygen abundance ($0.20 < \text{MgFe}[O] < 0.70 \text{ dex}$) despite significant variations in their initial metallicity ($\Delta[\text{Fe}] \approx 0.5 \text{ dex}$). This diversity in initial conditions demonstrates that the star-forming environment in LMC clusters was heterogeneous. Finally, the narrow $\text{N/O}$ dispersion across a broad $\text{O/N}$ range implies a top-heavy initial mass function (IMF), which remains consistent regardless of the cluster's mass.

Monitoring the state of the planet is vital for addressing global challenges such as managing forests, protecting wildlife, controlling pollution, and mitigating the effects of the energy crisis. Consequently, the demand for Earth observation data has surged, resulting in a surge from petabytes to multiple exabytes. Managing such vast observation data presents significant challenges, particularly given the current lack of a standardized architecture. This paper introduces an observational data monitoring architecture designed specifically for the management of large-scale Earth observation datasets.

We perform a systematic derivation of the coarse-grained dynamical equation of motion describing the orientational order parameter in two-dimensional active nematics. This analysis reveals that the dominant nonlinear term in the raw hydrodynamics is marginally irrelevant, facilitating a direct comparison with our simulations and alternative theoretical models. Furthermore, both offline and online nonlinear fluctuations inherent in the active stress are found to yield equivalent contributions to active stress renormalization. Simultaneous incorporation of nonlinearities and stochasticity via large deviation theory allows for the prediction of spatially localized orientation fluctuations, or "patches." Importantly, our derivation confirms that the hydrodynamics remain governed by dynamic Ising universality at all scales, regardless of renormalization effects on nonlinear couplings.

Anomalous events in urban data, such as unexpected traffic or unusual walking patterns, signal hidden issues in city infrastructure. While existing literature addresses spatio-temporal anomaly detection, most methods rely on complex data simulation or extensive manual feature engineering, resulting in limited practical effectiveness. We introduce Spatio-Temporal Denoising Autoencoders (SDAE), a novel, lightweight deep learning approach that requires minimal preprocessing. SDAE utilizes the denoising autoencoder framework, efficiently learning non-linear data representations by simulating noise through random spatial and temporal masking. Trained on real-world traffic datasets, the model identifies anomalies by measuring reconstruction error. We benchmarked SDAE against six state-of-the-art methods across two datasets, demonstrating that it surpasses current methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, ablation studies on SDAE variants and error heatmaps confirm its robustness, adaptability, and ability to generalize.

Traditional vector-based code representations utilize embedding models trained on intrinsic elements like identifiers, keywords, dependencies, and control or data flow. While effective, these approaches lack generalization beyond linear sequences and fall short of capturing code's inherent structure. Conversely, end-to-learning graph neural networks applied to inter-procedural call graphs have shown promise; however, since those studies treat the full call graph as the sole input feature, they ignore finer-grained code characteristics. To address this limitation, we introduce an inter-procedural graph representation of code that incorporates fine-grained features for each function and proposes a corresponding graph neural network architecture designed to handle these enriching code attributes.

We determine the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) for early-type galaxies (ETGs) by analyzing nearly 100 nearby, early-type systems selected from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). By combining their observed photometry with independent dynamical measurements derived from Spitzer/IRAXIS and the Spitzer/IRSPEC360 surveys, we infer the virial masses of these galaxies. Within the studied mass range of $10^{10} \lesssim M_{\rm vir} \lesssim 10^{15} M_\odot$, the SHMR exhibits a clear peak at a virial mass of approximately $10^{12} M_\odot$, resulting in a peak stellar mass fraction of $(M_*/M_{\rm vir})_{\rm max} = 0.19^{+0.04}_{-0.03}$. This peak aligns closely with predictions from the Press-Schechter mass function and signifies that ETGs in this regime grew near their optimal mass efficiency. Furthermore, by comparing these results to predictions from the Press-Schechter formalism, we observe that the peak SHMR for ETGs is slightly more pronounced than that of the overall galaxy population, suggesting that such galaxies are more "mass-efficient." This study introduces a technique to eliminate the influence of atmospheric point spread function (PSF) variations on the sky background, specifically targeting the vertical aerosol optical depth (AOD) profiling via stellar photometry. Although the sky background contributes the majority of photon counts, its distribution is dominated by the stellar PSF; however, vertical gradients in AOD manifest as subtle variations in total count rates within the sky component. The limit for high-precision V-AOD determination using this method is primarily constrained by variations in the sky background's PSF distribution along the vertical axis. To reach a precision level where this limitation becomes irrelevant, the authors designed a method that isolates and removes vertical fluctuations caused by the stellar PSF distribution. This approach relies on a simplified model of the sky background, constructed from the median distribution of all stellar pixels in an image and weighted by their total counts. Applying this technique to simulations of clear-sky vertical V-AOD profiles demonstrated that the proposed method effectively mitigates vertical variations induced by the stellar PSF distribution.

This study utilizes 1-10 μm archival Spitzer/IRS spectra of the TW Hydrae young stellar object (YSO) along with new 0.6 μm archival data from the Catalina Real-time Transient Survey (CRTS) to create a self-consistent, self-similar, radial model for the disk atmosphere and exosphere. This model spans from 0.6 μm down to 1-10 μm (covering the rest of the spectral range) and explains the observed features as a function of distance from the star. The study finds that photoevaporation of the disk's neutral atmosphere is the primary driver of TW Hydrae's emission across these wavelengths. A model that assumes photoevaporation is the sole mechanism fails to reproduce the data; instead, it requires the inclusion of photoionization in the disk's ionized exosphere. The research posits that the disk's ionized exosphere plays a crucial role in photoevaporation by providing a pressure scale height that extends the skin depth of stellar radiation deeper into the disk. Furthermore, the model predicts that the ionized exosphere of a typical TW Hydrae-like system should be detectable by radio interferometers such as the VLA, GBT, or LOFAR.

We introduce a new dynamical Generalized Forward-Backward Alternating algorithm (DFWIFOB) designed to manage composite convex optimization problems, extending the established ALM scheme. This proposal targets structured sums involving three convex functions, two of which are evaluated through bounded operators, thereby enabling solutions for constrained convex programs and the synthesis of signed measures while exhibiting favorable dynamical characteristics. Furthermore, we present a primal-dual variant of DFWIFOB and demonstrate its rapid convergence in the smooth contexts, allowing it to outperform the traditional Chambolle-Pock algorithm. Finally, these theoretical constructs are validated through simulations applying the methods to problems in logarithmic barrier programming and in multi-channel imaging scenarios.

We examine a theoretical framework where non-zero, minute neutrino masses emerge via the radiative mechanism, operating under conditions of exact $L_\mu - L_e$ gauge symmetry. In this model, neutrino masses originate exclusively at the one-loop level, proven to be tiny because the intermediate fermionic states involve heavy particles ($\sim$ TeV) that decouple completely. Additionally, the model demonstrates its capacity to reproduce the baryon asymmetry of the universe through baryogenesis occurring via out-of-equilibrium, first-order phase transitions, with these processes driven by differences in quark and lepton sector scattering.

Recent neural architecture search (NAS) efforts have predominantly explored surrogate methods within additive and DARTT-based design spaces, which limit exploration outside this constrained scope. Conversely, direct search within the space of computational graphs allows full search but suffers from high computational costs. We introduce SPHINX, the first direct method of searching high-performance architectures at the scale of computational graphs while efficiently navigating a broader design space. By employing guided beam search enhanced with a neural performance predictor, our method reduces evaluation counts by over 96% compared to random search, all without depending on trainable proxy models. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 dataset demonstrate that SPHINX reduces latency by nearly half, outperforming current state-of-the-art baselines by reducing their latency by nearly 50%.

Multicast beamforming is essential for enhancing spectral efficiency in communication networks. This study examines green multicast beamforning with energy harvesting (EH) in parts (Part I and Part II). This study focuses on Part II. We consider a scenario where a multi-antenna base station simultaneously serves a single multi-antenna EH user for information reception and a group of conventional user devices for communication. Our objective is to maximize the total spectral efficiency of the system by jointly designing the multicast beamfornning strategy and the receiver's energy harvesting process. We begin by formulating a non-convex maximization problem to improve system total spectral efficiency. To solve this, we propose an iterative algorithm based on successive convex approximation. Additionally, we develop a beamfornning approach using a low-computational method with a closed-form solution that ensures at least a suboptimal result. To further the work, we also evaluate a beamfornning approach using a low-computational method with a closed-form solution that ensures a suboptimal result. Simulation results confirm that the proposed method significantly boosts system spectral efficiency while meeting user constraints.

Communication efficiency stands as a critical factor for the viability of Federated Learning (FL). Although Distillation (DL) offers superior communication efficiency compared to standard Federated Learning (FL), it suffers from elevated computational costs per communication round due to multiple additional distillation phases. This study introduces FedDis, an enhanced communication-efficient federated distillation method that performs sequential knowledge distillation using student models. Feddis utilizes adaptive learning rates to mitigate catastrophic forgetting and incorporates regularization techniques to reduce the multiple communication rounds inherent in DL. Comprehensive evaluations of Feddis across multiple datasets and with various model architectures demonstrate that it achieves significant communication efficiency gains relative to conventional Federated Distillation and Federated Learning.

This research addresses the computational exponential stability of a stretched Euler–Bernoulli beam defined on a metric graph in the form of a star-shaped domain with one finite and two infinite edges. We demonstrate that for any positive self-adjoint boundary configuration, the system's eigenvalues are real and negative, ensuring exponential stability, while its eigenvectors exhibit odd symmetry. Furthermore, the eigenvalue spectrum consists of discrete states, and we formulate an explicit study on determining the precise decay rate associated with this stable dynamics.

This study examines whether inhomogeneous chiral phases exist within the quark-meson model, which incorporates explicit chiral-symmetry breaking. Results indicate that although the region permitting these inhomogeneities diminishes as pion mass increases, such phases persist at the physical pion mass. Furthermore, instability driving inhomogeneous matter formation manifests in the scalar channel, as opposed to the less favorable pseudoscalar modes.

Topological materials exhibit robust band inversion near the Fermi level, a feature derived from symmetry protection that ensures stability against certain perturbations. In this study, we explore hole-doped topological band inverters by employing a $\text{Bi}_2\text{Se}_3$ model to simulate the effects of hole doping within a band invertor based on $\text{Bi}_2\text{Se}_3$. We identify that creating a doping environment shifts the dispersion relation relative to the Fermi level, thereby promoting the emergence of topological bands characterized by non-zero momentum. Specifically, we observe the conversion from a 3D bulk band invertor to one that exhibits a topological nature in lower dimensions. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of chemical potential on the energy disbursement patterns observed during this transition process. Our results indicate that hole-doped inverters can be reclassified as either effective 2D or 1D systems exhibiting topological characteristics. These findings offer valuable insights into the mechanisms of hole-doped invertors and may advance the development of innovative applications for these materials in quantum information systems.

Recent studies have demonstrated that agents trained via reinforcement learning (RL) are susceptible to adversarial inputs, with existing defenses primarily addressing specific input perturbations. Our work extends this landscape by identifying and mitigating two critical vulnerabilities: first, samples synthesized by current adversarial generation models can completely freeze RL agents, causing severe performance degradation even without direct manipulation; second, we introduce the concept of white-box black-box attacks, where the generator is accessible to the attacker to optimize samples specifically for their target RL agent. This second approach achieves dramatically higher attack success rates compared to standard black-box methods. Our proposed mitigation techniques are robust across various agents, environments, and attack configurations, offering sustained protection while preserving minimal necessary interaction between the attacker and the generator while maintaining significant safety guarantees.

We introduce an exact analytic resolvent Green's function for the lowest-band electron holon lattice associated with a 2D square Hubbard model that includes a nearest-neighbor hopping defect. By analytically resolving the defects at the band edges and identifying isolated states within the band gaps, we demonstrate the formation of localized bands both above and below the main band. Furthermore, we examine the impact of defect dimensions on the positioning of these satellite bands and identify isolated bands specifically above and below the van Hove singularities for rectanglular lattices. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of hopping charges in the vicinity of defect states and clarify the relation to the magnitude of hole doping. Finally, we explore how varying doping levels influence van Hove singularity positions and analyze the consequences of this shift on superconducting pairing pairing symmetries.

This paper introduces two risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms capable of determining optimal policies within general stochastic environments that follow a Markov decision process, even when the underlying dynamics are unknown and non-stationary. To achieve this, we assume the existence of a "variation budget" that quantifies the total rate of change permitted for environment parameters over the simulation timeframe. By establishing theoretical performance bounds, we demonstrate that our algorithms match this bound, thereby confirming their effectiveness for simulation parameters constrained to stay within the budget limit. Additionally, we validate our methods through risk-sensitive RL tasks involving non-stationary Markov processes, including a time-series forecasting application for air quality.

Organizations utilize issue tracking systems (ITS) to monitor project tasks, analyze requirements, and manage defects. These systems, however, often suffer from excessive notification noise that hampers effective information consumption. This paper proposes a context-aware notification system (CANS) designed to mitigate such network noise within ITS implementations. An analysis was conducted on CANS using a newly developed, dataset-driven assessment methodology set to a proposed standard. The CANS was evaluated via this dataset and compared against two existing state-of-the-art note summarization approaches: one employing topic modeling and another using text similarity. The comparative results demonstrate that CANS significantly enhances users' ability to retrieve valuable information.

Distributed machine learning (DML) across time-varying networks enables collaborative model optimization by various stakeholders, such as mobile edge devices, with widespread adoption driven by rising demand for privacy preservation, bandwidth reduction, and resource efficiency. Nevertheless, existing edge-centric approaches struggle when applied to centralization-heavy tasks, such as large-scale deep learning, primarily because they rely on global synchronization and one-to-all data dissemination. This limitation hampers scalability and impedes application in environments with significant computational resources or strict latency requirements. To address these issues, this paper introduces ViMES, a novel vector-based information fusion framework designed to enhance both the scalability and efficiency of deep learning over dynamic networks. Unlike conventional synchronization methods, ViMES operates without global sync dependencies, utilizing a lightweight communication protocol that transfers minimal data through a distributed aggregation tree. Furthermore, the framework incorporates an adaptive network topology management strategy that dynamically adjusts based on communication bandwidth and computational capabilities to optimize convergence speed. Experimental results demonstrate that ViMES outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions in both convergence velocity and total training time.

This study presents an on-chip multi-grating apparatus designed to generate several optical dipole traps for sodium and single rubidium atoms. Utilizing a 10 µm silicon nitride waveguide as a compact compact beam splitter, the device splits an incident light beam into four distinct directions, each feeding a diffractive grating that shapes the resulting optical potentials for trapping atoms. Experimental results confirm the successful generation of these trap potentials, verified by trapping individual rubidium atoms. The resulting dipole traps feature a diameter of approximately 2.5 µm and a bottom of the potential well around -kHz. Furthermore, numerical simulations indicate that this configuration effectively traps single atoms and supports the trapping of two atoms, as demonstrated by a bottom of the potential well around -kHz.

Power consumption is a critical consideration across diverse manufacturing processes. The asymptotic behavior of random walks is heavily influenced by a graph's dimension. While this concept is well-defined for transitive infinite graphs, extending the notional of dimension to general weighted finite graphs remains ambiguous. This work introduces a graph's chaotic operator and a corresponding non-negative self-adjoint inverse known as the Laplacian. By examining asymptotic properties of stochastic walks, we define a graph's spectral dimension. This framework enables us to determine conditions under which conformal Minkowski embeddings exist and are unique for the graph, thereby establishing a link between graph theory and discrete differential geometry. Applications span computer science, machine learning, and physics.

By employing a novel approach grounded in $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing angles, we have identified the mass spectrum and decay constants for $J/\psi$-hybrid states with a fixed mass around 4.23 GeV ($m=4.23$ GeV). Under this constraint, the system yields two hybrid resonances: the $Y(4230)$ and the $h_{\chi}(4.23)$. While both share an approximate mass of this value, the $Y(4230)$ is a candidate hybrid due to its observed preference for decaying into $\psi(nS)\,\,\pi\pi$, a signature indicative of a hybrid nature. Conversely, the $h_{\chi}(4.23)$ exhibits a distinct preference for $\chi(nS)\,\,\pi\pi$ channels. Furthermore, the decay rates of these hybrid resonances into the $\chi_J\pi\pi$ final state have been calculated. We further investigate the $Y(4230)$'s behavior within the decay process of $Z_B^0\to J/\psi\,\,\pi\pi\,\,\pi$, suggesting that the $Y(4230)$ plays a significant role in this process.

This study examines the statistical characteristics of online signature templates collected from 109 individuals using a lab-based pen-and-paper system for data acquisition. We propose three complementary metrics to describe these signatures: (1) the fractal dimension of the convex hull, (2) the count of vertical crossings within the bounding box, and (3) the volatility index. Additionally, we validate a classification model developed using a Nearest Neighbor algorithm, achieving an accuracy of 89%. We also observe distinct statistical differences between the templates and those of online signatures written on a mouse, recorded on a touch screen, or produced by styluses. Finally, we discuss the significance of these findings in relation to using online pen-on-paper signatures for document authentication and forensic analysis.

This paper summarizes the arXiv publication [hep-th/0009179]. We examine the perturbative spectrum of N=6 supersymmetric T-fold background solutions to superstring theory involving O(d,Z) symmetries, which include discrete Lorentz transformations and various supersymmetries. We focus on the minimal case d=8, where N=6 supersymmetry is preserved. In this scenario, the method of momentum and null oscillation winding states is employed, supplemented by an analysis using Kac-Moody algebra representations. The study finds that the resulting spectrum is invariant under two distinct maximal finite subgroups: O(4,Z_2) and D8(2,2,Z). These symmetry groups correspond respectively to the arithmetic quotients of the Borweil-Hartman-Hartman algebra and a specific subgroup of the Dynkin diagram associated with K-M algebras. The work concludes that N=6 supersymmetry is sufficient to maintain this duality invariance within superstring theory.

We examine a dopant moving within the insulating phase of a Mott insulator, focusing on two key aspects: its confinement and its magnetic dressing. Employing an effective model that incorporates both electron-electron and electron-phonon interactions, our analysis demonstrates first that the confining phonon-induced potential scales consistently with results from an insulator in which electrons are prohibited. Regarding the magnetic dressing, our findings indicate that electron-phonon interactions strengthen the magnetic polarization observed in the metallic scenario. Notably, this enhanced polarization surpasses what would be expected merely by adjusting the electron concentration. These results advance the understanding of noiseless solitons within mixed valence systems, such as those found in doped cuprates, and offer fresh perspectives on how phonons influence magnetic solitons in solvable electron liquids and liquids incapable of being solved.

Secondary nitrogen enrichment is observed in both massive stars and AGB stars with high initial metallicity. This study explores how pre-existing metallicity influences these nitrogen production pathways. We utilized the GENESIS model, which simulates nucleosynthesis and element yields from a broad spectrum of stars and metallicities. Our simulations indicate that for massive stars, higher metallicity elevates secondary N yields because higher initial C and O abundances accelerate the C($\alpha$,$\gamma$)N reaction within internal shocks. Conversely, in fast-loose AGB stars, higher metallicity results in lower secondary N output since stronger third-channel forces prevent the de-excitation of carbon isotopes via $\alpha$-capture rather than allowing it to convert into nitrogen via the $\beta$-decay route. Overall, our results suggest that pre-existing chemical enrichment can significantly impact binary star and AGB star production rates of secondary nitrogen, thereby influencing the chemical evolution of galaxies at high redshifts where ambient metallicity levels were low.

Defined as advanced capability in two or more languages simultaneously, multilingualism frequently manifests in real-world interactions through code-switching or code-mixing—terms used interchangeably here—referring to seamlessly blending elements from different linguistic sources within a single utterance. To explore the potential for AI to master complex tasks like these, we created a comprehensive 混合 dataset consisting of 十 million labeled mixed-lingual Wikipedia articles written in various combinations of six base languages: English, French, German, Spanish, Turkish, and Russian. We then evaluated three leading large language models (LLMs) to determine their ability to reproduce accurate code-switches and successfully predicted the language identity of switches undetected by prior methods with high precision using our dataset. Our analysis demonstrates that even state-of-the-art LLMs struggle to correctly identify language boundaries within utterances composed of these six languages, highlighting a significant gap in current AI capabilities regarding real-world multilingual communication.

Biomedical graphs serve as versatile models for the various data types and relationships essential to life sciences, enabling significant advancements in machine learning over the last ten years. This review examines recent progress in linear algebra techniques for enhancing graph representation learning within life sciences contexts along with prospects. We begin by outlining fundamental representations of graphs in the life sciences domain, examining both adjacency and feature-based learning approaches, as well as their integrative potential. Next, the output of these learning strategies will be evaluated, along with their applications in the biomedical machine learning field. The discussion concludes by summarizing critical challenges and emerging opportunities within biocomputational graph machine learning.

We present an updated white dwarf luminosity function to explore constraints on relic populations derived from hypervelocity stars and Weakly Interacting Massive particles (WIMPs). This analysis begins by examining how accretion from an interstellar interstellar (IS) medium and the annihilation of surrounding WIMPs influence a single white dwarf's luminosity. Subsequently, we describe a revised white dwarf luminosity function that incorporates energy contributions from both IS accretion and WIMP annihilation. By comparing our revised model with Spitzer infrared survey data, we determine new bounds on these phenomena. Specifically, our findings indicate that white dwarfs subjected to significant WIMP flux would violate observational limits, implying that if WIMPs exist and possess annihilation channels like $\gamma\gamma$, they cannot be abundant near the Milky Way plane. Additionally, our derived limits on the IS accretion fraction are comparable to previous studies, remaining loose enough that further data is needed to clarify the nature of any dust-free stellar remnants.

Many individuals underestimate the privacy risks associated with uploading photos to the internet. While existing methods for assessing image privacy primarily rely on detecting sensitive objects, the Graph Privacy Advisor employs a gated graph neural network to determine privacy based on context, individual presence, risk factors, overtly dangerous elements, and the likelihood of harm. The model's performance is benchmarked against a publicly available dataset and traditional detection models, resulting in superior accuracy. The model's code and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/leewenyan/graphprivacyadvisor.git.

This work proposes an alternative model of a quantum radiator based on a simple coupling between a two-level system and its radiation field. The framework offers compelling arguments supporting the view that a particle maintains an inextricable connection to its own history. Furthermore, it-analyses, particularly in regimes with low photon detection probabilities, demonstrate that these quantum effects align closely with experimental observations. Crucially, exploring the quantum aspects of its classical limit reveals a connection between decoherence and information back-action: specifically that an observer's ability to decohere a radiation source is strictly constrained by the fact that they simultaneously acquire knowledge regarding the emitter's history.

Measurements of charged-particle fragmentation functions within jet substructure are examined using data from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s}=1\,3$ TeV, acquired by the ALICE detector at the LHC. Two event samples are analyzed: inclusive jet events marked by a forward photon and unbiased jet events. By comparing charged-particle fragmentation functions in these scenarios against Monte Carlo simulations, the study assesses how hard scattered particles influence fragmentation for both jet types following ALICE reconstruction criteria.

Solar atmospheric nanoflares are hypothesized to supply the heat sustaining a significantly hot corona. Although nanoflares are too minute to be detected individually by current instruments, they are expected to be abundant based on existing observational evidence. A proposed method to verify their prevalence involves searching for a measure-zero distribution in flux, though existing data has not yet confirmed this signature, possibly due to limitations in imaging resolution. We utilize synthetic data derived from a model of collapsing magnetic flux tubes to test a newly developed image analysis algorithm capable of simultaneously quantifying microflare numbers and energies in data sets containing such events. Our results show that the technique successfully recovers properties across all data sets examined, regardless of signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, applying this method to actual data from the Hinode/XRT observations of the solar active region AR11158 demonstrates that the algorithm functions effectively with real-world inputs. We conclude that nanoflare frequencies and energies can now be accurately measured using existing X-ray data sets and instrumentation through our new approach.

Social influence prediction involves forecasting an individual's likelihood of adopting a product or service within a social network, a challenge frequently addressed by Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Although these networks excel at incorporating relational data, their performance deteriorates as tasks become more demanding, ultimately causing significant waste of computational resources on large-scale graphical datasets. This study addresses these limitations in unsupervised settings and develops an effective data augmentation strategy for enhancing the accuracy of social influence prediction using GNNs. Specifically, we introduce a novel "graph memory network" that leverages historical social graph information to strengthen current predictive capabilities. Empirical analyses confirm that our proposed method substantially improves social influence forecasting performance across multiple benchmarks.

Defining quantum field theory complexity is challenging because it largely involves extending our understanding beyond free models and their Gaussian states or operations. This paper examines conformal field theories in spatial temporal dimensions (1+1) utilizing conformal field theory methods to establish complexity evaluations for both twisted and untwisted scenarios. We demonstrate that maximum complexity instances correspond to primary fields within the operator framework, whereas untwisted configurations align with the OpeRt complexity literature. Our findings are substantiated through numerical simulations of the Ising model at its critical point.

This research addresses pose estimation using a single camera observing a planar surface through four key contributions. First, we derive an closed-form expression for the corrected Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) regarding the error variables, accounting for sensor noise. Second, we determine the Cramér-Rao lower bound for the estimated parameters, enabling the calculation of minimum achievable estimation error. Third, we conduct simulations to verify the theoretical predictions of our error analysis. Finally, we investigate methodologies to reduce this estimation uncertainty. Specifically, we demonstrate through both simulations and real-world experiments that pre-integrating sensor data according to our proposed formula significantly lowers estimation error.

Various models rooted in string theory and supergravity feature hidden sectors that hold significant cosmological and particle physics implications, including dark matter, its stability mechanisms, and potential connections to inflation as well as neutrino masses. This document provides a concise overview of these theoretical frameworks, highlighting a proposed new paradigm for dark matter realized through the kinetic mixing between photon and hidden sectors.

This study details the measurement of same-sign W boson production via proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV using 139 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC. The analysis employs an optimized strategy to identify four-W boson events, rejecting the dominant single production channel富 by targeting events with exactly two opposite-charged leptons while isolating specific charge configurations for the remaining isolated neural hadrons and corresponding jets. This refined categorization enhances acceptance for both ZZ production and the interference term associated with WW scattering, with the latter being significant only within the diboson mass spectrum exceeding 500 GeV. Consequently, this method boosts the expected sensitivity to interference effects while maintaining robust acceptance for doubly charged Higgs boson pair events. The measurement presents first-ever acceptance-corrected cross sections for same-sign W boson pairs, covering integrated cross sections and differential distributions as functions of the boson system's mass, the single transverse momenta of the W bosons, and the pseud rapidities of the leptons. These findings are compared against standard Model predictions from POWHEG-BOX, DYNE, FEJNMAN, and DYGLU simulations, alongside models extending to BSM scenarios including ATLAS HEPMC and DYGLU generators.

This paper proposes the Co-DMD, a novel color-adding-monochrome dual-camera system designed for high-efficiency illumination restoration and spectral enhancement of ultra-slow-motion sequences captured by single-frame rates. By exploiting the complementary relationship between cameras, monochrome data supplies instantaneous illumination conditions through its high sensitivity, while color data supplies accurate chromaticity though remains frame-limited. Synthesis results demonstrate significant speed-up capability compared to traditional multi-capture methods, while preserving superior color detail through illumination harmonization.

This study extends research previously undertaken in collaboration with the second author and P. Daskalopoulos. That earlier collaboration, conducted alongside J.L. V\'{a}zquez, introduced the fractionable Yamabe flow relevant to fractional curvature and established existence theorems for mild (semi-group) solutions. The current article advances this research by demonstrating that for a specific set of data, the flow exhibits convergence within a broader framework. Our methodology draws heavy inspiration from strategies streamlinized in M. Struwe's book.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has emerged as an effective strategy to mitigate data sparsity and enhance recommendation performance. Nevertheless, existing single- or dual-task CDR models often struggle to fully activate the potential of cross-domain data due to heterogeneous domain characteristics and the scarcity of a fully shared domain space. To address these challenges, we introduce the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model. MSDCR establishes a common sub-domain space through multi-task sparse embedding techniques, enabling robust user and item representation learning despite sparse signals in both isolated and cross-domain settings. Furthermore, by integrating a mutual attention mechanism, the model captures critical interaction patterns across domains to generate high-precision recommendations. Extensive experimental results conducted on two extensive real-world datasets demonstrate that MSDCR significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines.

We establish that for any smooth projective scheme, the vector space capturing the first-order variations of a sheaf equipped with either an orthogonal (respectively symplectic) structure corresponds exactly to the first hyper-cohomology of a specific, derived complex intrinsically associated to that structure. Additionally, we present the corresponding obstruction theory for such sheaves, which is governed by an obstruction theory with target given by the second cohomology of this same complex.

Using a partition identity established by Bressoud and Hindley and a recurrence relation from Andrews and Zuckerman, we determine the average count of even parts in partitions of $n$ into distinct parts, as well as in mixed even/odd distinct part partitions, nearly always correctly and typically with only finitely many exceptions. Additionally, we introduce straightforward averages related to the presence of multiples of 3 within such distinct part partitions.

We examine projection methods used to approximate functions within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) based on noisy empirical data. We derive distinct upper bounds for approximation error (bias) and these bounds highlight a clear trade-off: increasing the dimension of the approximation space reduces bias noise but is susceptible to higher variance as sample size and noise levels vary. We further propose several external regularization schemes to control model complexity, resulting in regularizers whose performance is demonstrated to be statistically optimal in various scenarios regarding sample noise, approximation space choice, and its dimension. This includes providing strong theoretical guarantees for popular approaches like the spectral cutoff method. Additionally, we introduce new results for the so-called principal component regression method, showing its statistical optimality under noisy samples with kernels possessing undecaying eigenvalues, such as those found within Sobolev spaces.

We introduce a straightforward phenomenological framework to examine the transport behavior of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ mesons in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, building upon the concept of the transport coefficient. By calculating both the imaginary and real components of the meson self-energy, we derive and solve a kinetic master equation for the two-body process:
$$c\bar{c}+c\bar{c}\rightleftharpoons\gamma+ \gamma.$$
This equation accounts for both Pauli blocking and Pauli enhancement effects. The study employs two distinct regimes for $c\bar{c}$ interactions—either direct formation and dissociation or capture/dissociation—to track heavy quarkonium yields throughout ultra-relativistic collisions at the LHC and RHIC. This phenomenological method is validated against more rigorous quantum kinetic calculations and experimental yield data from those facilities.

Numerical simulations on finite systems reveal that disordered insulators belong to the random singlet (RS) phase, a state evidenced by spin-correlation functions that decay proportionally to $1/r$ at large distances. Consequently, to conduct effective finite-system simulations, we must define an effective Hamiltonian consistent with this behavior; specifically for RS phase insulators like the one-dimensional Heisenberg chain, the effective Hamiltonian's ground state must exhibit the characteristic $1/r$ correlation structure itself. This study presents the derivation of such ground states through continuous deformation of trivial product states. Specifically, we show how to generate RS ground states by applying the $\sqrt{S}$-root-rotation technique, where $S$ denotes the total spin of the system. Our research indicates that the root rotation angle must follow a specific distribution to reproduce the $1/r$ behavior. Furthermore, we examine the distribution of the total system spin within these generated states, observing a bias toward lower total spin values that tightens with increasing system size.

Robots employing inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn from real-world observations may encounter distractions beyond the human expert, known as confounding factors. While these issues are often disregarded in theoretical models, they pose significant obstacles when applied to actual robots. We introduce the concept of "noise observation" to model such disturbances and demonstrate how they degrade the performance of IRL. Our paper presents a theoretical algorithm that effectively mitigates the impact of noisy observations. Furthermore, we validate our approach through simulations involving a robotic arm and experimental trials with physical robots to verify the proposed methodology.

We propose a two-phased algorithm designed to overcome demanding control tasks by partitioning the solution process into a preliminary stage for establishing feasible subgoals and a subsequent stage for refining the ultimate solution. At its core lies a randomized, projection-based method for constructing control sequences that features an innovative hybrid approach to defining the projection space; this space aggregates multiple data-derived descriptors, each validated for existence of a solution through optimization goals. These descriptors ensure mathematical stability within the solution set and exhibit flexibility in defining the control objectives. Validating the algorithm's efficacy on various challenging problems demonstrates that this strategy successfully addresses scenarios where conventional techniques fail to locate any solution.

We introduce a novel, self-consistent theoretical framework that addresses the supermassive black hole (SMBH) mass assembly problem. This model addresses a longstanding discrepancy in galaxy evolution: while standard accretion via accretion disks fails to reach the observed SMBH masses in high-redshift systems, it simultaneously risks excessive feedback that would suppress star formation. These issues are resolved by recognizing that gas accretion through the radiatively inefficient (RI) channel is not only the most efficient way for black holes to grow but is also a natural consequence of the radiative properties of hot accretion flows. Specifically, the model establishes a direct link between the radiatively inefficient accretion disk (RIAD) formation and the observed $M_*$–$M_{\rm BH}$ correlation across cosmic time. Furthermore, it simulates the full lifecycle of a RIAD, beginning with gas dynamics in a subsonic shock, extending through the formation of a radiatively inefficient accretion flow (RIAF), and concluding with the transition to radiatively stable disk states. Applying this approach to $z \sim 2$ star-forming galaxies with initial masses around $10^{10} M_\odot$, we obtain SMBHs ranging from $10^8$ to $3 \times 10^9 M_\odot$, aligning well with observational data. Deep neural networks (DL) have proven highly effective in extracting patterns from extensive datasets, making them a popular choice for data analysis in CERN's LHC experiments. However, certain obstacles impede their widespread adoption across scientific fields. To address these challenges, researchers from the LHC experiments collaborated during a 2019 workshop to explore how DL can be successfully integrated into experimental science. This meeting produced recommendations outlining pathways to expand the use of data-driven methods. You can find these proceedings, representing a compilation of those workshop reports, here.

Preprints represent the dominant method for the rapid dissemination of scientific findings, yet their distribution remains difficult to quantify. This study utilizes a vast dataset of over 300 million articles to analyze preprint activities, covering more than 90% of arXiv submissions and more than half of bioArXiv submissions. Our findings reveal that preprints have grown exponentially across three decades, reaching approximately 10% of all research articles in various disciplines, a rate that varies by field. In addition to general conclusions, our analysis offers both preprint and citation data for individual researchers, demonstrating significant variations in publication patterns. Our tools are accessible at https://www.research-gapis.acs.org/preprint-analysis, and the comprehensive underlying database is maintained at https://www.acs.org/gapis/preprintdatabase, providing essential preprint and citation metrics for more than ten million scientists worldwide.

Robust research data management stands as a cornerstone of contemporary laboratory operations, a challenge that is particularly acute in fields relying on extensive datasets such as chemistry. This project addresses current chemical data documentation shortcomings by introducing "eLab," a digital laboratory book constructed within Notion. Its primary goal is to enhance research reproducibility through organized records, while also streamlining research development via automated scheduling and reminders designed to mitigate human error in experimental planning. To support development, a comprehensive workflow was engineered, integrating software like ChemDraw, Excel, and Chrome extensions alongside eLab. The application successfully demonstrated its utility by documenting the synthesis, characterization, and storage protocols for various organic compounds. Ultimately, the study confirms that eLab offers significant data organization capabilities, effectively supporting chemistry research and data analysis while allowing for straightforward customization to align with diverse research strategies and personal preferences.

High-entropy alloys represent a promising class of materials characterized by multiple key features: complex crystal structures, significant chemical disorder, and diverse chemical compositions. These characteristics render them exceptionally difficult to investigate using traditional methods. However, modern machine learning (ML) methods offer scalable computational advantages, allowing for the efficient handling of high-dimensional composition spaces and disordered systems. Consequently, ML-driven strategies have recently become powerful tools for the exploration, analysis, and rational design of high-entropy alloys. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in applying ML to these materials, covering fundamental concepts and numerous specific case studies. Furthermore, the text addresses current hurdles and proposed future pathways for utilizing ML in the context of these alloys.

Probabilistic frameworks are essential for state estimation, a critical component of coin generation tasks where the objective involves inferring latent causes responsible for observed data. This paper introduces a variational lower bound framework trained via gradient ascent to perform joint estimation of latent causes and observation parameters over time, addressed within an online setting presented as part of a dual-learning methodology grounded in probabilistic principles. Furthermore, the proposed online state estimation technique demonstrates superior performance compared to traditional online Expectation-maximization approaches when implemented in robotic systems, highlighting its practical advantages.

The nonlinearity of a multivariate Boolean function quantifies the maximum nonlinearity among all its component functions. In 2005, Dobbertin et al. demonstrated that using projective planes from fields of square roots of prime order, one could achieve near-optimal nonlinearity for multivariate functions with several variables. However, this technique did not apply directly to constructing symmetric prime-squared order projective planes. Subsequently, in 2009, Mesnager introduced another method based on Sidon sets within finite fields, achieving the same optimal or nearly optimal nonlinearity for multivariate functions. This multivariate function features components that are almost affine functions belonging to cosets of nearly affine sets. This paper focuses on refining Mesnager's work by refining both the structure within which we find elements of finite fields belonging to high-order difference sets and the specific difference sets themselves. This approach allows us to generate multivariate functions with a significantly larger variable set while maintaining high nonlinearity. Furthermore, we provide sufficient conditions under which the use of difference sets yields multivariate functions with components that are nearly affine functions. Finally, we establish a relationship linking the numbers of high-order difference sets identified through our approach with combinatorial designs known as high-order difference families.

Binary matrix sampling is widely applicable in diverse areas including privacy preservation and modeling. Established swapping algorithms are capable of sampling from any binary matrix distribution defined by fixed row and column sums. Although these algorithms function correctly, they often exhibit slow convergence, particularly when structural zeros are present in the data. This study introduces a local-structure swapping method that enhances convergence rates. By integrating the concept of a "swapping chain," we construct a corresponding Markov chain tailored to the local structure of the matrix. Our approach also demonstrates that structural zeros can be managed effectively. Empirical evaluations using both simulated data and real-world applications reveal that the proposed algorithm outperforms traditional swapping methods in terms of efficiency.

Achieving the fitting of Parton Distribution Function (PDFs) demands the unification of extensive datasets, drawing from both empirical observations and theoretical predictions derived from various computational frameworks. Consequently, the PDF-fitting code must support flexible imports of these theoretical models and perform rigorous cross-validation against experimental data. This capability is particularly critical for next-generation fitting efforts, which aim to quantify distributions for heavier quarks. To address this, the open-source Monte Carlo PDF-fitting framework `MC@PDF` has developed a unified interface for managing multiple input formats, including `fastapi` for API-based retrieval and specialized libraries like `up4ia`. Furthermore, `up4ia` supports library-based access. To demonstrate its versatility, `up4ia` has constructed a prototype service.

This document outlines the research background, development history, and functional capabilities of ELKI, a open-source Java data mining framework available at https://elki-project.github.io/. We specifically emphasize its extensive collection of nearly 200 spatial algorithms, designed to facilitate the rapid prototyping of new algorithms. The document also provides documentation on utilizing ELKI for both batch processing and the creation of bespoke interfaces.

This work explores parametric seeding to tailor the structures of microresonator frequency combs, showcasing a experiment where a microsphere was driven by a continuous-wave laser, resulting in a higher harmonic envelope formed via soliton dispersion management. Parametric seeding rendered the frequency comb's spectral spacing deterministic, parametric inversion imaging revealed a location-dependent phase relationship among comb lines, and controlling the seeding position allowed for linearity tuning within the spectral envelope. These findings demonstrate that parametric seeding offers a robust method for engineering microresonator frequency combs, presenting promising avenues for customizing their architectures and applications.

Extending the contributions of Ciardo, Clark, and Miller, we observe that every weakly mixing probability measure preserving (p.m.p.) action of a hyperlinear group remains faithful if it is essentially free; however, such an action may still fail to be essentially free.

Neural networks have become foundational in computer vision, yet computing real-valued weights and activations precisely is often impractical, leading to a widespread shift toward quantization where integer values are assumed. This brief discussion analyzes how quantization influences generalization capabilities. Our findings indicate that quantized networks face greater difficulty generalizing compared to their unconstrained counterparts, a hypothesis supported by the observation that quantization imposes an implicit prior on weight distributions. Furthermore, we propose a Bayesian quantization approach designed to enhance generalization performance.

This work examines the entropic relations governing bulk systems corresponding to the dual Boundary scenario under Holographic Logarithmic Correlation (HLC) and Bulk Logarithmic Cavity (BLC) conditions. A defining trait of our proposed entropic framework is its adherence to bulk entropy constraints, specifically requiring that all observed entropies be consistent with either the Holographic Entropy Cone or an extension thereof. Consequently, not every arbitrary set of such bulk entropes can constitute a valid solution. Our primary objective is to determine whether specific information-theoretic constraints, namely the Entanglement Wedge Cross Section (EWCS) and the Bulk Entanglement Wedge Entropy (BWE), inherently satisfy these relational requirements. By solving this problem for various scenarios and boundary configurations, we demonstrate that bulk entropies must obey the Holographic Entanglement Entanglement Relation (HBIR) and BIR, respectively, implying that bulk entropy relations are more restrictive than those found in the bulk logarithmic correlation and cavity contexts. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the monotonicity properties of bulk entropies and the monotonicity of quantum states, and we investigate the behavior of bulk entropies in the context of pure states versus mixed states, ultimately showing that while monotonicity may not hold universally for all bulk entropies under HLC and BLC conditions, it is universally valid where bulk entropies satisfy the Holographic Entanglement Entropy

This paper introduces a technique grounded in lattice duality to tackle large-scale instances of the TQA equation. We demonstrate findings for exceptional series LTTs up to scale $L=2000$. As the system size approaches infinity, we identify that crossing multipliers align with the characters of both 3D A-type and B-type conformal field theories. Furthermore, we numerically investigate anomalies associated with the conformal dimensions of exceptional series LTTs.

Signal recovery methods within the framework of compressed sensing have attracted significant attention over the past decade, driven by advances in hardware, the emergence of new applications, and the desire to enhance algorithmic performance. To address this, various refinement strategies have been employed, including relaxed constraints, the use of a sparsity prior, and relaxed monotonicity constraints. This paper investigates the impact of such approaches on compressed sensing algorithms through a simulation study, demonstrating their positive efficacy in distinguishing recovery methods and their potential for further optimization.

In this study, we evaluate the coadding schemes employed by the ZTF pipeline and conduct $\psfmat$-based PSF assessments for images generated through these methods. We determine that a linear combination is valid for producing a well-defined point-spread function only when image scaling involves a constant offset across all channels; our observations indicate the other scaling approaches tested here do not meet this criterion. Furthermore, although the combination method produces a composite PSF, it introduces significant non-linearities that complicate photometry. Consequently, we recommend utilizing the co-add produced by the stack_scales algorithm as our standard. We provide psfmat evaluations for all images in the 2021 Year 4 data release and have packaged these assessments alongside the data for user access via the public portal.

The present work extends this connection beyond Remenik's specific case by investigating the evolution of directed polymer fluctuations under the heat flow on one-dimensional directed polymers.

This work examines single-server models where a quantum server allows a quantum computation to be verified by a classical client. We introduce a fast, secure, and single-server quantum verification protocol with linear time complexity ($O(n)$) operating under the Random Oracle paradigm, representing an enhancement over the prior best-known efficiency upper bound of $O(n^{1})$. Furthermore, under the assumption of access to a quantum random access oracle, we establish that classical efficiency—specifically $O(n)$ complexity—is achievable for verifying quantum computations. Real cells and tissues frequently exhibit intricate and dynamic forms that standard mathematical models struggle to capture. While voxels offer a useful tool for representation, they lack the flexibility required to model complex shapes, and even when using polygon meshes, the necessary number of vertices for realistic simulation can be prohibitively high. In contrast, modeling cell forms through level sets of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) provides a balanced, multi-tool format optimized for computational efficiency. This approach facilitates the development of effective simulation strategies for cellular processes, such as cell division and cell death. To support these scenarios, we have developed a general, tissue- and cell-wide SDF library that defines the parameters for various cell types and organizational structures, enabling accurate representation of individual cells and various interactions.

While Cartesian space serves as the conventional framework for spatial perception and navigation in engineering and science, there is significant interest in alternative models such as metric, topological, and graph representations. This paper investigates these non-Cartesian approaches within the context of autonomous navigation, aligning with our broader research into a hybrid navigation system based on human-like heuristics. We examine relevant literature, assess the strengths and limitations of each model, and explore potential applications in robotics and navigation. The conclusion presents a recommendation regarding the most suitable choice or combination of spatial models for conceptualizing an effective agent-based navigation system.

This work benchmarks event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithms—recognized for their superior statistical sampling efficiency compared to local reversible Metropolis (MR) methods—in hard-sphere systems. Specifically, we assess performance relative to dynamical-systems (DYS), random-scan (RDS), and scan (scan, RSC) variants. We confirm that all irreversible ECMC approaches exhibit significantly enhanced sampling efficiency compared to their reversible MR counterparts; however, they differ markedly from one another in efficiency. Among them, the random scan variant matches or surpasses the performance of DYS and outperforms scan and RSC significantly. These results hold true for both two- and three-dimensional simulations.

This paper introduces a new dataset and benchmark for evaluating methods in sound event localization and detection (SELD), featuring recordings of diverse acoustic events captured within actual offices. Our collection, assembled from over 100 offices across five continents and spanning more than 50,000 hours of unsupervised audio, was enhanced with manual labels for just one hour of recording to support supervised learning models. Our approach leverages convolutional recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) alongside the previously published OSSS net architecture, both trained on our dataset. We also present an analysis of our results relative to the established 2019 OBSERVATION challenge and the earlier data used in that competition.

Traditional wireless communication relies on orthogonal transmission modes to distinguish users, but this approach limits spectral efficiency. To address this limitation, non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), which enables simultaneous transmissions by multiple users over the same orthogonal resource, has emerged as a promising alternative for enhancing connectivity in 5G networks. While wireless channel conditions introduce noise that complicates signal detection, machine learning (ML) offers a robust framework for mitigating these challenges. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the integration of ML with NOMA, beginning with an overview of both technologies followed by discussions on various ML applications within NOMA systems, including their operational principles. The work concludes by outlining current research gaps and potential future directions for advancing this converging field.

Montgomery and Siegel established an upper limit on how many real zeros Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs) can have, yet the complexity of their properties makes deep theoretical exploration difficult. In this paper, we simplify these complex aspects by providing a straightforward construction of a GAF featuring exactly $n$ real zeros. Additionally, we extend our findings to show that for any specified symmetric setup with $n$ points, there exists a suitable GAF configured accordingly.

This paper introduces a new class of localized standing wave patterns within driven networks of phase oscillators. We define these phenomena as "chimera states," standing wave analogues to previously identified dynamical states in networks of coupled identical or nearly identical oscillators. Through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we demonstrate the emergence of these standing wave chimera states in a specific parameter regime defined by weak noise levels and large system dimensions (characterized by the number of oscillators). Furthermore, we assess the stability of these states against variations in phase response curve asymmetries and noise intensity levels. We also assess the robustness of these phase-based standing wave chimera states regarding differences in natural frequencies within an oscillator network context.

We describe a newly implemented module designed to simulate physical systems with a stochastic influence over particle movement. This module may prove valuable for modeling planets and debris disks affected by turbulence. The module allows users to specify the magnitude of random kicks and the probability distribution they follow. We apply the model here with a Gaussian kick distribution and show that they can be applied effectively in circumstellar disk simulations.

Quantum science demands high precision due to inherent quantum fragility, resulting in feedback control being essential for numerous technological and scientific applications, particularly within quantum simulation contexts. This publication examines feedback-controlled quantum simulation from a theoretical standpoint, addressing continuous-time measurements as well. We propose a fresh theoretical approach to quantum trajectory simulation based on stochastic Liouville equations, specifically designing an adapted algorithm to simulate stochastic trajectories efficiently. Simulation experiments confirm that this method accurately captures the dynamics of various traceable quantum systems. Additionally, potential future directions in the field of quantum feedback simulation are explored.

We investigate a two-dimensional jammed system of disks restricted within a narrow channel, focusing on the discrete variables defining jammed macrostates: height, orientation, and order. Our findings indicate that the count of distinct single-particle orientations remains constant as a function of disk shape, while variations in disk dimensions alter both jammed density and available macrostates, which exhibit power-law scaling at extreme limits of confinement. Furthermore, we outline a phase diagram of disordered to ordered macrostates based on softness versus confinement width, capturing key features observable in discrete particle experiments and noise-free simulations. Ultimately, this disordered jammed state is proposed to represent the terminal configuration for liquid compression, offering a foundation to interpret the viscosity divergences associated with the glass transition.

This study examines historical and projected variations in how El Niño events impact global seasonal precipitation. We differentiate between East Pacific (EP) and Central Pacific (CP) El Niño types, analyzing their distinct influences on the Southeast Pacific, North Pacific, and North America for EP El Niño, and the Southeast Pacific, North Pacific, and Eurasia for CP El Niño events. Our findings indicate that EP El Niño events drive more pronounced and widespread rainfall anomalies across these key regions compared to CP El Niño. This disparity is attributed to the greater sea surface temperature (SST) warming associated with Eastern Pacific El Niño, which amplifies zonal wind shifts and subsequent atmospheric responses. Furthermore, our results suggest that future climate change will not significantly alter the relative impacts of El Niño types on global seasonal precipitation, despite potential modifications in the frequency or characteristics of specific EP or CP events.

Current observations reveal a population of massive black holes in dwarf galaxies that likely formed through collapse rather than dynamical streaming. We propose a testable strategy to constrain their formation mechanism by analyzing the observational signatures left behind in dwarf spheroidal galaxies today. Our model posits initial fragmentation of a massive gaseous halo during the cosmic dark ages; subsequently, a "rearrangement phase" occurs where a "re-stabilized stellar component" surrounds a newly formed massive black hole. Because these black holes eject surrounding stars, the dwarf galaxy becomes more compact than one without a black hole. Our predictions are consistent with the luminosity function and velocity dispersions observed in several dwarf spheroidal systems. However, a key prediction is a correlation between a system's present-day velocity dispersion and its degree of compactness—a signature unique to the black hole formation channel. If future observations of dwarf spheroidal kinematics and spatial structures confirm this relationship, it would provide compelling evidence that streaming collapsed to form these massive black holes.
