This study examines opinion dynamics within a framework where self-organized groups emerge through localized interactions. We analyze opinions evolving over graph-structured populations, where individuals restrict their comparisons to a limited circle of similar peers (bounded confidence). In our model, agents only incorporate data from their "friends," or neighbors, into their opinion formation. This bound of similarity acts as a dynamic mechanism that fragments an initial group into distinct opinion clusters separated by gaps of zero interaction. Our analysis demonstrates two critical outcomes: first, that such within-group dynamics always stabilize into distinct subgroups; second, the topology of these resulting clusters is dictated by the spectral properties of the opinion update matrix associated with various graph structures. Specifically for common models like small-world networks, star graphs, and others, we derive the precise outcomes of these opinion-forming processes by calculating the eigenvalues of their respective matrices.

This work investigates the interior structure of a newly identified family of asymptotically flat, charged black holes, which develop charged scalar hair when the charge-to-mass ratio is increased. Within the event horizon, the geometry mirrors an interior resembling those of uncharged black holes; specifically, scalar hair and electromagnetic fields decay exponentially, while the solution approaches a scalar charge configuration akin to Reissner-Nordström. We further detail specific scenarios within the asymptotic region's geometry to provide insights into black hole interior properties, noting strong similarities between our solution and the $\text{Re}^{*}$ model.

Although genes exhibiting similar transcriptional activation behaviors often display distinct temporal mRNA trends, the drivers behind these differences remain elusive. We present a mathematical framework to investigate how activation dynamics interact with transcription mechanisms within confined spaces, revealing that while activation dynamics dictate general patterns, specific features—particularly peaks—are governed by molecular parameters such that slower protein production and shorter RNA lifespans promote more pronounced spikiness. Furthermore, under conditions involving long activation durations, both spikes and anti-spikes can coexist, though only前者 (predominate) when transitions are gradual rather than abrupt. By simulating these models against bulk RNA-Seq data from yeast, we found that most genes with perturbed activation kinetics demonstrate anti-spiked responses during transitions, whereas those regulated through constant rates show anti-spikes less frequently.

This study utilized the Monte Carlo shell model (MCSM) to identify a low-spin architectural in the $^{64}$Ni nucleus. This framework encompasses the well-documented $4^+$ state at 4201 keV, as well as two newly identified excited $2^+$ states at energies of 4065 and 4660 keV. Consequently, the low-spin configuration spans from 0 to approximately 47 MeV. The inclusion of this newly proposed structure has refined the overall energy spectrum of $^{64}$Ni. Furthermore, the $4^+$(4201 keV) state is interpreted as the $\gamma_2_2$ member of an $\gamma$ unquadruplet, aligning with theoretical predictions from $\gamma$-vib models. MCSM calculations for electromagnetic transition probabilities $B(E2)$ demonstrate excellent agreement with experimental measurements; this success validates the integrity of the $\gamma$-vibrational model for the $4^+$(4201 keV) state and supports the accuracy of the derived $2^+$(4065 and 4665 keV) $2^+$ states.

This work examines the contribution of Kasteleyn orientations within a discrete formulation to both the partition function and various correlation functions involving internal Weyl fermions in $2n$-dimensional U($N$) gauge theories. A primary derived consequence is the "fugacity of pairs" and its connection to the 't Hooft anomalies of these gauge theories featuring Weyl fermions. Furthermore, by employing the lattice gauge theory framework, we offer straightforward proofs for two established results: the demonstration that U($N$) theories with charged fermions exhibit an absence of non-Abelian anomalies, and for $2n$ dimensions with U($N$) gauge theories with charged fermions, the presence of exactly one non-Abelian anomaly.

Let \(C\) be a \((G,\mathcal{H})\)-bilinear code consisting of subsets from the real group algebra \(\mathbb{R}[G]\), where \(G\) is a finite group and \(\mathcal{H}\) is a normal, often elementary abelian, subgroup. We introduce the notion of a "linear complementary pair" for such codes and establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which such a pair exists. Additionally, we define a specific construction to generate these codes within \(\mathbb{R}[G]\) and prove it is both necessary and sufficient. As applications, we present novel methods for constructing linear complementary pairs of code pairs over \(\mathbb{F}_2[G]\) and leverage these findings to build new designs. As a concrete outcome, we establish that the Mathieu design \(\mathcal{M}(2,77,10)\) can be realized using a code defined on \(D_{33}[G]\).

This paper introduces an efficient method for enhancing graphically modeled probabilistic models, specifically those defined by functions where the number of variables exceeds current computational limits. We propose leveraging deterministic finite state automata (FSA) to depict these functions more advantageously than traditional binary encoding methods. Our strategy involves modifying the structure of graphical models by substituting scalar parameters with appropriate FSAs. By alternating between representations, we can execute operations that eliminate variables, thereby enabling the computation of previously intractable conditional probabilities. To achieve optimal results, we must identify a way to construct an FSA with a compact state space. Finally, our work includes an evaluation of the proposed technique against established encoding standards to demonstrate superior outcomes.

This study introduces CARRIE, a new multi-modal object localization framework designed around a dual-agent collaborative reinforcement learning setup. In CARRIE, two agents—each with distinct roles and objectives—work in tandem to jointly determine target objects within a given 3D point cloud scene. The visual agent acts as a long-range agent that operates under a partial observability setting, tasked with object detection and the transmission of guidance information to its partner. The auditory agent, in contrast, serves as a short-range operator under complete observability, allowing it to actively collect auditory cues based on the visual agent’s input. By exploiting this cooperation, the visual agent can mitigate the excessive action space inherent in direct localization, while the auditory agent leverages precise directions from its counterpart to enhance its ability to gather auditory cues. Experimental results demonstrate that CARRIE significantly surpasses existing methods across a range of benchmark datasets.

Thickening agents are extensively employed to regulate the flow properties of dense suspensions, such as those comprising sand, ceramic powders, and food particles, enabling the control of yield stresses and flow behavior. Consequently, there is significant demand for predicting flow states across varying shear stresses, from quiescent conditions to high shear rates. This study investigates such thickened suspensions by analyzing pressure fluctuations in a confined geometry subjected to shear stress. We observe that while yield stress formation from quiescent suspensions relies on transient particle caging, shear-induced flow relies on a mesoscale cluster network; crucially, a transition occurs where dominance shifts between these mechanisms as shear stress increases. By characterizing acoustic emissions during shear experiments, we provide the first direct evidence of a interaction mode switch between frictional contacts and hydrodynamic forces under increasing shear rates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that shear flows are not merely characterized by reversible un-caging but by a more complex process. Therefore, our findings suggest that mechanical and hydrodynamic forces play comparable roles throughout the material's history, not just during shear deformation.

This paper examines the short-term forecasting of Ghana's电力 demand, a critical factor for grid operators aiming to prevent shortages and maintain stability, especially given the difficulty of predicting this non-stationary time series, which is exacerbated by limited historical data. To address these challenges, we employ advanced machine learning models—including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), and a hybrid variant combining LSTM with an extreme learning machine (HM-ELM)—alongside traditional benchmarks like ARIMA and Random Forest. Our results demonstrate that these proposed methods significantly outperform the reference models in forecasting short-term power consumption. Specifically, during crisis periods characterized by supply deficits in Ghana, we identify a distinct low-consumption regime that persists, on average, for approximately 11 days. Beyond its crisis analysis, our crisis-based detection approach offers valuable utility for load forecasting strategies worldwide.

A primary concern with search personalization is its potential to skew neutrality by suppressing certain results while highlighting others based on user profiles, thereby causing users to overlook critical data. Yet, quantifying the searches that suffer from such biased filtering remains a significant challenge. This study addresses that difficulty by introducing an innovative detection framework designed to identify the presence of bias in Web search personalization. By leveraging two distinct features, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, validating it through comprehensive evaluations on both the English-language query dataset from Microsoft and the multilingual dataset from Yandex. Our findings reveal that personalization policies from major providers like Microsoft, Yandex, and Yahoo exhibit varying degrees of bias; specifically, these policies potentially obscure relevant information in approximately 20% of personalized search cases while highlighting it in about 80% of cases.

Program synthesis remains a critical, yet unresolved, challenge in computer science, involving the creation of programs from flow charts—graphs where nodes represent actions and edges denote control flow. Existing literature predominantly focuses on single-language synthesis, whereas our work introduces a dedicated system capable of generating Python code based on flow chart inputs. Evaluation against a database of 1,000 problems yielded a solution accuracy of 60%. Furthermore, by leveraging a flow chart's inherent problem-specific data to precondition a language model our team achieved significant performance gains: experiments demonstrated a 20% average improvement in solving mathematical flow charts compared to baseline approaches.

We explore an ensemble of techniques, some existing and others potential candidates suited for linking climate model simulations at varying scales. These methods, where exact reduction applies to our focused discussion, reveal how each approach aligns with its specific target for exactness.

The creation of heavy nuclei through the $r$-process in neutron star-merger jets is a central focus of current astrophysics research. This study examines the dynamics and chemical nucleosynthesis of ultra-relativistic jets colliding with a circummerger medium (CM), a nebulina composed of neutron-rich and unbound material left behind from the binary system. We propose that jet penetration and the subsequent mixing of jets with the CM are critical for explaining observed electromagnetic counterparts. Furthermore, our NREHD simulations suggest a significant finding: collisionless magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) fail to accurately represent this scenario, as they underestimate both jet mixing and angular momentum transfer to the CM. Consequently, predictions regarding ejecta properties, ejecta composition, and overall nucleosynthesis may be inaccurate when derived using collisionless models.

Radiation oncology clinics are increasingly adopting MR-linac systems to enhance precision through real-time imaging capabilities that monitor patient shifts caused by organ motion and organ-specific deformations. While MR linacs provide superior monitoring accuracy, the process of planning therapy remains largely dependent on CT scans, which fail to capture soft-tissue deformation data. Consequently, the current methodology of calculating dose on MRI-coregistered CT data can introduce planning errors for moving organs like the tumor and prostate. Addressing this limitation, this study evaluates the advantages of utilizing deep learning techniques to segment tumors in real-time using MR linac acquisitions. The research employs a U-Net architecture trained on CT-MRI datasets of patients with prostate cancer to leverage this approach. Results indicate that the model achieves a Dice coefficient of 0.924 ($\pm\,0.042$) and a mean 3D Hausdorff distance of 1.49 mm ($\pm\,2.09$), demonstrating a high level of agreement between predicted and actual segmentation. These findings suggest that deep learning segmentation is a viable tool for enhancing treatment delivery and handling real-time tumor motion monitoring via MR linac systems.

Compositional Data Analysis focuses on multivariate datasets expressed as parts of a fixed total, frequently seen in fields like geology and ecology with 100% sums. While standard methods rely heavily on log-ratio transformations—rendering data incompatible with typical multivariate techniques—this limits access to common analyses like Principal Component Analysis. To address this, we propose a new suite of methods capable of handling transformed data directly. Our solution includes an eigenanalysis tailored to pre-log-transformed data (yielding a Compositional Principal Component Analysis), a framework for Multivariate Discrete Compositionals, and one for Multivariate Continuous Compositionals. Crucially, our compositional eigenanalysis allows for direct interpretation of original scale variables and surpasses existing log-ratio approaches.

Building internal states of environmental focus allows artificial agents to allocate attention efficiently, thereby enhancing learning and decision-making. While recent work demonstrated that such agents could master complex environments built on Minecraft using modular neural networks trained sequentially to solve specific sub-tasks, a critical limitation remains: these agents depend entirely on sequential training orders. Consequently, they often fail when faced with variations in environment parameters, such as altered difficulty levels or modified rules, because they lack generalization beyond their trained conditions. Addressing this, our paper introduces a foundation-based attention mechanism that enables agents to dynamically manage their attention even when their available information is restricted to partial and sequential observations within Minecraft. Through extensive experiments spanning simple to highly complex tasks and incorporating both naturalistic and nonsensical environment alterations, our attention-based agent demonstrated robust generalization capabilities without requiring sequential training procedures to adapt to these variations. Furthermore, our attention mechanism shows promise for applications in partial observability Markov decision processes that demand long-horizon planning capabilities.

This work investigates the phase structure of a composite dark matter candidate, modeled as a fermion with a strong coupling to a scalar, utilizing an effective $2+0$ flavor N.J.M. theory for analytical treatment. In its confining regime, the system exhibits chiral symmetry breaking, producing a dynamical scalar mass scale and requiring non-perturbative solution of the associated gap equation. Both symmetry-restored (unconfined) and confining phases are solved for, with the latter demanding a density-dependent cutoff density-filling mechanism. We further analyze the system's thermodynamics and identify a symmetry-confined fermi gas phase existing beyond zero scalar density; this configuration corresponds to a scalar condensate in the confined state. The phase diagram is established via the fermion density and temperature, with our findings benchmarked against an alternative framework involving a fermion interacting with a pion, demonstrating close alignment.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) serve as a foundational element for numerous natural language processing (NLP) applications. Although recent advancements have largely centered on deep RNN architectures, parameter-setting methods for non-static RNNs remain underutilized. In this work, we introduce an innovative weighting technique for RNNs termed "locally masked RNNs" (LM-RNNs), which apply masks to the fully-connected layers based on input locality. This approach enables data-dependent sparsity, yielding significant sample and training efficiency. Specifically, RNN-LM models achieve equivalent predictive accuracy to their fully-connected counterparts with 60% fewer samples, across various tasks including POS tagging, constituent parsing, and token classification. These results highlight the model's ability to generalize effectively. Furthermore, RNN-LM demonstrates a faster rate of convergence and can be retrained more rapidly when provided new training data. The model exhibits robust transfer learning capabilities across a variety of linguistic domains. Our results suggest a high degree of stability in performance, even in lower-resource settings. Additionally, we observe that RNN-LM models are less prone to overfitting compared to their fully-connected versions. The research code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyongchen/rnn-lm.

Relativistic jets emitted by Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are widely considered a primary mechanism driving the growth of Supermassive Black Holes (SMBHs) throughout cosmic history. This study examines the implications of persistent jet activity on SMBH evolution within a cosmological framework, utilizing persistent jet models to constrain supermassive black hole mass function (BMFF) data. This approach offers significant advantages over non-persistent assumptions, particularly for black holes lacking observable variability. By comparing persistent jet-injecting SMBHs with non-injecting counterparts, we can derive the BMFF specifically for jet-active galaxies. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between SMBH mass function slopes and redshift across different redshift epochs. Our findings indicate that persistent jet activity substantially influences SMBH evolution, with SMBH mass at a given redshift being significantly higher for galaxies hosting jets compared to those that do not.

We investigate the covariant series expansion of Einstein's 34ilbert action in a non-relativistic limit where $c \to \infty$. This approach treats Einstein's action as an series expansion analogous in nature to Madelung's expansion of the Dirac equation at zeroth order. Our analysis reveals that leading-order terms contain the Galilean Einstein 34ilbert action, which is found to be degenerate. At the next order, where powers of $c^{-2}$ are involved, the resulting hybrid covariant mixed structure contains a unique term incorporating time derivatives. This finding suggests the possibility of a finite relativistic transition occurring at second-order scales rather than strictly at the maximal velocity scale. Our results also suggest that even at the level of non-relativistic limits, quantum effects may remain relevant. Additionally, our series contains both positive and negative definite terms at the level of second-order scales. 3D active contours are 3D analogues to the well-established 2D level set method, yet they often fail to function correctly due to the absence of key characteristics found in their 2D counterpart, namely symmetric flux and isotropy with respect to local landmarks. This study introduces a novel 3D symmetry definition that applies to vector fields like contour normal flows and demonstrates how to realize it within the context of 3D active contours. Field duality underpins this definition and ensures a 3D equivalent to the 2im symmetric flux. We present a 1m symbol problem related to finding minimal symmetric partitions in fields with finite alphabets and illustrate its application to restructuring 3D active contours.

Global pooling represents a crucial computational step in machine learning, often serving as a bridge between localized processing and overall understanding. Although its simplicity makes it attractive for easy parameterization, existing theoretical insights remain scarce. This paper introduces a novel mathematical framework centered on graph theory to analyze global pooling within convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The proposed methodology offers deeper theoretical insights into both the mechanisms and functionalities of global pooling ops. Furthermore, the theoretical operations are contrasted against various global attention mechanisms to elucidate their relationships. Demonstrating empirical results in both image classification and object detection tasks confirms these approaches enhance representational efficacy without compromising speed, yielding marginal but meaningful performance gains across diverse datasets.

This paper examines general rotation surfaces generated by rotation around a point in a non-planar manifold, specifically on the Clifford torus. We aim to demonstrate that within this framework, the only non-planar flat general rotation surface is the Clifford torus itself.

Training deep neural networks for semantic segmentation demands extensive, meticulously labeled datasets, which are difficult and costly to assemble. Although data augmentation and transfer learning have eased this scarcity, their efficacy eventually plateaus. Recent studies suggest pre-training on unlabeled depth data derived from videos offers a viable solution. This paper evaluates using depth data from unlabeled video sequences specifically for pre-training. We observe that our approach, which utilizes depth estimates reconstructed via Monodepth1 from 230k unlabeled urban video frames captured in the CityScape benchmark, significantly enhances final segmentation accuracy when compared to models pretrained on synthetic depth data or those initialized with random weights. Additionally, we assess the influence of using distinct intermediate depth models versus a fixed, frozen depth model pretrained on the same source data. Our results indicate that pre-processing and extracting monocular depth estimates from diverse, high-quality unlabeled video datasets can substantially boost performance on dense object segmentation tasks.

Producing effective time-series narratives is vital for data visualization, yet existing text-based methods often fail to scale to large datasets and lack the flexibility for user customization. To address this, we introduce TCube, a narrative toolkit that enables interactive storytelling through temporal visualizations. TCube supports creating unique, user-specific narratives and generates insights by uncovering anomalies and trends in real-world datasets. TCube's interface facilitates time-range selection and suggests visualizations via a cube-like structure aligned with X, Y, and Z axes. Users can refine stories by adding, removing, or reordering visuals or making direct edits. Evaluation involving professional analysts demonstrated TCube's capacity to generate detailed narratives of complex datasets, with interactive customization proving particularly valuable for refining outcomes. Furthermore, usability testing among non-experts using raw, unfamiliar data demonstrated that TCube can produce meaningful narrations capable of guiding others toward understanding the information contained.

The ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has conducted precise analyses of mixing and CP violation within neutral B mesons, along with investigations into rare events arising from electroweak FCNC suppression mechanisms. Specifically, the study exhibits several significant findings: first, measurement results regarding CP violation in $B_d^0$ and $B_s^0$ systems align well with the Standard Model predictions; second, observed frequency rates for electroweak neutral current decays, such as $B_s^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B_s^0 \to D^+\ X$, conform to ATLAS projected limits.
We examine the Ising model within a Cayley tree context, discovering new weakly periodic measures that align with normal subgroups of index 2 from the tree-Cayley group's representations.

This study introduces a Japanese word segmentation model built on a deep neural network using only orthographic information. Since Japanese word segmentation differs from its Chinese counterpart by dealing only with orthogonous clues, it is challenging to achieve a high degree of accuracy. Furthermore, obtaining a large corpus of annotated data is expensive. Therefore, we aim to enhance performance by leveraging only orthotextual information and creating synthetic training examples through domain text manipulation. The results obtained from three different types of synthetic tasks demonstrate significant improvement over baseline approaches, with the best method yielding a 0.8% increase in F-score.

On Stack Overflow, users can utilize external links to attach additional information about programming queries, though relying on these external sources introduces security risks. This study examines how link sharing activities utilize web pages across the platform, revealing that 30% involve external resources and that 70% of user-shared pages load automatic images and scripts. Furthermore, 50% of these external links originate from just 5 percent of active questions, predominantly in Java and JavaScript contexts. Consequently, we argue for heightened caution when incorporating automatic resources from web pages shared by non-natives.

We introduce a new class of models for Self-Interacting Dark Matter (SIDM) that is highly sensitive to baryonic feedback mechanisms, unlike traditional Cold Dark Matter (CDM) or standard SIDM implementations. In these scenarios, mediated by dark matter interactions, low-mass states are converted into heavier ones within the potential well of the Sun, resulting in a significant concentration of high-mass dark matter states in galactic centers. This results in increased mass-dependent self-scattering cross-sections that generate cored density profiles in dwarf and Milky Way satellite galaxies while maintaining a cuspy profile suitable for larger galaxies. Although there is extensive research on communication strategies to effectively address climate change, such efforts rarely engage with the structural characteristics of communication networks themselves. This paper introduces a new conceptual framework for understanding effective climate change communication, one that synthesizes insights from both the scientific literature and network theory. By integrating these fields, the study outlines a set of design principles and offers a model for evaluating communication networks. We apply this framework to analyze two networks: a historical "famous scientist" social graph and a real-world "climate skeptic" network. By exploring specific communication pathways within these networks, the paper investigates the practical application of this conceptual framework.

Building upon the prevalence of labeled datasets, supervised learning has become a foundational element of autonomous driving research. Yet, as labeling costs escalate and the sheer volume of driving scenarios becomes nearly infinite, acquiring extensive labeled datasets is increasingly difficult. Our work addresses this limitation by enhancing the efficiency of labeled data usage through the expansion to semi-supervised learning frameworks. We introduce a scene-specific and task-oriented clustering technique designed to organize and structure large-scale, multi-view driving scenes—enrich further with clustering-level labels—to maximize information extraction from existing data. Leveraging this pre-clustering knowledge, we develop an adaptive, scene-dependent loss function that regulates model training based on the idiosyncrasies of different场景 types. Empirical results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showing a performance gain of 10% over baseline methods on the Argyle Drive dataset benchmark.

Over the past few decades, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have driven significant advancements in computational intelligence; however, their extensive memory requirements and high computational costs have limited their practical deployment on edge devices with restricted resources. A promising biologically inspired solution lies in Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), which offer superior computational and energy efficiency compared to ANNs. While prior research has focused primarily on digital neuromorphic architectures, recent strides in analog hardware have made substantial progress toward delivering true analog neuronal behavior and synaptic plasticity. These advances position analog neuromorphic systems as the most biologically realistic option, yet they have historically suffered from significant noise levels that have hindered their adoption. This study introduces a fully configurable, fully analog neuromorphic system designed with a robust low-no characteristics. By utilizing commercial off-the-shelf components, our design offers high reproducibility and supplies researchers with an important reference benchmark. Experimentation was conducted using both publicly available datasets and our own recorded neuron activity to validate performance. Results demonstrate that our hardware achieves an accuracy of 92.5% on MNIST and 90.1% on FMHand, and successfully processes real-world temporal patterns such as mouse whisker movements and human motion captured via electrophysiological techniques.

Pando offers both shared memory and distributed memory architectures for parallel execution across thousands of globally dispersed personal devices. Pando's initial deployment occurred in 2020 to run Bayesian optimization on a provided dataset. Subsequently, the platform was utilized to advance open-source initiatives including improving cryptographic hash functions for Cyclic Redundancy Checks (CRC32 c) and enhancing error correcting algorithms, as well as developing new machine learning models and designs. Pando's infrastructure and asynchronism allowed for the development of efficient scalable algorithms, which were designed to take advantage of the shared memory architecture in addition to the distributed one. $Q(\lambda)x=0$, where $Q(\lambda)$ denotes a matrix polynomial and the variable $\lambda$ is scalar.
The methodology combines minimal rational interpolation with the Cayley transform.
Specifically, the algorithm interpolates the matrix polynomial using a set of starting points,
then applies the Cayley transform to generate an approximation of the reciprocal characteristic polynomial.
Following this, roots are extracted from the resulting polynomial equation.
Although this technique belongs to the class of secular methods, it is tailored for scenarios
involving sparsely populated interpolation points.
The paper provides the convergence rate analysis for this algorithm.
Numerical examples are presented to demonstrate its practical performance.

We establish that certain intermediate $\beta$-transformations are conjugate to greedy $\beta$-transformants with a hole at the origin, as first hypothesized by H. Erd\H{s}. The proof strategy involves adapting the methodology developed by B. de Luca and M. Mendes da Silva. This finding validates and broadens an earlier conclusion drawn by Erd\H{s}, who demonstrated the same conjugacy for specific intermediate systems but unable to extend his approach arbitrarily.

We establish that confining $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories featuring vectors in their matter content exhibit confinement resulting from monopole condensation, which reduces the $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry via quark bilinears to $SO(N_{F})$. These findings arise from perturbing $\cal N = 1$ supersymmetric theories with anomaly-induced supersymmetry breakdown.

While tree ensemble methods are valued for their interpretability, understanding feature contributions for specific predictions remains challenging because feature importance is often continuous yet presented discretely via ranking or heatmaps, resulting in a loss of granular detail. This study introduces Disentangled Attribution Curves, which visualize feature contributions at the leaf node level and effectively visualizes feature interactions by disentangling them, thus preserving data fidelity. We provide a feature as effect framework wherein features are interpreted based on their outcomes. Additionally, we establish feature as risk by formulating it around the concept of feature stability to create a new interpretation metric.

Federated learning enables distributed training of machine learning models by sharing intermediate data, such as gradients, rather than private datasets. However, this process remains vulnerable to insider threats from malicious participants or untrusted network environments. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) mitigate these risks by providing a secure execution environment. In this paper, we introduce TEE-based federated learning, where the local training of these models and communications occur within the TEE. Our paper presents the challenges and opportunities of integrating TEE into federated learning and suggests future research directions.

Embedded systems are software-controlled programs deployed within physical machines ranging from simple sensors to intricate automotive control networks. During the past ten years, the volume of such software generated by vendors has surged dramatically due to heightened legal liability for manufacturers. These programs often interact with external hardware, including sensors, displays, and wireless modules, which complicates their simulation, verification, and testing. This paper introduces a simulation framework designed to bridge the gap between software development and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) validation environments by automatically generating control for actual hardware components while reconstructing the behavior of virtual peripherals. By leveraging this capability during the design and development phases, engineers can eliminate the need to halt progress for hardware availability, as tests can be conducted on physical infrastructure without delaying development workflows.

We introduce Timeloops, a novel approach that leverages dynamic analysis to automatically generate system call filters for microservices applications, a critical requirement for such applications to operate within sandboxed environments effectively. Timeloops distinguishes itself from existing static analysis-driven solutions by employing dynamic analysis to enhance precision in producing these filters. Its operation involves two phases: initially, it automatically identifies relevant system calls through multi-stage timeliness analysis, and subsequently, it utilizes a machine learning classifier to discard superfluous calls. Timeloops demonstrates superior efficacy, increasing filtering accuracy by 30% in comparison to the leading current static analysis method. Furthermore, it efficiently produces functional filters in a manner that is both user-friendly and requires minimal manual intervention.

Linear classifiers are frequently employed to demonstrate theoretical bounds regarding model capacity and to serve as interpretable alternatives to complex nonlinear classifiers in our theoretical understanding. However, prior research has primarily confined their analysis to Euclidean feature spaces, overlooking intrinsic geometry. This paper investigates linear classification within the product space formed by the Cartesian product of two Hilbert features—considering operators on feature operators defined by curvature—including Kernels Hilbert manifolds. We establish that linear classifiers become remarkably more expressive when composed within these product structures, matching the expressive capacity of neural networks possessing arbitrary nonlinearities and capacity across inner product spaces with any curvature. Notably, we demonstrate that an infinite collection of linear classifiers in such product spaces can exactly simulate a single neural network layer while simultaneously reducing training loss by at least a factor of 50 percent compared to using linear models alone. These results suggest that incorporating intrinsic geometric properties may substantially advance the design and interpretation of machine learning systems.

We introduce a novel analytical approach to determine the steady-state distribution of stars in close proximity to a galaxy's central supermassive black hole (SMBH). Unlike previous models that rely on ad-hoc assumptions, our method derives the stellar population from fundamental physical principles, specifically the balance between gravitational forces and stellar evolution. The resulting stellar orbit distribution is characterized by parameters representing the minimum and maximum specific angular momenta, which correspond to a power-law density in specific energy and, consequently, a cusp profile in position space. While earlier research suggested such cusps might fail energy conservation checks, our analysis reveals that this feature complies with both energy conservation and the various constraints imposed by stellar evolution. The resulting theoretical framework aligns well with observational data regarding SMBH mass and the core radii of galactic bulges, leading to the proposal that all galaxies possess a universal cusp slope for stars. For rotating discs, this extends to a similar relationship for gas, matching the "mass line" found in gravitational line profiles. This short overview focuses on stochastic model predictive control with an emphasis on probabilistic constraints, using a simple linear system affected by uncertainty as a case study and providing related MATLAB code online for reference.

Compressive learning achieves sparsity and structural properties within the learned solution—properties like analytic, geometric, or topological structure—by leveraging a prior regularity in the unknown. This strategy significantly lowers the complexity of learning tasks involving non-i.i.d. data by enabling efficient optimization. This work examines various compressive settings, including independent covariates, time series, adaptive learning, and adaptive covariates where iteratively learned structures are used to determine subsequent query choices. Furthermore, we extend these concepts into the realm of compressed reinforcement learning, where the agent acquires a compressed representation of the Markov decision process. Across all scenarios, we assess compressed performance against standard approaches using Minimax risk minimization. Our results demonstrate that compressed learning can achieve substantial compression with only minimal performance penalties. Additionally, we address the statistical robustness of these methods by considering adversarial perturbations in data queries and questions.

This study examines how emigration and immigration influence ecological models of competition by analyzing two specific migration scenarios. In the first, a well-mixed population competes with spatially distinct, localized invading populations. Second, space-completely uniform populations face immigration from heterogeneous, localized sources in variable spatial patterns. Both scenarios are examined using singular perturbation techniques under the assumption that the migration rate is small. The central goal is to assess how this round-trip flow impacts competitive exclusion or coexistence within a community. The findings indicate that for the emigration scenario, space-completely uniform populations exhibit the same fate as in a no-flow context: either exclusive competitive survival occurs or coexistence results from stable neutral polymorphism. In contrast, for the space-compatively uniform source scenario under low-flow flows, only two outcomes are observed via a singular perturbation: either competitive exclusion results in the winner being the spatially heterogeneous population or coexistence emerges where both populations persist.

A straightforward protocol is presented for enhancing entanglement within cavity magnomechanical systems, which typically suffer from limited entanglement generation due to interaction constraints. This method relies on modulating magnon-mechanical coupling strengths to initiate superradiant coupling, thereby inducing effective entanglement swapping between phonons and magnons. Notably, this form of swapping functions purely through linear coupling mechanisms, unlike most other cavity magnomechanical systems that require non-linearities. Consequently, this approach addresses several limitations, such as the inability of standard linear interactions to produce steady-state phonon-magnon entanglement. Furthermore, input control beams regulate the swapping process, enabling the creation of pure Gaussian quantum states.

We introduce the computationally efficient one-loop triple-collinear color and spin-space splitting operations for both collinear and soft limits within massless QCD. These findings build upon the factorization of multi-loop soft operators established in previous work arXiv:2012.03466 and complement existing color and spin-summed triple-collinear splitting variables for comparable limits (see arXiv:1705.04433 and arXiv:1703.10060). Verified through single loop nucleon matrix element calculations involving three particles with color and spin sums, our results are intended to enhance the efficiency of particle jet distribution computations at the one-loop level.

The sundial, a product of ancient technology, holds significant historical value. Classical Islamic civilisation placed great emphasis on the diurnal motion of the sun, leading numerous scholars to create various forms of sundials to determine prayer timings facing Mecca and align religious rituals with Islamic holidays. These devices ranged from simple types to complex assemblies requiring specialized mathematical knowledge. Although their origins lie in Hellenistic models, their application flourished within Islamic lands. This study examines the evolution of sundials from their Hellenistic foundations through the Renaissance, offering a comprehensive overview of their typology, design, and underlying mathematical principles. Furthermore, it analyzes their utility in timekeeping, solar observation, and day-length calculation, while also evaluating their contemporary relevance for educational purposes.

This paper introduces a dual-objective optimization framework for power allocation in device-to-device (D2D) networks sharing a non-orthogonal system with cellular users. By deploying an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS), the system aims to boost non-linear energy harvesting while simultaneously reducing interference to cellular users. Consequently, an optimization problem is constructed to maximize energy harvesting while minimizing total cellular interference, subject to diverse practical constraints. To address the resulting non-convex nature of the framework, a successive convex approximation (SCA) technique is employed alongside a hybrid approach combining particle swarm optimization and SCA. Extensive simulations confirm that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods by delivering higher interference tolerance through enhanced energy gains, validating its effectiveness in enhancing overall system utility.

Driven by the need to map mechanical behaviors triggered by stimuli such as gas exposure or temperature changes in "lab-on-a-chip" devices, this study demonstrates the application of 2-D Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) coupled with a Low-Coherence Vibrating Beamsplitter (LBBS). This innovative adaptation of classical Doppler vibrometry enables the detection of sample-induced vibrations across a broad frequency spectrum (10 Hz to 50 kHz) with high spatial resolution during both optical and non-optical interactions. Validation experiments were conducted on thin films and biological tissues to evaluate the system's capability, confirming its utility as a precise tool for tracking local deformations and observing dynamic phenomena like pore formation under controlled environmental conditions.

We investigate the spectral properties of first-order statements within the spectral logic framework, which utilizes k-variable logic combined with fixed relational predicates. By analyzing the spectra of sentences within spectral logic k-languages containing a symmetric binary relation, we establish that using multiple variables in place of variable-binding does not expand the spectrum available to express fixed first-order statements with specific structures. By generalizing work done by Ashby and Flum, we demonstrate that for any spectral logic 2-language containing a single symmetric binary relation, its spectrum aligns precisely with the spectrum of a specific spectral logic 1-language involving an equality relation. Consequently, for structures possessing a single such relation, the spectral capabilities of high-arity logics are not superior to those of spectral logic containing only 2 variables. By widening the scope of allowable atomic formulas to include relations of arbitrary arity, a significant increase in expressive power is observed; specifically, for structures involving a single k-ary predicate, the spectral capabilities of spectral logic containing k variables are not equivalent to those containing only k variables variables.

Although current developments in programmable electrostatic phase plates promise to mitigate various spatial resolution constraints within Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs), this study quantifies the spherical aberration ($C_s$) in such platforms using electron holography. By employing an embedded phase plate design, we achieved extremely low values of $C_s$ ($\sim 0.01\,\mathrm{mm}$), enabling detailed visualization of the corresponding electrostatic lens spherical aberration via electron holography. Through $C_s$ engineering, programable phase plates demonstrate the potential for an ultra-compact TEM capable of achieving a spatial resolution approaching $0.05\,\mathrm{nm}$.

We propose a framework for defining oracles representing physical resources and use it to model progress in theories regarding the computability and complexity of physical resources.

Human conversational speech is characterized by features derived from individual voices, speaker identities, emotional expressions, and contextual nuances. Establishing these attributes is essential for creating speech quality in speech synthesis applications. This study introduces a novel end-to-end framework utilizing neural workflows to generate paragraph-level synthetic speech via multi-task learning. By simultaneously optimizing for invariant voice quality, speaker compatibility, emotional consistency, and context relevance, the model produces natural, high-fidelity synthesis. Comprehensive evaluations against previous state-of-the-art methods demonstrate superior performance, evidenced by lower multi-dimensional speaker embedding distances and improved scores in objective quality metrics and subjective Mean Opinion Score (MOS) assessments.

Standard projection predictive inference swaps an intricate target model for a simpler surrogate to boost computational efficiency during inference. While this offers efficient pathways for posterior inference and variable selection in complicated models, it shares the same vulnerabilities to prior mis-specifications as other exclusion strategies. This research introduces an adaptive prior that performs well for both the simple and target models to foster mutual learning. Supported by theoretical analysis, this approach is demonstrated to be effective through evidence from simulations and practical applications.

Deep learning networks have emerged as a highly effective tool for pattern recognition, yet recent studies have exposed their susceptibility to adversarial examples—specifically, the ability to deceive such networks with meticulously crafted inputs. This paper investigates this phenomenon within the context of speech recognition, aiming to explain the emergence of such samples in this domain and develop robust protective measures against them. The proposed approach utilizes a denoising autoencoder to generate robust perturbations effectively. Experimental results across multiple datasets confirm that this method yields performance that aligns with state-of-the-art research while achieving superior defense capabilities.

A significant challenge in climate communication is the widespread presence of conspiracy theories. This study examines dominant conspiracy narratives within an extensive Twitter dataset, utilizing advanced stance detection techniques to determine if these narratives are predominantly spread by skeptics or supporters of climate action. The research identifies specific conspiracy theories experienced by Twitter users and investigates correlations between belief levels and sharing behavior on social media platforms.

This study examines resonance decay effects within the leptonic channel of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 13.8 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS detector at the LHC. Testing against the nonresonant hypothesis, the analysis scans for production events involving invisible final-state particles. No statistically significant excess is observed; consequently, at 95% confidence level, exclusion limits are provided for models where these mediators are assumed to be scalar or pseudoscalar particles. These constraints, derived from decays occurring outside the resonance, cover scalar mediations spanning masses from 2 to 100 GeV and pseudoscalers from 2 to 50 GeV, respectively.

Creating antihydrogen is a major objective for experimental antimatters research, as it allows researchers to detect signature signals like peaks or valleys in scattering cross-sections that indicate CPT symmetry violations. The primary hurdle in generating such antihydrogen is obtaining high-flux, cold, pure, and trapped antihydrogen—without which meaningful scattering data cannot be analyzed. Our proposal involves directing a laser-excited, cold antihydrogen beam at a target to observe scattering patterns, specifically suggesting the use of Rb* (rubidium) as a suitable candidate for low-relative-velocity interactions with various forms of trapped antiparticles. These include but are not limited to antiprotons ($\bar{p}$), antiprotonium ($\bar{p}n$), and even more complex assemblies containing antineutrons or positronium. Such experiments would provide valuable insights into fundamental particle physics while testing the stability of antimatters.

Young multiple star systems evolve through dynamical interactions that drive bound-to-bound or bound-unt binding transformations. Within the context of hierarchical triples, we evaluate whether a differential accretion rate among components can explain the prevalence of unequal masses. We propose and test the "differential accretion hypothesis," which posits that in hierarchical triples, the inner pair accretes significantly more from the third body due to its proximity. To address the resulting mass imbalances, we assume the system settles into a configuration where mass ratios are maximally unequal. Our findings indicate that this mechanism is viable only if the mass ratio within the inner binary is substantially lower than that of the outer comparison ($q_{\rm in} < q_{\rm out}$), a condition met in merely 10–20% of cases. While differential accretion can account for mass distributions in some cases, most systems ($\sim 80\%$) fall outside its explanatory scope, suggesting a more universal role for dynamical interactions.

"This work explores intrinsically flat spacetimes that exhibit symmetry under rotations and translations along a specific axis, which serve as promising candidates for early-universe models. We derive the metric for this class of intrinsically flat geometry and examine its singularity structure as well as its causal properties. Finally, we analyze the optical scalars associated with both null and timelight geodesic congruences interacting with matter to further characterize the domain of global flatness."

Image restoration and image segmentation represent two fundamental and extensively researched areas within computer vision. This paper introduces a new methodology designed to jointly execute image restoration and segmentation when inputs consist of single, blurry, low-light images. We propose a multi-scale architecture featuring two interconnected segments: a representation learning module and a task-specific module. Within the learning section, two networks—named respectively for their functions in restoration and segmentation—are integrated via collateral connections into a bidirectional generative framework responsible for producing restoration and segmentation outputs. This design enables each network to access multi-scale features and facilitates mutual enhancement between tasks. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing single-task models and joint algorithms, yielding superior results across diverse scenarios. Furthermore, our model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, delivering satisfactory outcomes even under challenging conditions involving low illumination and blur.

We describe a methodology for determining the mass and spin of black holes within Active Galactic Nuclei based on their electromagnetic spectra. This approach utilizes statistical distributions of observed luminous flares to formulate likelihood functions for geometric models. These models account for the distributions of black hole masses and spins, supermassive binary formation rates, and binary merger dynamics. By inverting this statistical framework, one can geometrically constrain these parameters. This technique complements traditional spectroscopic methods, such as those using the broad emission line region or relativistic reflection models, by providing an additional means to probe black hole properties in AGEs.

This document outlines the design, implementation, and assessment of an open-source programmable emulator intended to accelerate and facilitate the rapid prototyping of neuromorphic systems. Utilizing an extensive software library, this tool enables the creation of highly scalable custom architectures, allowing designers to substitute individual building blocks—ranging from single circuits to entire applications—with flexible options. Its applicability spans the entire design workflow, supporting concepts through to final verification. Key advantages include free access to the open-source codebase, which features extensive documentation and functional examples, and the capacity for swift, iterative architectural iteration. This stands in contrast to current neuromorphic system prototypes, which are typically constrained by the inflexible, predefined hardware structures of existing systems.

Solar type-I noise storms originate from Doppler-broadened emissions in the microwave band, caused by accelerated electrons trapped in magnetic field lines as they accelerate during microflares. This study investigates the dynamical evolution of a specific type-I noise storm source linked to a microflare using both 1700 Å extreme ultraviolet imagery from the Advanced Telescope for High-Altitude Solar Observations (ATHTHSO) and ATST microwave data. The research identifies two distinct evolutionary modes for the parameters governing the flare source: a rapid mode and a slower one. Furthermore, the analysis uncovers a consistent correlation between the trajectories of these microwave features and their corresponding ultraviolet manifestations in the ATSH ionospheric image.

This study presents a high-fidelity numerical simulation model for a magneto-optical trap (MOT) of rubidium atoms. The accuracy of this model was verified by comparing simulation outputs against experimental data, specifically the trap size versus center beam intensity relationship. Furthermore, we explored the influence of key parameters on trapping efficiency, allowing us to suggest specific adjustments to enhance the performance of the M-O-T.

We investigate the accretion of a spherically symmetric gas cloud with non-zero angular momentum onto a Schwarzschild black hole within the framework of general relativity. By employing the steady-state Euler equations, which incorporate Coulomb friction representing Coulomb collisions, we calculate the surface area of the circular orbit where the accretion flow transitions from subsonic to supersonic as a function of total mass and friction coefficient. This critical area is then substituted into the mass accretion rate formula using the Bernoulli theorem alongside the total energy density to derive the rate itself. Our findings demonstrate that, for a given set of initial conditions, the accretion rate is significantly lower in the case of a black hole compared to an infinite friction scenario, highlighting the impact of angular momentum and dissipative processes on gravitational collapse in strong fields.

We assess the probabilities for (de-)excitation and photon emission involving an approaching or moving potential barrier, treating this scenario as a conducting plane moving toward an excited state. Our findings indicate that while an observer at infinity detects zero photons, a co-moving detector would register significant photon counts, with emission events occurring at non-negligible rates. Consequently, we resolve the apparent paradox associated with the "probability crisis" of an excited atom that has neither undergone de-excitation nor emitted radiation. Our analysis pinpoints the moving plane not merely as modifying the standard spontaneous emission probability, but as a fundamental contributor to photon emissions itself, with this effect being further amplified as the plane approaches infinite speed.

Handwritten document images frequently suffer from degradation caused by factors such as poor pen pressure, shaky hand movements, and aging paper. This paper introduces a new recovery approach based on a two-step cycle-consistency training framework designed to create a shared embedding space for degraded written words and their source templates. The first phase involves a denoising autoencoder that maps degraded input sequences into denoized time-series, aiming to preserve linguistic characteristics while suppressing noise. The second phase utilizes sequence-to-sequence autoencors to project these denoized time-series sequences into the target embedding space. This phase learns to fine-tune the language model specifically for the document domain while ensuring cycle consistency between the original degraded sequence and the final recovered template sequence. Experiments conducted on two datasets containing handwritten documents demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance in enhancing word quality compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Accurately and rapidly extracting text from Intelligent Document Identification (ID) cards is crucial for border control within security contexts. This study proposes a new deep learning framework named TFLearn-based ID Name Extraction (TFLearn ID NE) specifically to transcribe names on ID cards using image data. The system utilizes TensorFlow as its backbone to automate the extraction of these names through a streamlined, multi-stage pipeline encompassing preprocessing, preprocessing for preprocessing, feature extraction, text recognition, and post-processing stages. Through comprehensive evaluation, the proposed model achieved remarkable results, reaching 95.82% accuracy, 95.82% precision, and an F-score of precision of 93.32%. These metrics indicate a high degree of performance compared to existing state-of-the-art models in the literature.

This paper addresses channel estimation in vehicular networks utilizing massive multiple-input multiple-output (massive MIMO) orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems with orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM). To mitigate high pilot overhead caused by massive MIMO/OFDM characteristics while ensuring adequate tracking accuracy for mobile user equipment (mobile UE), this study evaluates a suboptimal method that randomly distributes pilot allocations. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient M3/M/M/Queuing model designed to predict the randomness of channel tracking accuracy in massive MIMO/OFDM vehicular networks. Additionally, we derive a closed-form mathematical expression for the average channel estimation error in this context. Our findings indicate that the proposed performance metric for random tracking accuracy in vehicular communications aligns closely with actual results in this study. We further compare our proposed method against existing state-of-the-art techniques, demonstrating that our solution significantly reduces pilot allocation requirements without substantially compromising tracking accuracy.

Automated images colorization has become a popular research topic in machine learning due to its practical utility and ease of implementation. Despite these benefits, it remains a difficult problem because of inherent ambiguities and a lack of accessible color information. This paper presents a new two-stage method—named E2R-Colorization—that leverages an edge detection technique paired with a refined selective filling algorithm to facilitate automatic chromaticization. This method was tested using a variety of color images to verify its effectiveness. The findings indicate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, as evidenced by its higher scores on the RGB-V metric and its superior visual output as demonstrated by several sample images.

In addition, our method guarantees an upper bound on the number of weights and ensures that the solution remains stable regardless of noise inclusion. Learning from Demonstration (LfD) serves as a promising approach for cognitive robotic systems designed to acquire new tasks through observation. However, single-agent cognitive models have limitations in handling scenarios where interaction occurs between a robot and other entities. To overcome this, multi-agent learning within social LfD frameworks offers potential, enabling robots to infer changes in their environment caused by multiple simultaneous agents. This paper addresses two critical technological hurdles in developing such multi-agent socialLfD for cognitive capabilities: (i) generalizing learned behaviors across different human agents and (ii) inferring internal states, such as velocity and trajectory predictions, from external observations. To achieve this, we propose a unified multi-agent social learning from demonstration (slfD) framework designed to handle dynamic human interactions. Our solution integrates visual input with time-series motion forecasting to facilitate the learning of transferable skills. Extensive testing confirms the efficacy of our proposed model through comparisons with existing methods on both simulated environments and real-world data.

A bias-reduced estimator for the population-level mean is developed to decrease the bias in a high-volume regression model. This research investigates asymptotic bias and bias mitigation strategies under diverse scenarios, specifically causal inference with high-volume regression models and biased sample selection. Additionally, the researcher develops bias mitigation methods to improve methodical approaches, specifically for the mitigation method in all cases, such as the bias mitigation method for the population-level mean, which is particularly useful when the population-level mean is unknown. Although the bias mitigation method is more complex than the standard least squares method, simulation studies indicate that the bias mitigation method achieves superior performance in terms of bias, particularly when the high-volume of the population-level mean is large.

Relation extraction (RE) focuses on identifying the connection between a pair of entities within a sentence, whereas knowledge graph link prediction (KGLP) aims to determine potential relationships between existing entities using both explicit features and implicit knowledge within a knowledge graph. Although neural networks have advanced both RE and KGLP by leveraging extensive labeled datasets, these tasks often suffer from data scarcity in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we introduce a mutual benefit task called Joint Relation Extraction and Link Prediction (JTRELP), which integrates both NLP and recommendation system methodologies. Our approach consists of two distinct yet synergistic stages. Initially, we apply an attention-based link prediction mechanism to integrate knowledge graph information into the RE process, thereby enhancing the accuracy of RE through this preliminary phase. Subsequently, we employ a collaborative filtering technique to establish a bidirectional connection between the two tasks for joint optimization. This two-stage framework not only facilitates effective knowledge transfer from KGLP to RE but also yields superior performance on RE tasks even when data is scarce.

We investigate the finite-T dissociation of quarkonium states within an N-dimensional static background featuring an anisotropic metric. Using the NRQCD potential formalism and adiabatic approximation, we derive expressions for the screening potential in an anisotropic M^{N+1} spacetime (where N spatial and 1 temporal dimension) as a function of spatial momentum, temperature, and various metric parameters. Our findings for an 3+1 dimensional system with arbitrary metric parameters are compared against results from higher-dimensional scenarios under various assumptions, highlighting distinct topological features in all cases. Specifically, we examine how anisotropy influences the dissociation temperature of both ground and excited quarkonium states; notably, increasing anisotropy lowers this temperature for the first state but raises it for the second. Furthermore, we calculate the critical volume required for phase transitions in D-dimensional contexts, demonstrating a direct correlation where transition volume increases with the number of spatial dimensions.

This study details the magnetic ordering in Tb$_3$RuO$_7$, a material exhibiting anomalous electrical transport. Neutron diffraction and polarized diffraction analyses reveal that the Ru$_1$ and Ru$_2$ moments evolve from an initially disordered state to one that is mutually antiparallel and collinear with the Tb sublattice below 15 K. Specifically, the Ru$_1$ moment aligns antiparallel to the Tb moment, while Ru$_2$ adopts an antiperpendicular orientation. Furthermore, the evolution of these moments across the transition is explained as stemming from the temperature-dependent ordering of O 2p electrons, which facilitates their interaction with Tb 4f and Ru 4d electrons.

This work introduces a novel machine learning-based approach to signal representation for images and clips. The proposed method employs a dual-MLP design where two multilayer perceptrons collaborate to decompose a signal into a short set of short real values. These latent coefficients serve as input to both an encoding stage, which generates a compact vector in a low-dimensional latent space for storage, and a decoding stage, which faithfully reconstructs the original signal. Both networks are trained in a supervised manner, learning optimal mappings using large datasets of standard images and videos. This method is highly flexible, accommodating any signal format including standard images, videos, or other types, and supports both natural signals—such as clips of real scenes—and synthetic content—such as medical anomalies or audio defects. Extensive experiments demonstrate the technique's superiority over traditional transform-based systems across a range of tasks, including image denoising, video denoising, image super-resolution, video frame interpolation, and more.

Traditional covariate shift adaptation methods rely on estimating importance weights or conditional pseudo-labels, a dependency that often results in suboptimal performance. This study introduces a new approach by integrating adaptation strategies with semi-supervised learning, effectively mitigating both target domain importance and adaptation issues. Additionally, a novel module termed "module importance enhancement" is developed to refine module weights by leveraging original input data, offering more reliable parameters without incurring substantial computational overhead. Crucially, this proposed framework demonstrates greater simplicity compared to existing solutions and establishes a new state-of-the-art standard on the AdapTKB benchmark.

Recent research into the emergent behaviors of deep learning models has revealed systematic patterns in their training dynamics and architectural designs. This survey places such patterns within an emerging framework known as geometric machine learning, which emphasizes the inherent geometric structures of different deep learning models. We begin by outlining the core principles of geometric machine learning and then examine the geometric properties inherent in various deep learning systems. Subsequently, we explore how this perspective illuminates the training dynamics and performance of these models, along with the advantages offered by several prominent techniques. The discussion concludes by addressing current challenges and promising avenues for future research in this field.

The proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to standard DNN or attention-only architectures, particularly in discriminating subtle jet compositions consisting of quarks and photons. Consequently, it serves as a robust framework for integrating different tagging strategies, offering significant practical utility for physicists aiming to optimize detector performance.

This study presents a novel algorithm for the symbolic calculation of attributes within layer groups, leveraging reduced generator sets alongside general properties of the symmetric group to enable highly efficient computations. This approach facilitates determining every possible two-real-polarity layer group with up to tenfold rotational symmetry. The authors encapsulate the methodology in a user-friendly software tool applied herein, the code of which is released as open-source for public access.

This work presents a novel instance of intrinsically curved Heisenberg frequency momentum operators. Specifically, we define commutation relations for these operators using the exponentiated integral of a mean-value intrinsically curved surface. While analogous constructs were hypothesized by several physicists decades ago—most notably Fock in relation to infinite-dimensional unitary representations of the Heisenberg group—we establish here both the existence and uniqueness of a non-flat geometry supporting this specific operator configuration. We further analyze dimensions greater than two, demonstrating that such curved manifolds exist only in these higher-intrinsic dimensions. These findings have profound implications for quantum field theory and the foundational theory of particles.

Recent high-resolution numerical simulations have revealed that binary stellar systems are a prevalent feature of stellar populations. However, the specific physical mechanisms governing the generation of the resulting mass function—which spans from planets to brown dwarfs and low-mass stars—remain largely elusive. In this study, we investigate the correlations between the total mass of forming parent cores, the mass ratio of the binary system, and the masses of the primary and secondary fragments, utilizing a high-resolution cosmological hydrodynamical simulation. Our findings demonstrate that binary fragment masses are strongly influenced by the mass of the parent core, with primaries typically exhibiting $M_1 \propto M_{\rm core}^{0.87}$ and secondaries following $M_2 \propto M_{\rm core}^{0.72}$. We also observe a power-law distribution for the mass ratio, expressed as $q \propto q^{-1.5}$. These dependencies on core mass can be generalized through a self-similar scaling of turbulent collapse, where objects of different masses share equivalent relative initial conditions. Furthermore, we argue that this self-similar collapse mechanism, combined with the observed correlations, provides a consistent framework for reproducing the mass functions of both fragments within binary systems.

This research introduces the 'm-arcsinh' Kernel-based Independent Component Analysis (m-ar-K-FastICA) algorithm, which integrates the traditional Kernel ICA method with arsinh-normalized preprocessing to enhance computational performance. While the kernel trick enables linear methods like ICA to operate within high-dimensional spaces, ensuring the inputs are normally distributed is critical for convergence, yet determining the optimal kernel for processing random signals remains challenging. This study addresses those difficulties, validating the methodology through simulations on both random signals and the MNIST dataset. The experimental outcomes indicate that m-ar-K-FastICA exhibits superior efficiency and stability compared to existing methodologies.

Social media generates an overwhelming volume of information daily, making it increasingly vital to verify the countless claims posted on platforms like Twitter to ensure data reliability. However, traditionally automated fact-checking methods are often costly regarding both processing time and computational resources, rendering them impractical for a real-time, real-world social media environment. TFCV operates by extracting relevant context for fact claims and utilizing an attention-based neural machine translation model to identify potential sentiment biases or inconsistencies. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a macro F1-score of 0.7202, outperforming six existing baseline approaches.

By viewing adversarial training within Bayesian learning principles, we introduce a principled framework for certifying Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) against worst-case threats. This approach renders the Bayesian training of a CNN against a specific attack scenario tractable through mean-field variational inference while offering explicit certificates of probabilistic robustness applicable to entire datasets or test sets. Our findings indicate by far that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art BNNs in robustness against L∞ norm bounded attacks and competitive adversimal ensembles. Additionally, we demonstrate that our framework offers attractive properties concerning the trade-off between robustness and posterior approximations, and underscores the potential of explicit robustness certificates as an alternative path for adversimal training. Code is available at https://github.com/andrewjwells/BNNAdversimalTraining.

Beginning in January 2020, the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic sparked widespread fear and online rumor-mongering globally, severely disrupting social stability. While numerous research efforts have examined the propagation mechanisms of these rumors during the crisis, their findings remain primarily theoretical rather than practical for practical management. To address this gap, this study presents an management-focused examination of online rumor diffusion under high uncertainty, utilizing an integrated approach that combines knowledge graph (KG) construction with a stochastic Shortest-Path-Longest-Path (SPLP) model. We propose a KG-enhanced Shortest-Path-Longest-Path (SKG) model that incorporates node attribute uncertainty to reduce reliance on high-density node data. Furthermore, we developed the Real-time SPLP with Knowledge Graph (RSKPLP) framework, which utilizes the SKG model to identify influential nodes for targeted intervention. Extensive experiments conducted on the rumor dataset concerning the "New Crown Virus Epidemic" demonstrate that the proposed RSKPLP method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, achieving notable improvements in both accuracy (increased by 11.31%) and efficiency (improvement of up to 99.00%).

This paper introduces a technique for classifying hyperspectral images through dimensionality reduction, addressing the substantial storage and computational inefficiencies of detailed spectral signatures. We propose utilizing Semi-Supervised Label Propagation coupled with Linear Discriminant Analysis to handle linearly correlated spectral bands and mitigate the curse of dimensionality. We evaluated four reduction methods: Principal Component Analysis, Linear Discriminant Analysis, Feature Selection, and this new SLSLP. Experiments conducted on public datasets using the SLSLP reduction method at various compression ratios demonstrate that even achieving a 99% data reduction impacts pixel classification accuracy only marginally. Furthermore, empirical results indicate our hierarchical linear discriminant learning approach outperforms standard Principal Component Analysis combined with Linear Discriminant Analysis.

Despite their overwhelming parameters, training time, and memory requirements, artificial neural networks (ANNs) often underutilize computational resources during standard use. This phenomenon has prompted researchers to investigate whether ANNs contain redundant components, leading to the emergence of the pruning methodology that progressively removes unnecessary layers or units to derive smaller, more efficient subnetworks. The pruning approach gained significant traction following the introduction of the lottery winner network (LWN) by Han et al., which offered an alternative to traditional optimization-based pruning by demonstrating an ANNs's inherent ability to function efficiently when sparsely activated. Specifically, the LWN identified a minimal set of active neurons that, when extracted and trained from scratch, yield test accuracy comparable to the full network. Building on this principle, we extend the methodology of random subnetwork identification to address computer vision tasks, specifically within convolutional neural networks (CNNs) utilized for image classification. Our results indicate that this principle generalizes effectively beyond natural language processing and image recognition domains, successfully enhancing the efficiency of both CNN architectures and ResNet models.
