We introduce a Bayesian deep learning framework designed for two weak-lensing tasks: estimating cluster masses and generating additive and residual multiplicative shear estimates. Using Bayesian networks, uncertainty quantification is integrated into these deep learning models. A quantification method derived from the posterior distribution of parameters enables the assessment of cluster mass uncertainty as well as the confidence intervals for shear measurements. The findings derived from Bayesian deep learning networks are contrasted with those from conventional ones; results indicate that these approaches yield consistent outcomes. Contrariwise, incorporating uncertainty into the modeling process produces more conservative estimates. The analysis further demonstrates that both Bayesian models and one of their specific implementations outperform their respective non-Bayean counterparts across two specific weak gravitational lensing areas.

A key insight from R. Sz\"uzke and refined by P. Varju serves as a cornerstone for addressing numerous questions and conjectures regarding additive combinatorics of sets defined by irrational rotations. Consequently, this paper introduces a generalized criterion extending their original work. Our main result establishes the existence of a $\delta > 0$ for certain $1$-bounded $1$-periodic continuous functions $f_\alpha(t)$ with $\delta$-even parity distribution in relation to specific $1$-dimensional sets $\{n\alpha\} + \beta$. This $\delta$ depends solely on the properties of $f_\alpha(t)$ and remains independent of the irrationality measure of $\alpha$. This finding unifies and generalizes several established results and conjectures in the field of combinatorial number theory related to irrationality measures of real numbers $1$ and $\alpha$. Furthermore, we provide a specific $1$-dimensional example of a $\delta > 0$ for any $1$-dimensional sequence generated using functions $g_\alpha(t)$ with $\delta$-even parity distribution, showing even distribution for sets defined using rotation angles $\alpha$. Finally, we prove that every $1$-dimensional sequence has $\delta$-even parity distribution for some $\delta > 0$ and specific $1$-dimensional sequence and rotation angles $\alpha$.

We demonstrate that local complete intersection $k$-rational singularities exhibit the $k$-Du Bois property, while for hypersurfaces, $k$-rationality is characterized through the minimal exponent. Additionally, we prove certain local vanishing theorems concerning these $k$-rational and $k$-Du Bois singularities; similar findings have been independently discovered in reference [FL2].

We present evidence indicating that weakly associated layers of Heisenberg spins can exhibit Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) behavior, provided that interlayer spin-spin correlations are sufficiently long-ranged. Our theoretical analysis examines the emergence of local BKT correlations within these weakly coupled layers, specifically addressing scenarios where classical dipolar interactions synergize with quantum zero-point spin fluctuations to enhance those correlations. To experimentally validate dipolar-coupled Heisenberg layers, we identify the candidate material Eu$_{0.99}$Mn$_{0.01}$F$_3$(DMSO) through its uniquely tunable dipolar interactions and quantum effects. Furthermore, we propose that such weakly coupled layers satisfy both BKT critical exponents and demonstrate universal amplitude ratios, confirming their adherence to BKT criticality.

This study establishes a near-optimal upper limit on the optimal stabilizer rank $\chi_m(T,d)$ for $d$-copy sums of the magic $|T\rangle$ state, demonstrating that this rank is $O(d^4\log d)$. This finding surpasses and improves previous thresholds. Additionally, the paper introduces novel super-resolved versions of the classical Naimark-completeness theorem that underpin its primary arguments.

This work examines the evolution of the $q$-coupling parameter within the extended $\Lambda$-matter cosmological model. We demonstrate that $q$-chromodynamics (QCD) conformal matter exhibits a critical density threshold $q\rho_{c}$; beyond this point, the $q$-branching becomes non-physical. Our findings indicate that $q\rho > q\rho_{c}$, implying the model's inability to represent a realistic universe. Furthermore, we analyze matter and dark energy branches, proposing an alternative explanation for the observed cosmic acceleration. We conclude that the accelerated expansion of the universe can be attributed to the dominance of the $q$-parameter in the very early epoch. Finally, we explore several astrophysical implications of extended $q$-QCD matter.

This paper introduces a new SRAM-based TRNG that overcomes the limitations of current TRNG designs, which typically suffer from slow generation speeds, large footprints, and poor power efficiency. The proposed architecture exploits the unique properties of SRAM single-event upsets to deliver both high sampling rates and space-efficient design, with location and size decoupled from generation rates to support customization. A TRNG utilizing a single 128-KB SRAM block can achieve 2.5 Mbps, occupying only 0.02 mm² on a 130-nm process. The randomness is verified through NIST statistical tests and entropy analysis across four different chips, while a fully implemented random number generator (RNG) is presented as the final contribution.

We introduce an all-optical method for characterizing and controlling resistive switching in molecular assemblies on atomically flat surfaces, a material system previously unexplored. This methodology offers a versatile framework that enables the examination of molecular electronics within a contemporary test environment. By employing this technique for developing new molecular electronic components, we achieved resistive switching behavior using assemblies of 1,2-diaminobenzene molecules that are less than 1 nm long and can be reliably produced via a scalable approach. These molecular arrays exhibit superior stability, reduced variability, and enhanced performance—specifically lower operating voltages, less variation in resistance changes, and faster switching speeds—compared to traditional blast-patterning methods. This demonstrates that the proposed optical characterization and manipulation strategy facilitates access to previously unattainable performance metrics by exploring molecular electronic states previously out of reach of traditional fabrication methods, allowing us to create improved molecular electronic devices. Specifically, we achieved stable low-resistance states using molecules arranged in linear chains shorter than 1 nm, arranged on atomically flat surfaces created by electrochemical lithography of gold electrodes. This work establishes a foundation for further exploration into molecular electronics and nanoscale resistive switching phenomena using this new all-optical characterization and control technique.

Loop-Tree Dual (LTD) serves as an innovative and exceptional framework compared to traditional approaches for calculating multi-loop scattering amplitudes numerically. It has proven particularly advantageous in scenarios lacking real singularities within momentum space, a condition often met by employing momentum dual forms that exhibit significant enhancements through jet reconstruction techniques. This discussion utilizes LTD as a vehicle for addressing fundamental issues inherent to general momentum-space representation forms that do not adhere to Lorentz invariant structures, a characteristic feature present in various momentum dual variants.

This paper presents eigenfunction expansion formulas for 1D 2-state quantum walks where the connection probabilities are not constant, demonstrating a result that achieves optimal precision, as verified through comparisons with known results for the constant connection probability case.
It is worth mentioning that the result is sharp of precision, as shown by the fact that it has already been comparable to previous results on the case where the connection probabilities are not constant.

This study examines the internal structure of hybrid stars comprising hadronic matter (modeled using the relativistic density-dependent quark-meson model), gaseous quark matter (described by the three-flavor quark matter model), and potential exotic SU(2) quark condensates within a two-flavor context. We determine key properties for these constituent phases to construct corresponding equation-of-state (e-o-s) scenarios for the three star types: hybrid stars. To validate the model's realism, the maximum mass of the hybrid star is constrained to $M_{\rm max}=2.16 M_{\sun}$ to align with the observational data of the pulsar PSR J0740+6620 ($M_{\rm obs}\approx 2.07\pm 0.1\ M_{\sun}$), implying the pulsar exists below this upper limit. Additionally, the radius for a one-solar-mass configuration is restricted to $R\le 12.5\ \rm km$, ensuring compatibility with NICER measurements for PSR J0030+0450 ($R=14.36\ \rm km$). This study explores the properties of a bosonic ladder operator and a fermionic operator under $q$-deformation, applying these concepts to $q$-deformed optomechanical models comprising $N$ undeformed optical modes coupled to a deformed mechanical resonator, as well as $N$ paired fermion-mechanical modes involving a single deformed bosonic occupation mode. Our analysis reveals that $q$-deformation influences the magnitude of zero-point motion in the ground state and alters phase transitions in the thermodynamic regime by shifting critical thresholds for quantum-phasic transitions to super-radiance. Specifically, increasing the $q$-parameter enhances the critical photon number while reducing the critical mechanical ground state $q$-deformed occupation. Finally, we present graphical representations of wave functions and $q$-deformed partition functions to further illustrate these findings.

This study investigates classical two-rotor systems characterized by an R-negative scissors state using a two-theory approach. Initially employing a simple model with harmonic coupling, the analysis identifies only one excited state corresponding to R-negative scissors states, characterized by relative rotational motion, while excluding relative vibrational motion. Subsequently, applying a more complex anharmonic coupling model allows for decoupling rotational and vibrational modes via parameter tuning, resulting in two distinct R-negative scissors states that exhibit a mixed rotational-vibrational character. Overall, anharmonicity in coupling is shown to be essential for the existence of such mixed states in classical frameworks. Finally, the classical findings anagrammatically and align well with key features of corresponding quantum mechanical solutions.

Metallic transition-metal oxides typically become insulating when condensed into extremely thin films, a behavior opposite to what is observed in semiconductor transition-metal oxides, which often exhibit enhanced insulating properties at reduced dimensions. This inverse trend, where thin films remain conductive, arises specifically when there is an insufficient number of electrons to completely fill the thin-dimensional band gap. Consequently, this phenomenon serves as a reliable indicator of altered electronic and bonding structures within confined geometries. In this study, we examine Ag-doped La$_2$CuO$_4$ (Ag-LCO) using first-principles calculations to determine the critical Ag-doping level ($x_c$) required to maintain metallic conductivity in both bulk and thin-film forms. Our analysis reveals that the thin-dimensional band gap within Ag-LCO is exceptionally narrow. Furthermore, we evaluate the stability of the metallic state in these systems by conducting finite-temperature simulations of entropy.

This study investigates how the viscosity of fluids influences the characteristic exponent governing the transition from normal to anomalous diffusion within single particles traversing their boundary. Our results indicate that the connection between these diffusion characteristics and the underlying two-dimensional geometry is surprisingly straightforward and may be predicted using solely the conservative energy of the system's viscous fluid. Furthermore, by establishing this conservative link, our relationship clarifies and unifies previously proposed models of anomalous diffusion arising from both viscous and non-viscous scenarios.

This study examines the topology of cryptocurrency transactions, with a particular focus on stability, by analyzing 11 major blockchains and over 50 corresponding network realizations. The research highlights that these networks are not merely random; rather, they exhibit significant high-order statistical dependencies, suggesting that certain cryptocurrencies function as stability anchors. By testing two competing methodologies for inferring transaction dependency graphs, we demonstrate that these dependency structures exist consistently across all analyzed chains, implying a mode of operation akin to the payment finality found in traditional financial networks. Consequently, the paper argues that the transaction topologies of these major blockchain systems should serve as the basis for evaluating risk and exploring efficient stability maintenance strategies.

This study examines the statistical relationships among cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) concentrations, supersaturation levels, and droplet sizes within cloud droplet size distributions (CDSDs) and cloud optical thickness (COT). Utilizing a high-resolution 3D cloud model, we simulated wintertime stratocumulus clouds and analyzed the resulting CDSD, COT, and CDT data. Our findings indicate a strong statistical correlation exists between COT and CCN counts, alongside a consistent statistical linkage between supersaturation and cloud droplet size. Notably, the statistical profiles of supersaturation relative to both CCN counts and cloud droplet size remain unaffected by COT. Given that supersaturation is statistically tied to CDSD size, this implies CCN counts and cloud droplet size are statistically interconnected through their shared influence on CDSD characteristics.

A pair consisting of a vector space along with a linear family of functionals is defined as "perceptual" when its space of norms-gauged elements via these operators becomes totally bounded in any topology induced. Our findings demonstrate that every perception pair admits a unique topological tangent space composed of scalars and exhibits an isomorphic relationship to a subspace within $C_{b}(G,\mathbb{K})$, where G is a specific non-empty Hausdorff hyperstonean space and the operators act on $\mathbb{K}$ as either the field $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{K}$ itself. Furthermore, it is proven that any linear subspace embedded in $C_{b}(G,\mathbb{R})$ or $C_{b}(G,\mathbb{R})$ can similarly be equipped to form perception pairs, with their representation space X also supporting appropriate topological and analytical structures.

In this study, we investigate the influence of temperature and Gravitational fields on transport of Transverse Energy in solids. We find that variations in the Gravitational potential induce Transverse Energy currents, findings that align with recent experimental observations involving hot solids within Earth's field. Our analysis suggests these flows stem from gradients in chemical potential driven by Gravitational effects. We further propose that analogous mechanisms underlie both the observed Gravitational flows and the Hall thermoelectric effect. Leveraging our models, we forecast the magnitude of Spinning Gravitational Zoë effect energies, offering designed strategies for verifying such Spinning Gravitational energy currents experimentally.

Simpler models are often favored over more complex ones, as their behavior is easier to understand and predict; consequently, researchers strive to train neural networks by imposing various constraints to enforce such simplicity. This work introduces the concept of "geometric simplicity," specifically defined as the minimal tube volume a curve can occupy while traversing a dataset's input-output representation space, and outlines a novel optimization approach to achieve this geometric simplicity. We demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of our methods on the "geocomp" deep learning modeling task across various simple architectural types, including convolutional, recurrent, and attention-based models, validated through experiments conducted on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 benchmarks.

Automated essay scoring stands as a pivotal and enduring challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Although transformer-based language models such as BERT and RoBERTa have achieved significant advancements in this domain, their substantial memory requirements restrict the training of large-scale ensembles. This study addresses that limitation by enhancing the built-in encoder within transformer models to facilitate the training of substantial ensembles at full scale. We evaluate this proposed encoder against current state-of-the-art approaches across two datasets: the English TED Talks dataset and the Chinese Huazhong University dataset, demonstrating improved performance with our method when applied to the TED Talks dataset.

We adopt the combinatorial perspective introduced by Paesani and Sullivant to examine toric and marginal independence models. By employing a specific construction via a linear coordinate transformation, we can convert certain marginal independence models into toric ones. We analyze the coordinate transformations associated with particular graph classes—specifically bipartite graphs and those equipped with a modular endomorphism—and demonstrate how these transformations give rise to graph polynomial models and cubic polynomial models within the resulting frameworks. Furthermore, we utilize the linear coordinate transformation underlying the Halpern-Lafforgue model to demonstrate that, in general, there exists no continuous bijective mapping from the parameter space of a graphical independence model to that of its corresponding marginal independence model. Consequently, this finding implies the absence of an encompassing general coordinate transformation capable of mapping all graphical independence models to their respective marginal counterparts without exception.

Chances for upward mobility through education are not uniform; they depend heavily on where individuals begin life. This study utilizes data from the Opportunity Youth Project to explore how the chance youth have of moving up socially is related to the share of higher education attendees within their specific town of residence. It examines the extent to which higher education acts as a general equalizer across different regions or functions more like an exclusive club reserved for the privileged. By analyzing these dynamics in the context of access to opportunity, it reveals patterns regarding whether higher education serves as an equalizer or exclusive club for opportunity youth. It reveals differing outcomes based on whether higher education acts as an equalizer or exclusive club for opportunity youth.

We demonstrate that if probabilistic or deterministic nearly logspace algorithms designed for undirected Laplacian matrices could be extended to handle slightly broader subclasses of linear systems, they would become sufficient for solving all linear systems under similar space constraints. This extends previous work by Kyng and Zhang in the time-agnostic context, which utilized reductions between approxsimal solvers; here, we show these same reduction steps can be executed via polynomial-size constant-depth threshold circuits.

This study details an analysis of the triple production of massive gauge bosons via proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, utilizing 39 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV data acquired by the ATLAS detector between 2015 and 2018. An anomalous triple gauge coupling framework guides the search strategy, which targets configurations involving two leptons and one jet, focusing on events where a Z boson decays into electron- or muon-pair. Within specific fiducial regions defined by the kinatics of this signal region, the study addresses both the isolated charged jet and off-shell W boson productions. Using data-driven techniques, substantial background suppression is achieved specifically for QCD multijet events. Consequently, the analysis reports compatible measurements with standard Model predictions for these specific processes. Furthermore, by employing a simplified mass spectrum model for an anomalous coupling scenario, limits are established on the magnitude of such effects, achieving a sensitivity corresponding to a 3$\sigma$ confidence level.

Hebrew NLP has progressed significantly over the last few years, building upon robust linguistic databases and machine learning techniques. Key tasks such as tokenization, POS tagging, constituency parsing, and semantic parsing have applied cutting-edge ML methods. This study presents the first application of neural network-based sequential and tree-structured neural network models to Hebrew for performing Hebrew Named Entity Recognition (HEBNER) and Hebrew Constituent Parsing (HCP). This study examines the generation of ground sound during rigid-body collisions, addressing a phenomenon underrepresented in current literature. While existing research often treats ground sound as negligible, our findings demonstrate that ground-generated sound can become perceptible when factors like surface compliance or impact velocity meet specific thresholds and must therefore be accounted for in scenarios resembling footstep production. This paper presents both an analytical model and a high-fidelity simulation framework designed to quantify ground sound in the context of rigid-body collisions. Additionally, we introduce a perceptibility metric to establish the conditions under which ground sound emerges and is audible. The proposed solutions were validated against a highly accurate full-waveform simulation model, confirming that the results align well with reality. The standard demonstration of quantum entanglement without invoking inequalities, exemplified by the "all-versus-nothing" proof of Bell nonlocality, bifurcates into two categories: the "always" variant and the "sometimes" variant. Prevailing research has predominantly concentrated on the "always" type, under the assumption that such proofs necessitate perfect correlations within at least one measurement context. Surprisingly, our investigation reveals by examining the context of quantum supersolidity—specifically conjoined solid and superfluid phases of quantum matter—that perfect correlations are not a prerequisite for an "always" type no-inequality proof of Bell's theorem or for establishing entanglement itself. By relaxing this dependency, we offer a refined proof of Bell's theorem and clarify the nature of Bell nonlocality in its most general form.

Flat bands characterize the energy landscapes of strongly correlated quantum many-body systems, a property that significantly suppresses the degree to which these bands exhibit itinerant behavior. Within this work, we provide an overview of the theoretical frameworks that explain the emergence of flat bands, paying particular attention to their consequences for magnetic ordering. We explore magnetic structures that can arise from itinerant electrons, contrast them with magnetic systems comprising a substantial magnetic moment, and investigate how orbital magnetism emerges via flat bands formed in the absence of half-filled states, a phenomenon exemplified by half-filled Landau levels and kagome lattice systems.

The C2v-symmetry hydrogen boride (borane) monolayer is proposed as a novel room-temperature superconductor, exhibiting zero in-plane resistivity and an anisotropic critical field. Its unique structural arrangement features a boron layer intercalated by hydrogen atoms, creating distinct electron-acceptor and donor layers that facilitate strong covalent bonding and pronounced anisotropic electronic behavior. First-principles calculations indicate that superconducting coupling arises from enhanced electron-acceptor donor interactions and elevated electron-acceptor donor overlap integrals. Notably, the material demonstrates high anisotropic electronic properties, including robust donor-acceptor overlap integrals. Furthermore, the robust donor-acceptor overlap integrals enable strong donor-acceptor overlap integrals. Additionally, the robust donor-acceptor overlap integrals facilitate efficient charge transfer. These factors collectively contribute to the emergence of superconductivity.

Research on flattened partitions was initially prompted by my inquiry into the sequence OEIS A124324, which enumerates these structures with distinct parts summing to $n$. This note extends the analysis to partitions where no two parts differ by exactly $k$.

This study investigates amenability within arithmetic groups, extending earlier concepts developed by Corcoran, Corrales, and others who linked group properties to dynamical behaviors like stiffness and flexibility regarding stationary measures, as well as shidong properties. By employing the corresponding definition for actions of arithmetic groups on their associated quotient spaces, this paper demonstrates that our extended stiffness framework aligns with, and thus implies, the condition identified by Corcoran, Corrales, and colleagues. Specifically, we prove that arithmetic subgroups of $SL_n(\mathbb{R})$ for $n \geq 3$ satisfy our stochastic stiffness criterion. Further, we establish a stochastic stiffness analogous to stiffness for groups involving direct products of free groups. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive account of our general theoretical framework, including a detailed definition of Schidong actions within the probabilistic context.

Fail-operational systems for highly autonomous driving must maintain operational capabilities despite the partial failure of any single component, typically achieving this goal through redundant architectures. Consequently, detecting failures within these redundant setups is critical; such capabilities are often assumed to be standard yet remain unquantified for most failure detection mechanisms. This study investigates several failure detection approaches in the context of highly automated driving and explicitly evaluates their degrees of redundancy. Empirical evaluations confirm that certain failure detection strategies do not inherently provide full redundancy and therefore cannot satisfy fail-operational requirements.

Extensive research has been conducted over several decades on clustering dynamic systems to extract meaningful groups characterized by similar trajectory patterns. Existing methodologies generally fall into two categories: those that adapt static clustering techniques designed for data points to execute on time-series or those that employ specialized dynamic methods. We argue that only approaches leveraging dynamic characteristics yield significant clusterings and present new unsupervised clustering techniques for time-series. Specifically, we extend the widely used self-organizing map to execute directly on data points and then adapt this formulation specifically for 1D time-series signals. Our method's temporal dynamic adaptation relies on the concept of effective centers, a generalization of static cluster centers that explicitly accounts for signal dynamics. We introduce a streamlined and efficient algorithm implementing these self-organizing principles directly on 1D time-series signals. We introduce the term "temporal clustering" to differentiate our approach from techniques applied to static points or other dynamic strategies. Empirical testing on both synthetic and real-world datasets, including the electroencephalogram signals and music audio clips, indicates that our algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

A sequence of vectors $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is termed *almost linearly independent* (almost LI) if there exists a basis $\mathbf{b}_1, \dots, \mathbf{b}_d$ such that each $\mathbf{x}_k$ is arbitrarily close to some $\mathbf{b}_j$. We establish that if a sequence $\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is ordered and grows quickly enough to be $R$-regular, then it is almost LI provided that $n \ge (1+\epsilon)d$ for any $\epsilon > 0$, given sufficiently large $R$. Furthermore, we introduce a notion of "bipartite almost LI" and demonstrate that ordered vertex sequences growing rapidly on the 2-dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^2$ can form an ordered pair sequence that is bipartite almost LI on $\mathbb{T}^4$ despite failing to be fully almost LI on $\mathbb{T}^4$.

This study introduces a novel deep learning framework for recommender systems, designed to enhance prediction accuracy by leveraging user-item interactions to establish effective user profiles and interests. To tackle data sparsity, we incorporate knowledge graph information to fill critical gaps. Our proposed interest propagation mechanism utilizes candidates from the knowledge graph to mitigate limitations inherent in traditional approaches. This framework, named PIRK (Propagation of Interest from Relations in Knowledge graphs for recommendation), features users and items as core elements along with their relationships within the graph structure. By integrating element embeddings with relational propagation, the model refines user interest representations and strengthens user profiles through this process. Furthermore, we refine the final recommendation list via an interest retrieval step grounded in the learned profiles and relational interests. To validate our approach, we conducted comprehensive experiments on two large-scale datasets: Alibaba's e-commerce interaction data and Amazon's product knowledge graph. Our findings demonstrate a notable improvement in accuracy, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods by approximately 3%.

This study investigates asymptotic freeness among subalgebras and freely generating variables within a family of random matrices. Our methodology builds upon the concept of multilinear forms for operator-free probability, which facilitates the analysis of joint distribution shifts when variables merge with those of different algebras.

This paper examines the monitoring of real-time systems for properties formulated as Metric Interval Temporal Logic (MITL). To address monitoring, we reduce the problem to a satisfaction check involving an augmented Region-Dividided-Automata (RDA), which combines the product of an MITL product automaton and the region automaton associated with timed regions. We evaluate monitoring efficiency by analyzing the computational complexity inherent to this mitigation and introduce a practical, executable prototype to validate our findings.

This study examines potential causes of isospin breaking during meson-meson transitions, focusing on two meson species that are nearly degenerate in mass but differ in isospin. We demonstrate that quantum chromodynamics (QCD) contributions arise solely from quark mass differences, whereas electroweak effects stem exclusively from electromagnetic penguin operators. In contrast to previous research, our findings regarding the relative magnitude of these sources are quantitatively consistent with existing literature. Furthermore, our analysis of meson pairs involving the $f_0(980)$ and the $a_0(980)$ identifies significant isospin breaking effects, suggesting a possible influence on their exceptional narrow widths.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera fulfills four optical functions within the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) of ESO: guiding each of the four telescopes via a "pick-up" system, performing on-acquisition guide star selection, and providing image acquisition for astrometry and relative source positioning. As an active element of the VLTI and EXPRess Interferometer for Images (EXI) project, it relies heavily on specific design and performance specifications to meet these diverse observational needs. This paper outlines the optical design principles and results, specifically the analysis of the three lens elements and their corresponding glass materials, along with an evaluation of field of view and pixel scale characteristics. Furthermore, it includes a analysis of linearity and includes simulation results for linearity and point spread function (PSF) to ensure operational precision.

This paper introduces a model featuring a massive fermion subject to a time-dependent $U(1)$ background and two interacting bosons that possess interaction terms governed by a parameter $\alpha$. We demonstrate that this system facilitates photon emissions in pairs. Parity symmetry ensures these parity-checks remain paired, while time-reversal symmetry accounts for the energy conservation of these photon pairs. Moreover, because the coupling is non-Abelian in this model, it provides valuable insights into superradiance effects involving dual photons.

We introduce a analytical framework for the equation of state (EOS) valid for pure alkali metals across a broad spectrum of compressive and expansive pressures extending up to megabar regimes. By introducing two empirical parameters—one governing density behavior under zero pressure and a universal compressibility factor shared among all alkali metals—we establish an equation of state across an expansive pressure spectrum. This proposed model accurately reproduces experimental data and existing high-pressure results for lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, and cesium, further aligning with density functional theory calculations within the random phase approximation. Furthermore, we examine significant thermodynamic derivatives and properties for these metals; our predictions for compressibility factors and specific heat capacities across densities from zero to approximately 3 times normal density closely match literature values and theoretical calculations. This study presents a simplified, efficient method for generating an analytical EOS for pure alkali metals that achieves high precision and extensive applicability.

This work investigates the mass spectrum of light vector mesons under conditions of non-equilibrium quark matter characterized by a chiral imbalance ($\mu_5$). employing the Quark Meson Meson (QMM) model, where interactions between vector and axial-vector mesons arise from their common coupling to scalar ($\sigma$), pseudoscalar ($\pi$), and pseudoscalar ($\omega$) components of the meson fields, along with their respective interactions. A crucial innovation of our methodology is incorporating a time-dependent information for the condensates within our quantum thermodynamic framework, allowing us to analyze how such dynamics influence vector and axial-vector mass spectra. Following the identification of equilibrium solutions for condensates, we examine the mass spectrum of vector and to axial-vector mesons as functions of temperature and $\mu_5$. Our findings indicate that increasing the dynamical influence of $\mu_5$ results in a convergence of vector and to axial-vector mass spectra. Consequently, the mass difference between these states diminishes at higher values of$\mu_5$, suggesting a potential restoration of chiral symmetry. This research offers significant insights into the exotic phase of quark matter present in neutron stars and other compact objects.

This study addresses the distributed card counting problem within a graph-structured setting, where each participant holds a private integer between 0 and $m$, with the goal of collaboratively determining the count of non-Byzantine nodes possessing a value less than the threshold $m$. We propose an algorithm capable of resolving this issue in synchronous environments despite the presence of adversarial actors. It achieves both correctness—guaranteeing every honest participant converges to the true count—and privacy (ensuring honest agents cannot deduce the $m$-values of other honest participants). Notably, the method endures up to $\min\{\frac{n}{3}, \frac{2}{3}n - \frac{m(n-m+1)}{2m}\}$ manipulative nodes. Assuming a common randomness prior to execution, the algorithm further delivers $O(\log(n/\delta))$-bit error independence against any distribution of corruption strategies such that no single coalition of $f$ nodes shares a consistent false narrative ($1-\delta$ success probability). Additionally, we establish a matching lower bound for achieving correctness combined with $(f+1)$-out-of-$\delta$ security properties under such constraints.

Numerical relativity simulations requiring precise solutions to the Hamiltonian constraint with non-trivial matter configurations are frequently approximated using pseudo-spectral methods. While these approaches are efficient, they demand that the initial data be smooth enough to avoid aliasing artifacts. This study presents an innovative approach utilizing the Chebyshev spectral differential operator to solve the Hamiltonian constraint. This novel method utilizes multi-resolution finite-difference grids for the matter configuration and employs the Chebyshev spectral operator for solving the constraint equations. We demonstrate using grid-convergence tests and comparisons with previous pseudo-spectral spectral methods that this hybrid technique achieves high accuracy and is suitable for use in numerical simulations. Furthermore, we show that this method can be used to solve the Einstein constraint equations with success.

Long sequence time-series forecasting plays a critical role across various sectors, including supply chain management, weather prediction, and health monitoring. Despite the significant volume of research dedicated to this task, current methods often struggle with accuracy due to their reliance on recurrent or convolutional architectures, which fail to effectively capture long-term temporal dependencies. This study introduces a new deep learning model, TFLA-LSTM, for long-term forecasting. It combines the strengths of Transformer networks and LSTM models to address the limitations of existing approaches. Specifically, it utilizes the Transformer architecture for global temporal feature extraction through self-attention mechanisms and employs an LSTM-based local differential attention mechanism for sequential forecasting. Experimental results confirm that this method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across 10 long-term forecasting benchmarks.

This paper details the design, fabrication, and assessment of an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector (ADC), a compact optical device engineered to mitigate atmospheric dispersion effects for compact telescopes. The ADC functions as a prism-pair assembly that refracts light through a variable angle to compensate for wavelength-dependent atmospheric distortion. Because the refractive indices of prism materials differ across the electromagnetic spectrum, these instruments generally provide precise correction only for a specific target wavelength; however, the solution proposed in this study involves optimizing a dual-prism configuration to significantly extend the effective bandwidth of the ADC. The refractive indices and dispersion coefficients for all prism components were obtained via spectroscopic measurements. The resulting ADC demonstrates effective correction across a broad spectrum of visible light. The instrument was further validated through comparative spectroscopy of Rigel ($\alpha$ Ori) at two distinct airmasses, demonstrating its utility in high-fidelity wide-field imaging and spectroscopy for amateur observatories.

Ultralight bosonic dark matter (UBDM) theoretically predicts oscillations in its wavefunction with an energy proportional to $\cos(m\phi t)$, where $m$ is the mass. These fluctuations induce tiny shifts in the masses and coupling constants of standard model (SM) particles, acting as an oscillating background that can be measured using quantum sensors to monitor correlations between different signals. Since the relative frequency between the mass shifts and the induced frequency differences falls within the near-zero-frequency regime, this range is uniquely suited to detect ultralight masses situated at extremely low values ($\sim 10^{-22}$ eV). Consequently, measuring these ultra-slow-frequency signatures allows experiments to probe the occupation numbers of the bosonic dark matter fields interacting with SM particles, thereby offering superior sensitivity under certain conditions compared to traditional methods that look for resonances at higher frequencies.

We examine various characteristics essential to packet processing—包括 parsing actions, forwarding logic, queuing mechanisms, and both single- and multi-table pipeline structures—and derive static properties tailored to each, leveraging characterizations of parsing, action applications, and packet classification to ensure reliable performance.

The significant ethical challenges of deep learning, including its potential for bias and threats to privacy, have prompted a surge in recent literature addressing these issues. Notable interventions range from regulatory frameworks to design patterns, all aimed at ensuring the private and fair utilization of these technologies. The authors describe a systematic review strategy designed to compile and analyze existing studies on the intersection of deep learning, its ethical implications, and privacy matters.

Analysis of $pp$ collision data, totaling $39\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ and collected by LHCb at center-of-mass energies ranging from $\sqrt{s} = 7$ to $\sqrt{s} = 13\,\mathrm{TeV}$, reveals an observed excess in the spectrum of oppositely charged B-meson pairs ($B^+\bar{B}$) within the invariant mass region corresponding to the $B_c^+$. This indicates the presence of an excited $B_c^+$ state, denoted as $B_c^{*+}$. The reported signal significance is 3.9$\sigma$, with a reconstructed mass of $M = 6.330 \pm 0.004\,(\mathrm{stat}) \pm 0.006\,(\mathrm{syst}) \pm 0.002\,(\mathrm{theory})$ GeV.

Recent advances in efficiently solving Hamiltonian numerics resulted in introducing a family energy-conserving Runge-Kutta techniques called Hamiltonians Runge-Kutta Boundary-Integral Methods. This new method class has interesting properties related to continuous-stage Runge-Kutta techniques that were revisited here for a broader range of general derivatives problems.

We introduce an unsupervised method for neural network weight visualization that extends Saliency Map techniques to visualize input feature trajectories throughout the network. This approach utilizes end-toend gradient computation relative to feature maps and local critic networks designed to evaluate the significance of specific layer group states toward the final output. By maximizing the contribution of each layer group, our method calculates attributes crucial at that intermediate stage. The proposed feature importance metric is then aggregated across all layers to produce a comprehensive feature trajectory for a given input. Ultimately, this input-specific visualization input can be averaged over a dataset to identify which features are most critical for classification. When applied to visual inputs, the input's feature representation evolution is clearly depicted.

This study examines open Hamiltonian dynamics within a 3D system, focusing on the Metropolis rollup algorithm applied to basin boundaries. Our analysis reveals that initial boundaries lacking the Wada property become non-Wadarsis when subjected to mild dissipative effects. Conversely, initial Wada partitions evolve into non-Wada structures under similar dissipative influences. Consequently, boundary geometry characteristics—specifically the presence or absence of the Wada property—are not intrinsic but depend on the system's dissipative context in such dynamical flows. Our findings suggest a mechanism whereby dissipative forces can suppress fractal boundary features and facilitate the stabilization of coherent structures in three-dimensional turbulent flows. Our approach offers a new, physically based perspective on fractal boundaries and their potential role in the dissipipating dynamics of three-dimensional turbulent flows.

Specifically, it enables extensive lifetimes and propagation distances for $\nu_R$ and Higgs bosons ($X$ decay into SM particles) even though they were produced in collisions at $e^+e^-$ and $pp$ accelerators respectively under conditions where their masses are relatively small. Recognizing human activities in unstructured video remains a pivotal challenge in computer vision. This paper introduces a new Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) model that efficiently captures the intrinsic temporal patterns specific to video, particularly the hierarchical nature of those structures, to benefit from more accurate action classification. To achieve this hierarchical focus, we integrate a bi-directional Long Short Term Network (LSTM) with two specialized layers: Hierarchical Attention and Temporal Segmental Pooling. Furthermore, to address data scarcity issues, we implemented a new technique called synthetic voice activity detection for improving HAN's robustness on speech action recognition. Our method is evaluated on two public benchmarks: UMD Action with Audio and a newly created UMN Action dataset.

The dynamics of the non-extremal Reissner-Nordström–Anti-de Sitter black hole demonstrate the presence of a critical threshold separating the formation of naked singularities from black hole creation. Across the entire parameter space, a critical radius exists; when the horizon radius exceeds this critical value, the final black hole remains stable and non-extremal. However, scalar perturbations applied during the black hole formation process can either extend the black hole's lifetime or cause a transition to an extremal state, depending on whether the scalar charge is positive or negative, respectively. While an upper bound determines the maximum allowable scalar charge to reach the extremal limit, no corresponding lower bound restricts how quickly an extremal black hole can form under these conditions.

This piece provides a brief overview of the principles surrounding star formation and its evolution based on observational evidence, showing that it is particularly meaningful in this light as the creation of planets is simply a side effect of stellar processes. Consequently, the entire inquiry regarding life throughout the universe and its origins can be approached from an innovative standpoint.

We introduce two novel techniques for determining the parameters of a multivariate Gaussian distribution. The first method employs Shannon entropy on the probability density function, yielding a unique set of variables through its solution. Our second method utilizes mutual information between specific components; here, calculating entropy from the resulting marginal distributions yields a non-linear system of equations with unique solutions. These solutions are expressed via closed-form equations and are verified as correct. Furthermore, our findings are extended to the multivariate probability box framework.

We introduce a new mathematical framework for modeling semiconductor manufacturing systems, utilizing a system of hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) coupled with ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Unlike prior approaches that rely on constant flux—which fails when velocity is discontinuous—our proposed approach employs conservation laws compatible with velocity discontinuities. These velocity variations result from fluctuations in upstream arrival times and fluctuations in speed caused by changes in wafer thickness during the deposition phase. To handle this, our model assumes deposition velocity depends inversely on the current wafer thickness. We prove the existence and provide a numerically constructible solution for this problem, establishing the uniqueness of solutions within a specific unit interval by analyzing the associated initial-value ODE. Finally, our work demonstrates how to solve the related WKB problem by applying our established ODE solution method.

Animals move for various purposes including foraging, escaping predators, and reproduction. Understanding the mechanisms and controls behind animal locomotion is vital for gaining insights into both biological movement and its applications for robotics. This paper reviews recent research on fish swimming and aerial vehicle flight by examining the principles of swimming and flying. It begins with a general overview of fluid dynamics as they apply to both media, then analyzes the specific aerodynamics and hydrodynamics relevant to flight and swimming. The document explores the mechanics, control strategies, and experimental outcomes concerning swimming and flying organisms before concluding with implications for robotics and further directions for research into animal motion.

Optimizing excess electricity stands as a critical function within transmission power grids. This paper details an approach to resolve the resulting multi-objective optimization problem, specifically tailored for surplus electricity in Japan's network. We introduce two complementary methods: an epsilon-based technique for generating Pareto-optimal solutions and a randomized search tactic for identifying discrete, representative points across the objective function's landscape. Field-testing our optimization framework against actual grid data from verification runs demonstrates both the Pareto optimal front's geometry and the proposed scheme's computational efficacy.

Machine learning and AI techniques offer a range of methods for extracting physical laws from data, but these approaches face significant challenges. These methods struggle to distinguish between underlying universal principles and noise or artifacts from specific experimental setups, as they typically analyze surface-level measurement data without access to the raw underlying information. Consequently, current ML/AI algorithms are ill-equipped to separate universal laws from measurement artifacts. This paper proposes a foundational step toward overcoming that limitation: formulating these laws implicitly through constraint optimization. We demonstrate the power of this approach using Newton's law of universal gravitation, showing how it can be derived from both noisy synthetic data and real-world measurements involving planetary and stellar motion.

This work details a search conducted by the ATLAS detector at the LHC for hypothetical heavy, electrically charged particles with extended lifetimes. The analysis examines these potential new particles based on a unique signature consisting of energy deposits in the hadronic calorizer combined with no tracks or hits found in the silicon tracker's inner layers. Conducted using proton-proton collision data collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 36.1 fb$^{-1}$, the study reveals no evidence suggesting these massive charged long-lived particles exist. Consequently, upper limits for their production cross-section were calculated at the 95% confidence level, showing no discrepancy with theoretical predictions, as these particles do not currently appear in the Standard Model. Furthermore, constraints on various decay mechanisms were established: these limits significantly surpass previous sensitivity achieved by the D0 andCDF experiments regarding similar charged long-lived particle signatures, and they align well with existing constraints derived from other ATLAS analyses that utilize different topologies.

This study introduces a practical approach for generating photons on demand, achieving nearly unity indistinguishability and a high Purcell factor of 73 via coupling colloidal quantum dots in a microfluidic chip to a ring resonator. Inelastic neutron scattering (INS) offers a method to characterize glass structure by measuring the vibrational density of states (VDOS) around the region known as the boson peak. The growing application of optimization methods highlights a persistent challenge: existing algorithms typically locate only one or a few high-performing solutions, whereas many practical scenarios demand a diverse range of competent agents that excel in different capabilities. The concept of Matching with Three Partners extends the classic Stable Roommates problem by facilitating pairwise matching among individuals within groups of two, leaving one person unmatched. This study investigates how various static strains influence valley Hall responses in two-dimensional materials. In software system development, modifying a component can inadvertently cause existing parts to malfunction, leading the system into an inconsistent state. We propose a deep learning framework designed for this purpose; however, prior work indicates that long-term EHR data often fails to yield satisfactory performance. We conducted a retrospective study on 202 patients exhibiting high suicide risk, who provided both their medical records and weekly EMA assessments over a 30-month period. Our analysis reveals that incorporating EMA significantly enhances predictive capability, particularly when combined with clinical data, whereas utilizing EMA alone yields limited efficacy. Specifically, our models leveraging the fusion of patient EMA and clinician data demonstrated AUC improvements of 0.127 to 0.177 compared to those using only clinician data. These findings suggest that our EMA-integrated deep learning approach effectively harnesses the complementary strengths of both data sources, offering a robust method for predicting suicidal ideation.

Three-dimensional topological insulators (TIs) are defined by a quantized magnetoelectric coefficient, yet this linear coupling between electric fields and magnetization is suppressed by topological surface states that enforce time-reversal symmetry. We introduce and experimentally validate a novel non-linear magnetoelectric effect in 3D topological insulators, derived from the cross-product of an applied electric field and magnetic field to generate a magnetic polarization density. This non-linear interaction is uniquely allowed at the surface due to the coexistence of bulk topology and gapless states, providing a robust signature of the modified Maxwell equations in the topological regime where time-reversal symmetry holds. Crucially, this non-linear effect is not merely a bulk manifestation of the quantum Hall effect induced by field-induced time-reversal symmetry breaking, as it persists even when the bulk response remains diamagnetic. We further demonstrate that this phenomenon serves as a powerful probe for surface physics, effectively revealing the presence, orientation, and topological protection of TI surface gap states.

We investigate a standard category involving delayed nonlinear systems, which demonstrate chaotic diffusion. Results indicate that periodically varying the system's time-lag can amplify the constant force acting upon it, triggering chaotic motion even when the intrinsic delay is minimal. Numerical simulations point to potential applications in control systems and propose a novel mechanism for generating oscillations in timing circuits.

**Paraphrase:** We introduce various structural semantic frameworks for process-like entities employing coinductive definitions. Our primary findings include an adequacy theorem that links all formal models—based on both operational and structural methodologies—to denotational semantics, along with limits for these formal definitions in the context of contextual and observational equivalences. Our approach utilizes coalgebraic processes, where entities like processes, functions, and abstract streams are represented as streams and defined via coalgebraic structures. Specifically, functions and streams correspond to weak streams (infinite lists of integers), while processes are defined as subsets of this category, equipped with additional properties. By applying coalgebraic properties, our approach provides unified proofs that simplify the demonstration of standard results such as compositional semantics, equivalences, and optimization rules.

While program analysis has long focused on reverse-engineering existing systems, program synthesis is increasingly taking a similar trajectory by looking forward. Design mining represents a specialized form of synthesis where artifacts are generated to enforce a specific architectural design within a codebase. In this work, we introduce a general approach combining abstract interpretation and constraint solving for design mining. By abstracting away implementation details, this method extracts crucial aspects necessary for constructing programs that integrate cohesive elements into the target system without replacing its existing code. We examine various design enforcement scenarios, including refactoring challenges and creating custom interpreters. In doing so, we identify and resolve limitations related to analysis precision, synthetic tool versatility, and the practical viability of generated outputs. Through workflows mirroring actual engineering processes and evaluating against real-world datasets, we demonstrate the approach's potential.

Proximity algorithms are effective at revealing hidden substructures in nonsmooth optimization tasks, and in many cases, extracting these structures via the proximity operator holds independent significance. We introduce and investigate the concept of "dual structures," analogous to widely used primal structures, and provide sufficient conditions guaranteeing that dual structures emerge from proximal algorithms when applied to composite objectives composed of two parts: a genuinely smooth dual component and a truly structured dual norm that is conditionally imposed. Specifically, near-optimal objectives yield dual structures that are permutations of conditionally structured vectors containing smooth variability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these associated dual structures can be pinpointed through Sylvester rank-sign patterns of Hessians related to the proximity mapping. These insights yield streamlined, accelerated methods for solving convex problems that enforce sparsity-specific constraints.

This study explores a property of commutative rings with unity named the "weakly 1-absorbing prime" and its associated characteristics. Initially, a novel condition is provided to identify such ideals. Subsequently, the paper examines the behavior of these ideals concerning weakly prime multiplicative sets and valuations, alongside presenting several examples and theoretical results regarding their distribution and distribution.

This study introduces an on-device machine learning approach for integral image spectral unmixing, enabling real-world photonic sensing. By leveraging photonic components traditionally used in spectroscopy but adapted for minimalization through image processing techniques within an image sensor, we achieve a 1000-fold reduction in size compared to standard spectrometers. These photonic devices, though smaller, capture light intensity data across a range of wavelengths, producing "hyperspectral images" that facilitate the distinction of various chemicals across specific areas. To handle the resulting large datasets from intense calculations on individual devices, we implemented a decentralized learning strategy that trains machine models independently and transfers knowledge to a central system to refine accuracy. This approach eliminates the need for a large centralized database, allowing the system to process information locally. Ultimately, we created a chemical identification system using a machine learning model to distinguish ten distinct chemicals across a 10x10 grid on 10x10 surface unit cells using only 100 data points per test instance. This system, trained using a combination of synthetic and real-world data, was able to accurately identify ten test chemicals with 99.9% precision.

Lately, various machine learning models addressing tasks such as polypharmacy adverse effect recognition, predicting drug interactions, and planning combination treatments have been developed. In this work, we offer a cohesive theoretical perspective on relational machine learning models capable of managing these specific objectives. Furthermore, we define key concepts, contrast prevailing architectures, evaluate strengths and limitations, and suggest promising avenues for future research.

This paper introduces the 2022 Road Damage Evaluation Challenge. Motivated by the growing application of computer vision for quality road inspection, our challenge seeks to assess the current capabilities of this technology. Participants receive low-resolution images captured from vehicles during routine municipal maintenance trips and must classify road defects into categories while specifying their locations. The 2022 section of the challenge focuses exclusively on two tasks: cracking detection and pothole identification. We provide detailed problem descriptions, establish public training and validation datasets, and offer a baseline using the Least Cost Path approach. Participant submissions were compared against ground truth annotations via F1-Score metrics; we granted three grand prize teams per task and recognized ten top solutions for each track. The study concludes with an analysis pertaining to the challenges, prominent patterns in the generated images and patches, and methods employed by the leading solutions.

Imitation learning has become a prominent approach for training reinforcement learning agents, particularly because crafting effective reward functions for intricate environments is often challenging. Despite this, the sample efficiency of imitative learning typically falls short of that of standard reinforcement learning. A primary reason for this discrepancy is that agents trained via imitation may converge to suboptimal behaviors that do not yield maximal cumulative rewards unless a carefully engineered, custom-final reward allows for proper optimization. This paper introduces a novel strategy that enhances both demonstration quality and learning outcomes by integrating a reinforcement learning component into the imitation learning workflow. Our method begins with demonstrating how to identify an optimal perturbation to maximize the policy's expected immediate reward, thereby refining the demonstration policy. Subsequently, it refines this approach to optimize demonstrations within short horizons by aggregating immediate benefits. Finally, by incorporating these optimized demonstrations into the behavior policy, the method generates superior performance. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that this framework significantly boosts the quality of demonstrations and yields significant gains in return metrics for policy learning.

A significant concentration of magnetic fields is presumed to have existed in the early universe, potentially playing a critical role in the large-scale structure of matter. However, due to current observational constraints, it remains difficult to determine exactly when this magnetic field was last amplified. We propose a new theoretical framework to estimate the last amplification stage, focusing specifically on how it impacts the rate of early protostar formation within secondary gas clouds. Additionally, we investigate the potential connection between the timing of this final amplification and current observational limits, exploring its implications regarding the relationship between the Universe's large-scale magnetic fields and local ones found within our own Milky Way.

Association rules constitute a fundamental concept in data mining, frequently employed to reveal significant correlations among variables within large datasets. A rule is generally expressed as $X \Rightarrow Y$, where both $X$ and $Y$ represent collections of items; such a rule signifies that the presence of $X$ elevates the likelihood of $Y$. Standard association rule learning seeks to uncover all viable relationships by defining minimum thresholds for confidence and support, thereby generating an vast number of rules that can overwhelm users. While numerous methodologies have emerged to constrain results for specific analytical goals—such as maximizing confidence, minimizing confidence denominator values, or limiting the cardinality of item sets—these existing filters often yield outputs that are redundant or logically trivial. This research introduces a novel filtering criterion designed to generate rule candidates that are both diverse and non-obvious by targetting maximal variety in associations that maintain a uniform level of confidence, rather than simply maximizing it.

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately experience mental health disorders. To evaluate whether addressing these conditions reduces recidivism, this study utilizes difference-in-differences analysis alongside population-level administrative data from Florida probationers. Drawing on data from 1998 to 2011 and a cohort of nearly 50,000 offenders, the research compares recidism rates between those ordered to participate in probation mental health clinics versus those serving standard probation. Furthermore, by integrating a registry of clinic participants, the analysis examines recidism outcomes across varying durations of clinic attendance. The findings reveal that access to mental health clinics significantly lowers the probability ofre-offending within one year among property crime offenders, particularly for those with extensive prior contacts to the criminal justice system. Additionally, sustained attendance proves more beneficial than brief participation. Consequently, expanding access to mental health clinics shows promise as a cost-effective strategy within the broader criminal justice framework.

This research introduces parameterized variations of generalized Apostol–Bernoulli polynomials alongside their corresponding generating functions, examines various properties and relationships within these polynomials, and establishes connections with additional special polynomial families.

Radio maps are essential for situational awareness in next-generation wireless communications, including UAVs, by providing spatial information about channel parameters and the radio environment. While existing research suggests their utility, no comprehensive solution has yet been implemented for actual generation and subsequent use. Addressing this gap, this paper introduces a complete framework for radio map generation and consumption, focusing on non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) systems. The work evaluates LOCATION-based interference (spatial) noise maps, which track interference variability per user, demonstrating their potential to inform intelligent NOMA user scheduling. Results indicate a significant reduction in NOMA scheduling complexity and an improvement in resource allocation efficiency. Furthermore, a novel scheduling strategy is proposed that leverages these radio maps to enhance network performance.

This article introduces HMM4Time, a novel advanced framework for detecting anomalies in multivariate time series data. By leveraging Hidden Markov Models, the system identifies significant deviations by analyzing transitions between hidden states and residual errors. Designed to be highly adaptable, it accommodates diverse characteristics of time series data, including periodicity, seasonality, and various trend patterns. Since installing detection rules directly is often challenging due to the indirect nature of state-based outputs, a specialized method has been developed to translate these constraints into viable anomaly detection protocols. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through comprehensive case studies and numerical simulations, validating its effectiveness. Additionally, we outline specific considerations for applying this method across different types of time series environments.

This study introduces a novel trimodal person verification framework combining visible light images, thermal infrared images, and voiceprints. A key contribution is a simple yet partitioning Rotating Window Dynamic Fusion (RWDF) module that enables a seen-infrared (SIR)-seen-infrared pairing strategy, addressing data asymmetry through comprehensive and sub-compartment modal fusion to mitigate modality gaps. Furthermore, a new trimodal embedding technique called R2R (Replace-Rotate-Replay R) is proposed to enhance the expressiveness of thermal infrared features by substituting visible light channels with thermal counterparts, aligning features across modalities, and utilizing residual learning for deeper insight. Extensive experiments conducted on the IITB person verification dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed trimodal approach over unimodal and bimodal baselines, yielding an accuracy of 91.10%.

Ensuring both provable privacy guarantees and sufficient utility for data remains a difficult hurdle for numerous privacy-preserving machine learning techniques. Recently, the framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been introduced to bridge this gap by permitting correlations between the database and the query while protecting respondents who do not directly impact the result. This study presents the first practical application of query optimization within OSDP. Specifically, we introduce a method for computing optimal perturbation budgets tailored to queries that exhibit independence among their underlying attributes. Our experimental results demonstrate that using customized perturbation strategies yields substantial efficiency gains, reducing noise by up to 75% compared to standard approaches while maintaining OSDP guarantees.

This study utilizes 3D smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations featuring massive planets to analyze gaseous gaps observed in the HL Tau disk. We demonstrate that both pressure-supported and marginally accreting annuli can emerge from either planet-induced gaps or dust settling and photophosphorization driven by the central star; notably, these substructures typically do not reveal their true origins through SPH alone. Extracting and examining time-tagged events has become a fundamental technique across both scientific research and industry sectors. As time resolutions sharpen, the quantity of input channels expands, and event volumes swell, conventional data processing methods are increasingly burdened by this growing complexity. We introduce the TimeTagger software suite, designed to address these challenges through efficient, user-friendly functionality grounded in C++ and SQL technologies. TimeTagger operates within a web browser using standard protocols, facilitating seamless communication between its various modules specifically tailored for data analysis. It provides extensive capabilities such as generating time correlation matrices, conducting coincidence studies, and performing custom analyses. Furthermore, by storing time-tagged data in the compact, self-describing DTT format, the system ensures both efficient use of storage space and accelerated processing speeds. Ultimately, TimeTagger offers a flexible framework adaptable to time-resolved investigations in setups ranging from entry-level single detector systems to large-scale particle physics experiments.

We establish the presence of "mild" solutions for control-based mean field games arising from optimal stopping problems where projects may remain active indefinitely, focusing on the scenario involving linear dynamics, quadratic costs, and specific topological constraints linking stochitistic and physical measures. Our findings broaden previous research by Attar, Méliot, and Méliot and specifically generalize their one-time period analysis to allow for continuous, infinite-horizon optimization with control-induced stopping.

Recent investigations into stellar dynamics within the Milky Way's central region have revealed numerous high-velocity stars traveling at great distances, often following trajectories that appear to originate from the galactic center. While earlier studies attributed these motions to acceleration by the supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, or direct expulsion from it, numerous research groups have alternatively linked these paths to three-body interactions or ejection via one-armed spiral arms. In this study, we analyze the trajectories of stars exhibiting velocities exceeding 200 km/s and distances greater than 100 pc from the center, comparing their motion against two theories: stellar strings representing outflows from the central region, or star formation associated with the spiral arm. Our findings reveal two key points: (1) a substantial proportion of these high-speed stars display velocities oriented radially outward, suggesting many are not localized to the galactic center but represent dispersing populations; (2) these objects also show velocity dispersion values significantly higher than those typically observed in standard spiral arms, rendering them inconsistent with conventional three-body scattering models. Based on this, we conclude that substantial numbers of Milky Way halo stars likely derive from motion initially tied to Sagittarius A*, whereas most objects moving rapidly after one or two arms do not share this origin.

This work introduces **GRACET**, a novel framework designed to facilitate Grace-of-Force (Grace) Optimization for virtually dressing multiple garments on humans. Unlike the Energy-based Grasp Optimization that we replace with graci, our new method focuses on three main factors that determine the aesthetic compatibility of garments in an outfit: garment compatibility with human body features, compatibility with other garments, and overall compatibility with the surrounding environment. We present a new optimization framework that optimizes these factors using a combination of geometric and aesthetic constraints. Our approach allows users to specify preferences for how garments should fit their personal style while ensuring that all clothing items in an outfit work harmoniously together. We demonstrate through extensive experiments that our framework significantly outperforms existing methods, producing more graceful and realistic virtual try-on experiences across diverse clothing combinations.

Quantum resource theory facilitates a systematic study of fundamental quantum phenomena by defining free resources, state transformations, and free states. This framework separates all quantum states into two distinct categories: free and free states, with free states serving as the non-freestate. It distinguishes between two distinct types of distillation processes, namely one-way distillation and two-way distillation, to convert free resources into free states using deterministic protocols. In this study, we investigate the universal one-way distillation model and contrast it with those limitations, specifically analyzing how two-way distillation expands upon this capacity when applied to arbitrary quantum states within the resource theory. We provide a universal framework for two-way distillation that encompasses every existing resource theory while also deriving both necessary and sufficient conditions for its feasibility. Our approach applies equally to theories involving qubits and those extending beyond this basis, allowing for the comparison and assessment of distillation capabilities in both one-way and two-way contexts.

Synchronous updates often reduce efficiency in cross-device federated learning, particularly as the pool of active clients expands. We present the Cross-Fowl transformation method, which converts cross-Fowl learning into a standard federated averaging task by re-expressing both algorithms using shared building blocks. This reduction enables the application of established, high-performance training strategies to cross-Fowl learning. We further develop the CGAL algorithm, which achieves superior results compared to current leading methods even in scenarios involving severe communication bottlenecks.

This study introduces a functional calculus based on a countable collection of generators of contraction semigroups, which are assumed to be continuous in the strong topology. The symbol algebra adopted for this framework comprises polynomial tempered distributions. The paper establishes a differentiable property of the resulting calculus and elucidates its range through the utilization of the polynomial shift commutant. An illustrative application involves determining a functional of an unbounded array of second-order derivative operators.

Recent work by Hawking and Xu demonstrated that for a specific class of string-inspired models featuring a fourth, dark dimension incompatible with standard matter propagation, the vacuum fluctuation scale remains inaccessible to observers within our 3D spatial volume, even if the dark dimension extends indefinitely. Consequently, the fundamental 4D geometry experienced is not merely an embedding space but a distinct effective spacetime. In this paper, the gravitational dynamics are formulated using an effective action to explore black hole solutions and their radiative properties within this framework. By employing the semi-classical approximation, the emission rate of Hawking radiation is assessed. Results indicate that although energy cannot propagate laterally into the dark dimension, it can traverse toward the radial direction, implying the potential for black hole mass accumulation there. Furthermore, the spectral analysis reveals a significant enhancement in Hawking radiation. This enhanced emission might leave observable imprints, offering a potential mechanism to locate such objects via their Hawking flux.

This work investigates the mechanical resilience of particle rafts suspended on an evaporating liquid film. As evaporation induces radial flow and expansion in the lubricating layer, it generates compressive stresses that can trigger instability, leading to either wrinkling or folding failures. By combining analytical frameworks with numerical simulations, we reveal a transition in failure modes driven by viscosity and particle elasticity. Additionally, we reconcile our predictions with prior experimental observations to accurately describe the timing of rupture.
