Scientific research increasingly relies on data-driven approaches to develop and validate new theories. While data-driven benchmarks are essential for advancing computational methodology, their limited availability often hinders meaningful comparisons. We introduce *CompModRank*, a Python library designed to facilitate rigorous benchmarking through competitive ranking of models against the same dataset, ultimately aiding in the selection of the most appropriate tool for a given task. We demonstrate the library's utility by analyzing two real scientific datasets: one concerning turbulence modeling within astrophysical jets and another involving the prediction of rainfall from cloud resolvable simulations. Although each dataset uniquely highlights specific model strengths, we observe that their correlations are unique and, in certain instances, inverse to one another. Consequently, we recommend researchers develop a custom competitive ranking system tailored to the particular dataset they wish to evaluate.

Hadwiger's conjecture posits that for every integer $k$, any graph with a $k$-core chromatic number possesses a $k$-coloring minor. Building on a recent finding that establishes an equivalence between this conjecture and the existence of specific large substructures within $k$-decomposable graphs, our paper introduces an alternative proof of this result. Specifically, we demonstrate that in any graph with chromatic number $k$, a vertex subset $S$ of size at least $k$ can be identified where every graphically connected component within the remaining vertices $G - S$ meets an node in $S$. Our approach primarily utilizes a theorem by P. W. Wilson, which guarantees subsets possessing induced degrees characterized by desired properties.

This paper introduces a robust adaptive algorithm utilizing local kernels for multichannel signal recovery on graph structures. The methodology defines an adequate update of kernel width and height by employing a Riemann kernel in the objective loss function along with the principle of minimizing this loss function. Furthermore, it is appropriate to apply this robust kernel-based adaptive technique for signal recovery in the graph when impure data signals are present. The proposed method was tested and compared to other methodologies in terms of its performance. The simulation results show that it is more competitive than other methodologies in terms of its performance.

This work provides both an example of how technical noise can be used to generate atomic coherence between two different positions of an optical lattice and shows that the resulting atom interferometer is technically noise-resilient. This study determines sharp constants within a refined P\'{o}lya-F\"{u}rer type inequality concerning the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. Furthermore, it establishes the precise asymptotic behavior regarding the growth of the first Robin eigenvalue for the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator, derived from expanding domain sequences that satisfy the requisite smoothness conditions.

To explain the design choices behind Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNN), this paper offers a fresh perspective on graph convolution. We introduce a generalized definition of graph convolution as operations between two functions, which enables a unified framework for understanding these layers. Within this framework, standard operations like local filtering in signal processing and spatial convolution in image analysis, along with popular application-specific designs such as Graph Convolution, Graph Convolutional Networks, Graph Neural Networks, Graph Convolutional LSTM, and Graph Convolutional Pooling, can all be interpreted as particular instances of the functions. By examining these well-known variations as specific cases, the paper elucidates the architectural decisions. Ultimately, this theoretical understanding aids in assessing different GCNN architectures for various applications and can guide the creation of specialized graph convolution types optimized for particular tasks.

Neural dependency parsing has demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional methods; however, acquiring sufficient labeled data remains essential for models to generalize effectively to unlabeled text. To address this limitation, we introduce an approach employing data augmentation and a sequence-to-sequence encoder-decoder architecture to synthesize dependencies from labeled input. Specifically, our method introduces three distinct pseudo-dependency tasks to enable the model to learn representations from these generated outputs. To mitigate issues related to memory efficiency and sample quality, we implement a custom data augmentation strategy alongside a pseudo-dependency filtering step for synthesis. Evaluations on English and German datasets confirm that combining synthetic and real data yields significant improvements in model performance, with our methods further enhancing results compared to baseline approaches using label sets alone.

This paper examines the CFI-query across graphs featuring bounded graph parameters, specifically determining its CPT-definability across various classes such as planar graphs, trees, chordal graphs, and others. Through various transformations including vertex splitting, edge subdivision, and changes in adjacency semantics, trees are utilized to instantiate instances involving multiple graph types. Furthermore, the results extend to classes parameterized by distance to trees, with the core logic relying on a characterization of the trees themselves. A distinguishing element of our methodology is leveraging stable room graphs to establish lower bounds, utilizing room graphs as the fundamental construction. Leveraging room graphs also facilitates defining variables that capture path existence while negating cycle existence. Consequently, the upper bounds presented in this work appear nearly optimal, given that the definitions of the respective room graph variants are concise formulations of six-edge cycles.

Eu2Ir2O7 serves as a prototypical Kondo lattice system, exhibiting a thermal conductivity peak at elevated temperatures alongside a resistivity maximum and anomalous entropy release near the phase transition from a resistive to a Kondo hybridization state. Substituting Eu2Ir2O7 with Bi leads to a substitution at the Eu site, which suppresses this traditional thermodynamic signature associated with the Kondo state. Surprisingly, however, a similar phase transition emerges in the Eu2-xBi_xIr2O7 series at x=0.5. Spectroscopic evidence indicates that this transition stems from the emergence of a novel small pseudogap in the density of states near the Fermi level, an effect driven by a substantial downshift of hybridization bands in the bulk material caused by Bi-induced band structure modifications.

Consider a metric space $X$ and another $Y$ equipped with the Hausdorff distance. We study single-valued Lipschitz functions $F: X \to Y$ that serve as selections for a given set-valued mapping $S: X \to Y$ defined as $S(x) = \{y \in Y \mid d_H(Y, Y) = 0\}$. In this context, $S(x) = \{y \in Y \mid d_H(Y(x), d_H(Y(x)))$, where $d_H$ denotes the Hausdorff distance between two sets. Specifically, a Lipschitz selection refers to a function $F(x) = \{y \in Y(x), d_H(Y(x), d_H(Y(x)))$. We provide a formula for the minimal Lipschitz constant of such selections. This formula extends results previously established by Klee and Morgan when the metric space $X = \{0, 1\}$ is a subset of the real line with the standard metric topology induced by Euclidean distance.

Given an $n$-tuple $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ of random variables that are jointly distributed with exchangeable properties, its characteristic function is defined as $\tau(\mathbf{t}) = \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left\{ \mathrm{i}\sum_{k=1}^n t_k X_k \right\}\right]$ for $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^n$. This paper establishes the existence of maximal cyclic $n$-tuples—those for which the inequality $\left|\tau(\boldsymbol{\delta})\right| \ge \tau(1,\dots,1)$ holds for all rotations $\boldsymbol{\delta}$—and demonstrates that such tuples can be constructed by selecting each $X_k$ independently from a two-point distribution.

Many software platforms allow runtime customization through mechanisms like command-line parameters, enabling users to tailor systems for specific use-cases. While existing research has explored compile-time configuration specialization to optimize features such as binary size and performance, the effects of altering runtime configurations on these non-functional properties remain under investigated. This study examines how modifying the runtime configuration of a representative Java framework influences its non-functional attributes across a range of distinct configurations. The findings confirm that specializing a system's runtime configuration can yield significant improvements in binary size and performance, with the extent of these gains depending on the specific configuration variations.

Sub-GeV dark matter particles pose significant challenges for direct detection due to their low recoil energies, which lead to tiny expected signals detected by current experiments operating in the MeV scale regimes. Indirect detection methods, constrained by the astrophysical background, lack the sensitivity to detect such low recoil signals. In this study, we examine the detection capabilities of low-mass dark matter particles using ultra-high-energy cosmic ray accelerators. Our proposal involves utilizing a time-of-flight measurement technique within the High Energy Cosmic Ray Accelerator to distinguish dark matter signals. Our analysis demonstrates that even detections yielding only statistical evidence at the $2\sigma$ confidence level would provide substantial scientific value. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of conducting such experiments using existing facilities, specifically proton synchrotrons and cosmic ray proton accelerators.

This paper outlines a method for producing entangled states via anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction using only linear optical components. Our scheme relies on Rabi oscillations rather than the typical energy oscillations found in anti-Rabi cycles. Notably, due to the absence of reabsorption during this process, the generation of entangled states—whether pure or mixed—is less constrained by initial mixedness of input resources compared to protocols driven by population oscillations.

Monitoring variations in the intervals between heartbeats (HRV) serves as a critical method for assessing cardiovascular health through non-invasive, continuous assessment. Traditional methods for estimating HRV typically rely on electrocardiogram (ECG) data, whereas this work introduces a technique for HRV analysis conditioned on action potentials (APs) or depolarization events in both normal and pathological myocardial tissue. By deriving metrics based on these key temporal markers, the proposed approach effectively eliminates noise-induced artifacts and compensates for dropped detection signals. Furthermore, comprehensive analysis demonstrates that HRV metrics calculated from APs exhibit strong correlation with those derived from standard ECG data.

This study investigates the large deviations of active forces generated by Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles (AOPs) in both free space and confining potential fields. Specifically, we derive the rate function for energy injection in the context of a Brownian particle coupled to passive thermal reservoirs and subject to internal active forces. Our findings demonstrate that the topology of the imposed potential influences key characteristics of this rate function, notably the maximum power output and the curvature of the rate function evaluated at zero power output. Additionally, we examine power absorption dynamics by considering time-reversed realizations of the system. Consequently, these observations open avenues for further research into fluctuations of thermodynamic quantities in systems governed by equilibrium or nonequilibrium dynamics.

Although natural language processing models have gained widespread success in English, expanding their application to non-English languages remains inherently complex. To address this, we introduce a general model for transferring English-trained neural systems across various languages. This approach employs multilingual knowledge graphs to guide model adaptation by modifying the vocabulary embeddings of pre-trained models to align with target languages while preserving underlying feature correlations. Validated through experiments on six task-driven datasets spanning machine translation, question answering, and natural language inference, our method consistently outperforms zero-shot zero-training baselines by substantial margins. In multi-task reinforcement learning, learning across related tasks simultaneously accelerates the process by leveraging task similarities. Conventionally, this approach transfers knowledge by training on unrelated, "easy" tasks first, progressively moving toward more complex and related ones. This study examines information flow within multiple fully connected deep reinforcement learning networks trained in parallel. Our observations reveal significant differences in benefit sequences between network types: recurrent networks often require knowledge from simpler tasks, whereas policy gradient methods often benefit more immediately from the characteristics of simpler tasks. Based on these findings, we introduce a training protocol for networks employing the policy gradient method that learns by training across both simple and related tasks in parallel simultaneously. Our results confirm that this approach accelerates learning, and our method demonstrates improved performance in a specific robotic control application.

This paper examines finite-time heat engines constrained by fixed bath temperature and either constant or linear scaling parameters linking optimization variables to this temperature. The study focuses on optimizing work production under a limited cycle duration while analyzing the characteristics of protocols that achieve thermal efficiency, those maximizing power, and those delivering the highest efficiency alongside fixed cycle times, considering systems governed by the same stochastic thermodynamic dynamics. These findings are verified through simulations of an underdamped Brownian heat motor, composed of a single degree of freedom acting as a spring mass interface between two baths at distinct temperatures. Furthermore, we assess the sensitivity of the optimal, maximum-efficiency, and power-optimal protocols to variations in cycle time for each respective category under finite-time conditions.

This study examines the impact of storm surges generated by the 2018 Hurricane Dorian on a coastal electricity grid. The analysis utilizes a surge model to identify vulnerable power substations along North Carolina's shoreline and evaluates substations' resilience by assessing component reliability under varying water depths and exposure durations. Findings indicate that substations in Dare and Currituck counties experienced the greatest risk, with survival rates dropping below 50%. In contrast, counties further inland, such as Dare and Currituck, exhibited longer lasting resilience, maintaining a 95% chance of withstanding the surge even after several hours. The research concludes by suggesting that substations' ability to remain operational correlates directly to both water depth and time exposed, implying that substations' resilience can be significantly prolonged through rapid and complete shutdown procedures.

Following the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson, the Standard Model of particle physics has faced significant experimental testing, prompting urgent needs to refine and enhance detection and analysis methodologies. A primary motivation for advancing these tools is the SM's inability to fully describe nature's scalar sector, particularly in light of ongoing theoretical research suggesting its extension. These ideas are explored through simulations of scalar system interactions using 2+N dimensional SM frameworks at the Large Hadron Collider. By implementing this SM extension in our SM-event generator, we can investigate how accurately and completely models containing only a single Higgs boson represent SM event data in various observables. These models are then benchmarked against multi-Higgs SM event simulations at the LHC to identify which production-channel-specific observables can most effectively distinguish multi-Higgs scenarios from the SM Event Generator, ultimately refining event-modeling techniques to capture complex scalar dynamics more precisely.

This study introduces a novel pitch-adaptive dilated convolutional neural network designed for efficient and high-fidelity audio synthesis. Our proposed Pitch-Adaptive Dilated Convolution (PADConv) integrates two pivotal elements: dynamic dilation training (DAT) and a pitch-aware multi-scale bank. First, DAT automatically adjusts dilation patterns based on training samples, leveraging them for better feature extraction in layers without dynamic overhead, as they remain frozen at inference time to save resources. Second, the pitch-sensitive multi-scale bank utilizes local dilated convolutions with various fixed dilation rates to capture acoustic properties at different temporal resolutions, specifically targeting pitch variability by merging sub-band outputs through element-wise multiplication, as illustrated in Figure 1. Experimental evaluations on the F0-Aware WaveGAN benchmark reveal that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in both automatic and manual assessments. Our code and models are accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuanzhu/PADConv.git.

Collaborative Filtering (CF) has become a primary method for addressing Recommender Systems (RS) challenges. However, its utility is constrained by the cold start, sparsity, and scalability issues inherent in its reliance on user-item interaction data. To overcome these obstacles, various hybrid approaches integrating Content-Based (CB) techniques have emerged. This paper proposes an enhanced hybrid model that leverages Deep Neural Networks to analyze diverse user behavior indicators, including rating history, item popularity, view count, and cultural background. By capturing these specific signals, the system aims to boost performance and offer more accurate recommendations. Experimental results indicate that including these specific user behavior metrics yields superior performance compared to models utilizing solely user-item ratings or ratings and item data.

Doppler techniques face significant challenges when searching for Earth-like planets due to stellar noise; specifically, understanding how starspots and other cyclic phenomena affect radial velocity measurements is critical. This study employs both synthetic and realistic data to assess whether current and upcoming spectrographs can identify potential Earth analogues around active G-dwarps using these datasets. Using spot cycle models to calculate synthetic spectra alongside observed OGLE data for OGLE-TR18 in realistic simulations, the results indicate that viable planets (0.5-1.5 M$_\odot$) within the habitable zones of these stars remain undetectable with present-day and next-generation instruments. Consequently, the next phase of exoplanet research must prioritize investigating how stellar cycles and variability influence observed signals to refine detection methodologies.

To investigate topologically protected Majorana zero modes (MZMs) arising from the hybridization of a topological superconductor with quasi-zero-energy bound states (QEBS) near the edge from a non-equilibrium perspective, we conduct theoretical analyses. First, we calculate the tunneling conductance as functions of energy, temperature, and superconductor size, revealing that the Majorana peak's height grows with smaller systems and cooling temperatures, eventually saturating to the maximum quantum conductance limit. Secondly, we examine the local density of states (LDOTS) to pinpoint the origin behind these findings. This analysis indicates that the saturation behavior stems from the distinct evolution of quasi-particle excitations compared to the emergence of a true topological superconductor (TSC) phase, alongside contributions from the bound state(QB) near the transition zone from QEBS to MZM. These results underscore the critical role of finite temperature effects on the stability of the majorana mode, highlighting the necessity of achieving low-thermal environments to experimentally verify Topological Protection of Majorana zero modes (MZMs).

Many practical image operations, such as editing, enhancement, or inversion, often lack a uniquely determined solution. For example, when restoring a black-and-white photograph to color or deblurring a motion-blurred shot, multiple plausible outcomes typically exist. Although it is desirable to select a specific solution aligned with user preferences, traditional methods have struggled to incorporate such customization. To address this, we propose a novel, parametric approach grounded in partial differential equations (PDEs) capable of selecting an arbitrary number of solutions based entirely of user preferences. Our method extends existing variational P frameworks by adding a flexible control term that allows for flexible and practical adjustments. Evaluations using various real-world scenarios—colorization, super-resolution, and deblurring—demonstrate that our approach successfully generates multiple distinct results and allows users to selectively choose the one best suited to their needs. Source code can be found at https://www.github.com/Pranav12345/MUSE.

This report details the 2nd-ranked submission to the LongVideo2021 challenge, focusing on long-form video comprehension. Despite attracting significant researcher attention due to numerous established benchmarks and challenges, deep learning approaches for comprehensive video analysis often struggle with limited dataset sizes, extensive video durations, elaborate temporal relations, and intricate visual contexts—factors that made previous non-deep-learning methods ineffective in prior contests. To address these limitations, the authors proposed a hybrid architecture integrating conventional computer vision techniques, graph-based modeling, Transformer mechanisms, prior knowledge graphs, and generative models. Specifically, short segments were encoded using efficient traditional vision algorithms, while a Graph Attention Unit handled temporal alignment. Furthermore, the work demonstrates how pre-existing knowledge graphs mitigate the scarcity of training data by restricting model search spaces through learned representations. Last, a slow-generator technique segment was implemented to distill essential information for scene-level localization. The team secured the second-highest rank in the competition.

This paper presents a large-eddy simulation (LES) study examining the settling of coarse snow particles within turbulent atmospheric flows. The study reveals that vortex structures form the "core" regions of turbulence, creating particle-rich zones that accelerate settling due to the absence of particle suspension. These observed phenomena align with previous experimental findings. Furthermore, we quantify the impact of both turbulent quenching by solid particles and aggregation on the settling process, noting that while existing experiments support these mechanisms, the relative contributions require additional experimental validation.

Active inference serves as a unifying theoretical framework that addresses fundamental challenges in perception, action, and learning by biological agents. It posits that agents—ranging from molecular structures to humans—reliably navigate complex conditions through the continuous cycle of updating their internal models of the world and executing behaviors that align with these models. By doing so, agents facilitate the conditions necessary for beneficial outcomes, effectively driving their environmental reality toward their internal representations of how things ought to be. At its core lies a hierarchical process where agents employ their internal mechanisms to selectively induce specific causal pathways, thereby achieving favorable states. To investigate this theory, researchers have developed various implementations, generating rigorous quantitative and qualitative predictions that span from cellular responses to neural activity related to healthy brain function, all the while addressing disorders characterized by maladaptive behavioral loops. This document reviews the historical roots, principles, and predictions of active inference, noting that despite significant progress, critical unresolved issues remain. Furthermore, it outlines promising directions for future research aimed at refining the theory and leveraging its applications toward advancements in biomimetic robotics and artificial intelligence.

Gathering scientific data in real-time presents significant challenges within the contemporary era. As examples, projects in high energy physics and cosmology often require processing vast volumes of information from diverse sources, necessitating both sophisticated hardware and advanced software solutions. This paper introduces a software framework designed to address such difficulties by leveraging the power of Apache Kafka for message queuing and distributed messaging. The proposed method is validated through a use case involving the real-time processing of data from multiple sources for the ATLAS experiment, an LHC facility at CERN.

This study applies Finzi's novel gravity theory—which predicts enhanced attractive forces at cosmic scales—to the thermodynamics of the Finzi-Finzi-Trotta (FFT) model of the universe. We treat the universe within General Relativity, assuming a perfect fluid and an adiabatic, adiabatic expansion. By determining the temperature and pressure evolution under this framework, we investigate the thermodynamic behavior of dust matter, radiation, and cold dark matter under significant modifications from standard cosmology. Specifically, we find that dark energy's equation of state deviates from the standard $w=-1$, a result with implications for the cosmological constant problem. These deviations in Finzi gravity also alter the critical density threshold separating dark energy and dark matter phases, as well as the universe's expansion rate and total energy budget. Because of these changes, we must re-evaluate the timing of key cosmological events, such as matter-radiation equality and the onset of dark energy domination, within this new gravitational context.

A subset collection of segments of strictly planar convex point sets defines what is known as a convex geometric hypergraph, where each point serves as a vertex and every segment acts as an edge connecting them. Distinguishing itself from standard geometric graphs, this structure allows multiple edges to exist between any two points, though only one can appear as a specific pair of convex geometry points. This paper explores the concept of $(2, s, t,)$-saturation within these structures. We establish that every such convex geometric $n$-vertex $H$(convex geometric $G$) contains at most $O(s+t+1)$ edges if removed no such $K_3$s exist. Conversely, we construct examples demonstrating that this upper bound is tight when considering larger values of $s$ or $t$.

This study utilizes the ab initio N* code, specifically the Local Coupling Approximation (LCA), to analyze alpha-particle generation in neutron-alpha collisions. The scattering calculations are refined by integrating continuum antisymmetrization to ensure physical accuracy. Primary attention focuses on the $s$-wave channel, specifically the $^0$S$_0$ state, which is found to account for the majority of alpha production. Total cross-sections are analyzed across an alpha energy spectrum from 0.5 to 5.0 MeV, revealing excellent agreement with experimental data.

This work presents an experimental investigation into a 3D-printed robot named "Trident," designed for vertical surfaces. The prototype achieves significant advancements in climbing performance by integrating real-world observations of vertical movement with engineering principles derived from both marine and terrestrial animals. Specifically, the design emulates the lateral undulatory motion of lampreys found in aquatic environments alongside the stick-on capabilities characteristic of geckos from terrestrial contexts.

Trident successfully executes surface tracking via 3-degree-of-freedom joints at its head while simultaneously generating propulsion through body undulation. This mechanism proves particularly effective when the robot encounters surface irregularities such as crevices or ledges, successfully maintaining traction with both anterior and posterior appendages.

The reported data indicate a peak vertical stride displacement of approximately 1.15 cm, corresponding to an average vertical climbing speed of 1.3 cm/s. Furthermore, the robot demonstrates a remarkable load-lifting capability, supporting its own weight in air (equivalent to 1.0 N).

These observations collectively underscore the potential for biomimetic strategies to enhance the adaptability of ground effect robots across varied terrains.

This study introduces a novel stochastic approach to understanding cancer dynamics by utilizing an Itô stochastic differential equation. Our goal in developing this framework is to analyze and characterize the probability density function of the associated state space, which naturally leads to an infinite-dimensional Itô Fokker--planck equation tailored for this cancer model. To overcome the challenges posed by infinite dimensions, we transform equations into a finite dimensional setting using proper truncation techniques. We then apply standard numerical methods for solving partial differential equations. Our simulation results effectively demonstrate the validity of our proposed scheme.

This paper tackles the problem of scheduling device-to-device (D2D) links within a macro cellular network, aiming to balance system throughput and user energy efficiency. The study first establishes the total system objective function along with individual power and rate constraints, noting that both the users' total power consumption and link activation decisions are binary variables. The scheduling task is formulated as a mixed-integer non-convex optimization problem, which is subsequently approximated as a convex problem to ensure accessibility. An efficient algorithm is proposed to maximize the user utility function by iteratively updating the optimal power allocation and D2D activation decisions until convergence. The approach leverages the majorization/minorization (MM) method to approximate the user utility, employing a block coordinate descent framework that alternates between optimizing power allocation and D2D activation. The resulting power allocation updates rely on closed-form solutions, while determining the D2D activation pattern involves solving a linear equation, both ensuring a globally optimal solution within the reformulated problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly surpasses conventional methods in achieving high energy efficiency and system throughput, particularly for D2D links. Furthermore, it exhibits robust performance even under substantial channel estimation uncertainties.

Building on the work presented in \cite{KlSjSt20} regarding complex geometric optics solutions for d-bar equations in electrical impedance tomography and for the large-$k$ scattering theory of the integrable Davey-Stewartson equations, this article broadens the analysis to include reflection coefficients. Specifically, for compactly supported potentials $q$ within a domain $\Omega$ featuring a smooth and strictly convex boundary, enhanced asymptotic estimates are established.

We introduce a technique to calculate spin-averaged final eccentricities for inspiraling binary systems of compact, non-spinning objects that begin with moderate to high eccentricities. By leveraging recent advancements in tidal interactions between twin twin-accelerated bodies and gravitational drag effects, this approach reaches accuracy up to second order in the gravitational coupling constant. Results indicate that when two directly inspiraling high-compactness objects start with the same angular momentum loss rate and eccentricity, their final states differ by up to 12%. This value is roughly 6% larger than predictions made without considering reaction terms, such as those from gravitational drag. Notably, including these terms is essential for achieving even a first-order estimate of their final states, as their collective behavior in nature cannot be ignored.

The x-ray free-electron laser (X FEL) has become a highly valuable instrument for contemporary research, yet its efficiency is limited by low electron beam energy recovery. Countermeasures such as two-pass energy recovery have successfully enhanced the X FEL's output, but they simultaneously decrease the efficiency of the recovery process itself. Our simulations indicate that a circular energy recovery approach offers a more promising future. Specifically, we propose an innovative circular electron beam energy recovery scheme utilizing RF cavities arranged along a spiral trajectory to achieve high-efficiency energy recovery for spiral X FEL systems containing RF cavities. To further improve the recovery efficiency of the spiral X FEL system with the proposed scheme by 20% compared to the two-pass approach, the energy recovery efficiency by 20% was achieved. This study offers valuable insights into the design of spiral X FEL systems and provides a foundation for the further development of X FEL technology.

Event detection on dynamic graphs is a critical component of event-driven inference. Existing deep learning architectures, however, often fall short in this area due to their reliance on heuristics and rule-based methods. Addressing this limitation, we propose a novel deep learning framework that models event detection as a time-series classification task. By employing a novel encoding technique for dynamic graphs, we capture the structural nuances necessary for detection, complemented by innovative data generation methods to support experimental validity. Validated through comparison with baseline approaches and other detectors on both real-world and synthetic datasets, our results highlight the effectiveness of this framework.

This work examines the resolutions of the Guderley problem within an ideal gas featuring a power law for density and characterized by an implosion-driven intense shock front. The investigation focuses in detail on the unique self-similar solutions—particularly the scaling exponent governing the acceleration rate—in the contexts of both spherical and cylindrical geometries, spanning a broad scope of adiabatic and spatial density indices. Furthermore, we show these analytical predictions can be replicated in hydrodynamic simulations operating within Lattice-Boltzmann frameworks.

Explainability has been identified as a critical factor for enhancing stakeholder trust in AI alongside ensuring system reliability. While establishing that an AI system is trustworthy is essential, it remains unclear precisely which characteristics contribute to this trustiness. Addressing this knowledge gap, our research proposes a rigorous framework for defining and assessing the trustworthiness of AI systems relizing that trustiness can be compromised by a lack of explainability. We also develop a comprehensive evaluation metric capable of measuring how much an AI system violates or upholds this framework. Finally, to validate the practicality of our approach, we apply the method in a case study involving a deep reinforcement learning model designed to control robotic manipulators.

Characterizing colorectal polyps through histopathology allows clinicians to determine personalized treatment plans and predict patient risk, thereby preventing future occurrences. A typical method involves a specialist manually moving a microscope to various polyp sections for histopathological analysis; however, this process remains labor-intensive due to the costliness and scarcity of available microscopes and pathologists. To address these limitations, our work introduces a novel approach to automatically localizing colorectal polyps within histopathological slides. The proposed system employs the Lasso method for sparse regression to identify specific morphological features indicative of polyp presence. Furthermore, our new classifier is evaluated using a comprehensive dataset of 444 colorectal polyp sections, each containing 100 visualized images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm surpasses current deep-learning and traditional machine-learning techniques regarding classification accuracy.

This work addresses optimal source coding schemes designed to mitigate an adversary's guesswork. We focus on a $(n, d)$ source coding framework, defined as one that generates a codeword of length $n$ capable of allowing an adversary to guess the codeword successfully with at most $d$ attempts using the Han-Kobayashi guesswork measure. Given a source alphabet of size $d+1$, we establish lower and upper bounds on the maximum achievable rate within this setting. Under the single-user model, we prove bound equivalence to the best single-user scheme and demonstrate that random coding achieves within a logarithmic gap of optimal performance given the appropriate alphabet. For multi-user scenarios involving $k$ independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) sources, we derive lower bounds on an extended rate by applying single-user techniques repeatedly. We also consider the case of $k$ sources possessing unequal i.i.d. distributions, where a closed-form lower bound on the adverse rate is provided. Finally, we examine a specific scenario with $k=2$ and $k=3$ users, where sources have distinct but concentrated distributions. In this concentrated $k=3$ case, we propose both single and joint decoding strategies.

Deep generative models, which have recently gained widespread attention, offer significant promise for enabling imaging transitions from dense data acquisition schemes to sparse undersampling while maintaining superior reconstruction quality. Our paper introduces a novel framework utilizing generative prior knowledge to transform undetermined underdetermined imaging systems into solvable problems. Specifically, our proposed method employs a deep generative prior to define a data-driven manifold of realistic image trajectories, thereby guiding the iterative optimization process of traditional undetermined inversion methods. By integrating this generative prior into the computational undetermined inversion step, our approach undifferentiates the constraints inherent in the deep prior undetermined generation method, effectively eliminating the necessity for undifferentiated optimization. We validate the method's effectiveness through extensive experiments on various undetermined inversion scenarios, including magnetic resonance, computed tomography, and super-resolution, demonstrating that the method significantly enhances reconstruction quality compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) stands as a leading near-term quantum method for addressing combinatorial optimization problems. It functions by varying the parameters of a variational circuit to optimize a cost function, a process that can be executed via gradient-based methods or derivative-free search. While gradient-based searches generally offer faster convergence, they are often hindered by sensitivity to initial parameter guesses and the difficulty of accurate gradient estimation in low-shot regimes typical of Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. Conversely, derivative-free strategies boast robust initial performance but typically demand a substantial number of circuit executions per step. We introduce a novel hybrid strategy that leverages both approaches by employing gradients solely for initial global exploration followed by iteration without further updates. Our evaluation demonstrates that this hybrid protocol outperforms purely gradient-based methods when implemented on limited-shot NISQ hardware. Furthermore, this combination effectively bridges a critical performance gap between pure gradient-based and derivative-free techniques within the context of QAOA.

This paper introduces methods for calculating the area of an ellipse segment defined by its boundary points derived from the inverse ray tracing (IRR) technique. These points, obtained via IRR using standard elliptical equations, define the secant line for each segment. Since a precise closed-form solution is unavailable, we compute the segment area by applying standard calculus to evaluate the definite integrals of upper and lower elliptical arcs bounded by the secant. Furthermore, comparing these calculated areas allows for determining the respective lengths of the major and minor elliptical arcs formed by three distinct points. When extended beyond two dimensions, comparing multi-point segment areas facilitates the calculation of the total elliptical area enclosed by $n$ points. Additionally, we examine how varying semi-axes lengths influence segment areas and compare the computational accuracy of the proposed method against conventional approaches such as the midpoint algorithm and central difference algorithm (CDA).

We present an L-loop exact magnetic mean-field theory to explore Hubbard model excitations on a triangular lattice. This approach identifies that accidental zero modes arise for a wide parameter range, corresponding to completely flat magnetic bands. We further demonstrate an extensive region in parameter space featuring strongly correlated ferromagnetic order characterized by long-range order within spin structures. These findings indicate that the zero mode behavior stems primarily from geometric frustration effects rather than strong electron-electron interactions.

Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are critical for various clinical applications, including spinal pathology monitoring, surgical planning, and differential diagnosis. Nevertheless, this process is frequently complicated by common anatomical pathologies such as osteophytes, degenerative disc disease, disc herniation, and herniated discs. To address this challenge, this study introduces a robust deep learning framework designed for robust vertebral handling. This method employs a specialized loss function that normalizes the Cross-Entropy function through per-vertebra standardization, effectively mitigating prediction bias inherent in class imbalance. Additionally, a data augmentation strategy is developed to synthetically generate images of vertebrae lacking pathological features, thereby enabling the model to learn characteristics related to current abnormalities. Experiments conducted on the publicly available MRCVertebrae dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms.

Stochastic Thermodynamics models random fluctuations using Markov processes, where transition rates often obey constraints imposed by fluctuating drive protocols. While these constraints ensure that probability distributions remain invariant under cycle relabelled permutations—a property known as gauge invariance—stochastic models typically fail to preserve this when describing continuous time trajectories. This work demonstrates that this limitation also applies to scaled cumulant-generating functions, which are pivotal for characterizing rare event statistics in stochastic thermodynamics, unless the protocol is time-transversal symmetric or the system is uncoupled from external drives. We achieve a restored gauge invariance by redefining scaled cumulant-generating functions through an alteration of the underlying Markov process definition, resulting in a universal asymptotic limit for joint first-passage-time distributions for both open and closed cycles applicable to arbitrary protocols.

This investigation examines the behavior of relative quantum cohomology, a notion introduced by Tseng and Yu, across the context of toric complete intersection singularities. By demonstrating that the axioms defining this concept remain valid under the small crepant partial blow-ups of such singularities, the study establishes the isomorphism between their relative quantum cohomorphism rings. Consequently, the isomorphism serves as our primary result, indicating the stability of relative quantum cohomorphism under the specified birational transformations. As an illustrative application of this theorem, the study analyzes the rings of relative quantum cohomorphism for the Calabi-Yau complete intersection singularity defined by $xy-zw+a=0$.

This study examines all-optical, semiclassical modeling of polariton condensate formation within an excitonic reservoir. We demonstrate that both the reservoir's excitation density and its resulting chemical potential are governed primarily by the nonlinear profile of a high-energy, nonresonant pump. When this localized excitation beam propagates through the bulk, it undergoes significant radial expansion due to diffusive spreading. We provide a semiquantitatively accurate description of this motion using a simple Gaussian model. Following absorption, excitons from the beam populate the surrounding region, creating a centrally concentrated excitonic non-equilibrium reservoir. We calculate that for typical experimental conditions, this condensate forms roughly at the focal spot's edge rather than its core, a position dictated by the competing dynamics of thermal diffusion and exciton recombination. Our theoretical findings align well with recent experimental observations of resulting polariton condensates.

The disintegrating planet K2-22b shows evidence of vaporized silicate dust, suggesting an environment where its surface interacts with its stellar host. This current study utilizes a probabilistic approach grounded in a physical model to examine how the star and planet collide. By analyzing transit data from K2 and the TESS mission, we evaluate our model's effectiveness in understanding the debris environment surrounding the system and infer the precise timing and angle of the impact. This model performs better than earlier methods when fitted against TESS data, highlighting its superior accuracy. Additionally, we explore how this technique can enhance the study of other disintegrating planets through analysis of their respective transit curves to reveal more details about the debris field interactions.

This approach applies to holomorphic functions defined on $\mathbb{C}^n$, represented as the quotient of a group of holomorphic functions under an equivalent relation, by calculating specific variables derived from these relations, and for sums of products of squared linear forms.

I argue that it is crucial to view Galileo's mathematical talent as integral to his scientific endeavors, offering a fresh perspective on his career. Rather than seeing his emphasis on mathematics as a sudden shift marking the beginning of modern science, I propose that it should be understood as a gradual development within his career. Consequently, his early works, which lack a strong focus on mathematics, need to be reevaluated, and his later, explicitly mathematical writings should be appreciated for their contentment of long-standing inquiries into motion and light, which finally provided satisfactory answers to these age-old questions.

A generalized thermodynamic framework is proposed for a quantum gas with a degenerate, power-law distribution, defined by an infinite set of conserved generalized variables derived from maximum entropy. This theory is applied to an extended Saha equation, where traditional thermodynamic parameters are replaced by their corresponding generalized counterparts, resulting in a generalized Saha equation applicable to plasma physics and astrophysics. The system's infinite set of generalized variables are expressed explicitly in terms of standard thermodynamic parameters through a quantum statistical mechanical derivation. As a demonstration, the behavior of an ultra-relativistic Bose gas is examined. In the non-degenerate and classical statistical mechanical regime—where the nature of the distribution and associated conserved quantities become irrelevant—the generalized Saha equation converges to the standard form. In the Boltzmann limit, both equations yield identical outcomes.

Collisionless magnetic reconnection is a central focus in space and plasma physics, as it is fundamentally a kinetic process. In this study, we utilize the Harris sheet to evaluate a low-order fluid model against low-order kinetic treatments against full kinetic simulations. We demonstrate that a simplified model which ignores pressure anisotropy fails to capture key reconnection physics, whereas versions incorporating an isotropic or anisotropic pressure in the inflow direction both align well with full kinetic results and capture the essential features of the magnetic reconnection.

This document outlines the syllabus for a Stanford Course of Excellence in Machine Learning (CEML) on designing problem solvers, a 10-week supervised internship conducted under the direction of Prof. Felix Xiaoyang Zhang. The program involves a 40-hour weekly commitment split between 20 hours of in-person instruction and 20 hours of independent project work. CEML aims to equip you with the knowledge and skills to build problem-solving agents capable of tackling diverse challenges by emulating the problem-decomposition strategies human experts employ. You will gain experience enhancing your project through digital assistant interactions that mimic expert collaborators, including through various dialogue interactions such as providing hints, checking work correctness, and explaining feedback. Over the course of the program, you will focus on problem decomposition, state representation, and search algorithms, and by completion, you will have developed problem-solving agents capable of handling more complex tasks through hierarchical decomposition, and even domain-specific knowledge and strategies.
